# Thingstudio documentation

> Thingstudio is a node-and-wire visual editor for microcontrollers. You build a flow on a canvas; it compiles to MicroPython and runs on the board. To write flows without the editor, start with the page 'Writing flows with an AI assistant' (ai-authoring), then the node catalog, and check each flow with the thingstudio-compile command.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/

# ThingStudio

ThingStudio is a visual, low-code way to program microcontrollers. You build a program, called a flow, in a
node-based editor in your web browser. Nodes are functional blocks, and wires carry data between them. The design is
inspired by [Node-RED](https://nodered.org/).

ThingStudio converts the flow to [MicroPython](https://micropython.org/), a version of Python for microcontrollers,
compiles it, and sends it to your board. The flow is saved on the board. It will then run without the editor connected, and
will start again after a reset or power cycle.

<figure markdown="span">
  [![The ThingStudio editor, showing a three-node flow: timer, function and gpio out](images/editor.png)](images/editor.png)<figcaption>The editor: nodes to drag in on the left, your flow in the middle, and on the right the selected
  node's settings and the board's console. Click to see it full size. [Tour the editor](editor-tour.md) labels every
  part.</figcaption>
</figure>

!!! tip "In a hurry?"
    [Getting started](getting-started.md) takes you from a new board to a blinking LED in six steps.

ThingStudio is designed to be private, and as open and hackable as possible:

- **Fully local.** Development happens on your computer. There's no cloud service and no account.
- **Works offline.** Once installed, it needs no internet connection, docs included.
- **Git friendly.** ThingStudio's files, your programs and your board definitions, are plain, indented
  JSON that you save where you like. They diff cleanly and sit happily in a git repository. Passwords and
  other credentials are stored separately, so a committed program holds no secrets.
- **Made to be extended.** Write your own [custom nodes](custom-nodes.md), and add your own
  [boards](boards.md#adding-a-board) and [processors](boards.md#adding-a-processor). You drop their files into
  a folder. There's nothing to rebuild.
- **Free and open source.** ThingStudio is under the
  [Apache 2.0 license](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/blob/main/LICENSE). You can use it, change it and
  build on it, including in commercial products.

!!! tip "Already know the background?"
    If you know Node-RED, MicroPython or Arduino, read what's different for you, or go straight to
    [Getting started](getting-started.md).

    - [Node-RED](coming-from/node-red.md)
    - [MicroPython](coming-from/micropython.md)
    - [Arduino and C](coming-from/arduino.md)

## Who ThingStudio is for, and who it isn't

ThingStudio is designed for developers with a reasonable amount of programming experience, it doesn't aim to teach programming fundamentals.
You should also have some level of experience in working with microcontrollers. You don't have to be an EE graduate, but you should be comfortable wiring a breadboard. You should also be able to do basic commands from the terminal or PowerShell.

## What's different about programming with ThingStudio?

A typical microcontroller program, in Arduino for example, has a `setup()` section that runs once at boot, then a
main loop that runs forever. The loop might:

- read the sensors
- check the buttons
- update the outputs
- check the network
- go round again

Each new job makes the loop longer. A slow step, such as a network call, holds up everything else, and the timing
gets hard to reason about.

ThingStudio programs respond to events instead. When a button is pressed, turn on a light. Every ten seconds, read
the temperature. When a message arrives from the network, update the display. Each response runs only when its event
happens, and the board waits for many events at once. This is
[event-driven programming](background/event-driven.md).

MicroPython supports this style natively with
[`asyncio`](https://docs.micropython.org/en/latest/library/asyncio.html). An `asyncio` program no longer reads top to
bottom, which makes it harder to see what it does. ThingStudio's graphical editor of events, functions and outputs
makes an event-driven program easier to build and follow.

## Events, nodes and wires

A program is made of **nodes** joined by **wires**. There are three types of node:

- **Sources** start messages when something happens: a timer fires, a button is pressed, an MQTT message arrives.
- **Transforms** take a message in and send a message on: a function, a filter, a delay.
- **Sinks** act on a message: switch a pin, update a display, publish to MQTT.

A wire joins one node's output to the next node's input. The nodes and wires together make a **flow**. A flow can
hold any number of chains, each starting at a source.

Nodes pass **messages** along the wires. A message is a dict, with its main value in `payload`. Messages are covered
in more detail in [flows, nodes and messages](background/flows-and-nodes.md).

This way of working comes from [Node-RED](background/node-red.md), a popular tool for home automation and IoT. In
Node-RED, flows run on a server or a Raspberry Pi. In ThingStudio, they run on the microcontroller.

## Including your own code

There are a number of ready made functions available built-in [nodes](nodes/index.md) . There is also the
[function](nodes/function.md) node, which will take regular MicroPython and runs your it on each message that arrives:

```python
# payload arrives in degrees C, leaves in degrees F
msg['payload'] = msg['payload'] * 1.8 + 32
return msg
```

`msg` is a dict, with the main value in `msg['payload']`. Return it to pass it on, or return nothing to stop it. A
function node can also keep state between messages and have more than one output. The only rule to remember is not to use blocking calls in a function node, that would make the entire flow wait on the operation.

To reuse code across flows, make it a [custom node](custom-nodes.md). A custom node has its own place in the palette
and its own properties in the property panel. It can access custom hardware, transform messages, act on them, or send them on a schedule.

You can also stop the flow and run the python REPL directly on the board from the editor for debugging. See
[Commands and the Python prompt](debugging.md#commands-and-the-python-prompt).

## Running on the board
The microcontroller runs a [MicroPython](background/micropython.md) image with a ThingStudio runtime on top. You can flash the image from the editor or use one of your own choosing. The runtime sends the flow to the board and manages running it.  It also sends back status and debugging information. We also provide custom Micropython images with the runtime included, which are more efficient in memory usage.

When you click **Deploy**, the editor converts your flow into MicroPython and compiles it. It sends the compiled flow to
the board over USB or WiFi, and the board swaps it in, and starts running it. There's no new firmware to flash, so
changing a flow and trying it again takes seconds. The board keeps the flow and runs it again after a restart.

## Built on standard parts

ThingStudio tries not to reinvent the wheel.

- MicroPython's [`asyncio`](https://docs.micropython.org/en/latest/library/asyncio.html) provides the event-driven
  primitives.
- Tried and tested libraries provide extra functionality and hardware drivers, such as Peter Hinch's
  [`mqtt_as`](https://github.com/peterhinch/micropython-mqtt) and
  [`micropython-async`](https://github.com/peterhinch/micropython-async), and drivers from
  [`micropython-lib`](https://github.com/micropython/micropython-lib).
- What comes out is plain MicroPython. You can read it in the editor's **Compiled source** panel.

## What you need

- A board with one of the processors in [Supported hardware](supported-hardware.md). Other boards that run
  MicroPython may work.
- A USB cable that carries data, not only power.

## Next

[Getting started](getting-started.md) lists the steps from a new board to a blinking LED, and starts you on the first
step.

The docs on [docs.thingstudio.net](https://docs.thingstudio.net/) follow the latest code. The docs installed with ThingStudio
(**Help → User guide**) match the version you have installed.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/background/event-driven/

# Event-driven programming

An event-driven program waits for things to happen, and runs a piece of code for each one. A button press,
a timer tick and an incoming network message are all events. The code that handles one is often called a
handler.

## The loop you may know

Most microcontroller programs start as a loop:

```python
while True:
    if button.value() == 0:
        led.on()
    temperature = sensor.read()
    time.sleep(0.1)
```

Every job lives inside the loop, and each one waits for the others. A slow sensor read delays the button check.
A `sleep` long enough to pace one job stalls all of them. Adding a job means reworking the timing of the rest.

## The same program, as events

Written as events, each job stands on its own:

- when the button pin falls, turn the LED on
- every 10 seconds, read the sensor

Nothing is checked in a loop. The board sleeps until an event arrives, runs its handler, and waits again. Jobs
with different timing don't get in each other's way.

## How ThingStudio does it

ThingStudio is built on `asyncio`, MicroPython's built-in module for event-driven programming. It provides an
event loop: one scheduler that runs many tasks, switching between them whenever one is waiting.

In ThingStudio, each chain of nodes that starts at a source (a `timer`, an `interrupt`, an `mqtt subscribe`) is
one handler. When you deploy, the flow is turned into MicroPython code in which each source becomes an `asyncio`
task. While one task waits, for a timer or the network, the others run.

## The one rule: don't block

Everything shares one event loop. A handler that stops and waits without handing control back stops every other
handler too. In a function node, that means no `time.sleep()` and no long loops.

To wait, use a node built for it: [`delay`](../nodes/delay.md) waits, [`timer`](../nodes/timer.md) repeats. They
hand control back while they wait. Inside a function node, `await asyncio.sleep(1)` does the same:

```python
await asyncio.sleep(1)
return msg
```

## More

Further reading:

- [MicroPython's asyncio](https://docs.micropython.org/en/latest/library/asyncio.html)
- [Peter Hinch's asyncio tutorial for MicroPython](https://github.com/peterhinch/micropython-async/blob/master/v3/docs/TUTORIAL.md)


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/background/flows-and-nodes/

# Flows, nodes and messages

A ThingStudio program is a **flow**: a set of **nodes** joined by **wires**. You build it by dragging nodes onto
a canvas and wiring them together, rather than writing a program top to bottom.

## Nodes

A node does one job. Most fall into three kinds:

- **Sources** start things off: `timer` fires on an interval, `interrupt` fires when a pin changes,
  `mqtt subscribe` fires when a message arrives.
- **Transforms** change or filter what passes through: `function`, `filter`, `delay`.
- **Sinks** do something at the end: `gpio out` switches a pin, `display spi` draws, `mqtt publish` sends.

Each node has properties, set in the editor's property panel: a pin number, an interval, a topic.

## Messages

Nodes pass **messages** along wires. A message is a Python dict with two standard keys:

- `payload`: the main value, such as a reading, a count or a string
- `topic`: a short label saying what the message is about

```python
{'payload': 21.5, 'topic': 'kitchen/temperature'}
```

Nodes may add other keys. A node reads the ones it needs and passes the rest on.

## Wires

A wire joins an output to an input. One output can feed several inputs, and each gets its own copy of the
message. Several outputs can feed one input, and the node runs once per message, whichever wire it came in on.

Each port has a type, such as `int`, `number`, `bool`, `string` or `any`. The editor refuses a wire between ports
whose types don't fit.

## Config nodes

Settings that several nodes share, like a WiFi network or an MQTT broker, live in a **config node**. You set it up
once and pick it from each node that uses it. See [Editor in depth](../working-in-the-editor.md#config-nodes).

## Background

Node-and-wire programming has a long history, from J. Paul Morrison's
[flow-based programming](https://jpaulm.github.io/fbp/) to tools like LabVIEW, Max and Node-RED. ThingStudio
follows [Node-RED](node-red.md)'s version of the idea, with the same message shape and very similar nodes.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/background/node-red/

# Node-RED

[Node-RED](https://nodered.org/) is a free tool for wiring together devices, web services and APIs. You build
programs, called flows, in a browser by dragging nodes onto a canvas and wiring them up. It was created at IBM in
2013 and is now an OpenJS Foundation project.

## What people use it for

Node-RED is popular for home automation and IoT. A typical flow might take sensor readings from MQTT, check them,
store them in a database and send an alert when something is out of range. It has thousands of add-on nodes and a
dashboard for building web UIs.

## Where it runs

Node-RED runs on Node.js, on a server, a PC or a Raspberry Pi. Microcontrollers usually talk to it over the
network, often by MQTT, and run their own separate firmware.

## Where ThingStudio fits

ThingStudio takes Node-RED's way of working onto the microcontroller. The flow runs on the board itself, so the
board doesn't need a server to decide what to do. The two work well together: a ThingStudio board can publish
readings over MQTT to a Node-RED flow on your server.

If you already use Node-RED, see [if you know Node-RED](../coming-from/node-red.md) for what's different.

## More

Further reading:

- [Node-RED concepts](https://nodered.org/docs/user-guide/concepts)
- [Node-RED getting started](https://nodered.org/docs/getting-started/)


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/background/micropython/

# MicroPython

[MicroPython](https://micropython.org/) is a version of Python 3 made to run on microcontrollers. It fits in
hundreds of kilobytes and runs directly on the chip, with no operating system underneath.

## How it works

You flash MicroPython onto the board once, like any firmware. After that the board runs Python files from its own
filesystem, and gives you a Python prompt, the REPL, over USB. You can type Python at the board and see the
result at once.

MicroPython keeps most of the Python language and part of its standard library. It adds modules for
hardware: `machine` for pins, I2C, SPI and PWM, `network` for WiFi, and `asyncio` for running several tasks at once.

```python
from machine import Pin
led = Pin(15, Pin.OUT)
led.on()
```

## The limits

Microcontrollers are limited. A board typically has hundreds of kilobytes of RAM, and MicroPython itself uses some
of it. Python is also much slower than C, though fast enough for most sensing, switching and networking jobs.

## Where ThingStudio fits

ThingStudio runs on top of MicroPython. It installs a runtime onto the board, and turns each flow you deploy
into MicroPython code. The function node runs your own MicroPython. See
[installing MicroPython](../installing-micropython.md) to get it onto your board.

If you already use MicroPython, see [if you know MicroPython](../coming-from/micropython.md) for how ThingStudio
uses your board.

## More

Further reading:

- [MicroPython documentation](https://docs.micropython.org/en/latest/)
- [MicroPython quick reference for ESP32](https://docs.micropython.org/en/latest/esp32/quickref.html) and
  [for RP2](https://docs.micropython.org/en/latest/rp2/quickref.html)


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/coming-from/node-red/

# If you know Node-RED

Most of what you know carries over. You drag nodes onto a canvas, wire them, set properties and click Deploy.
Messages carry `payload` and `topic`. Config nodes hold shared settings like an MQTT broker. The differences come
from where the flow runs: on a microcontroller, not on a server.

## Where the flow runs

The editor runs on your computer, but the flow runs on the board. Deploy compiles the flow to MicroPython and sends
it to the board, which then runs on its own. Close the editor, unplug the USB cable, and the flow carries on.

## Function nodes are Python

Function nodes run MicroPython, not JavaScript. A message is a Python dict, so write `msg['payload']`, not
`msg.payload`.

```python
if msg['payload'] > 30:
    msg['topic'] = 'alarm'
    return msg
```

Much else is the same. `return msg` passes the message on, and returning nothing stops it. Return a list to route
to several outputs. `context.get()`/`context.set()` and `flow.get()`/`flow.set()` work as you'd expect. There's no
`global`, since there's only one flow. See the [function node](../nodes/function.md).

Don't use `time.sleep()` in a function node. It stops the whole board, not only that node. Use `await asyncio.sleep()` or a `delay` node
instead. See [event-driven programming](../background/event-driven.md).

## Messages

A message carries a `payload` and usually a `topic`; the built-in nodes that start a flow set `topic` to an empty
string. Ports also have types, such as `int`, `bool` and `string`, and
the editor refuses a wire between types that don't fit. See [Editor in depth](../working-in-the-editor.md#wiring).

## Nodes

The palette is smaller, and made for hardware. `timer`, `interrupt`, `gpio out`, `pwm out` and the sensor and
display nodes work with the board directly. `inject`, `debug`, `function` and `delay` will look familiar, and so will
the network nodes: `mqtt publish`, `mqtt subscribe`, `http request`, `http in`, `http response`, `udp send` and
`udp receive`.

A flow has one MQTT broker and one WiFi network, set on any MQTT or WiFi node and shared by all of them. Node-RED's
broker per node doesn't carry over. See [Config nodes](../working-in-the-editor.md#config-nodes).

You add node types by writing a JSON file and a Python file. See
[writing custom nodes](../custom-nodes.md).

## Debugging

`debug` output appears in the editor's console, not a sidebar. An error in one node is reported in the console,
saying which node, and the rest of the flow keeps running. See [debugging](../debugging.md).

## Using both

Node-RED is the better place for dashboards, databases and cloud services. A common setup is ThingStudio
boards publishing over MQTT to a Node-RED flow on a server or Raspberry Pi.

Next: [getting started](../getting-started.md).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/coming-from/micropython/

# If you know MicroPython

ThingStudio sits on top of the MicroPython you already have. It doesn't replace your firmware. It adds a runtime
and a way to write programs as flows, while the REPL and your own Python stay within reach.

## What goes on the board

**Tools → Install runtime…** copies a set of Python files onto the board's filesystem, including a `main.py` that
starts the ThingStudio runtime at boot. The runtime listens on USB or WiFi for the editor, and runs the last flow
you deployed.

If your board already has a `main.py` of your own, copy it off first.

## What a flow becomes

When you deploy, the editor turns the flow into MicroPython source. Each source node, such as a `timer` or an
`interrupt`, becomes an `asyncio` task. The other nodes become `async` functions that each task calls in turn. The
editor compiles the result to `.mpy` bytecode with `mpy-cross` and sends it to the board, which swaps it in without
a reset. Compiling on your computer means the board never needs RAM for the compiler.

The board saves the flow and runs it again after a restart.

## Your own code

- **Function nodes** run your Python on each message. They're called from the event loop, so don't block: no
  `time.sleep()`, no long loops. See [event-driven programming](../background/event-driven.md).
- **Custom nodes** turn your own code, such as a sensor driver, into a node with its own properties.
  See [writing custom nodes](../custom-nodes.md).

## The REPL

The command box under the editor's console runs Python on the board while the flow runs, for checks like
`gc.mem_free()`. For the full `>>>` prompt, click **Stop flow & open prompt**. To use Thonny or `mpremote`, click
**Disconnect** first. See [commands and the Python prompt](../debugging.md#commands-and-the-python-prompt).

## Memory

A flow, its nodes and the runtime all share the board's RAM. If a deploy fails for lack of space, the console says
so. See [debugging](../debugging.md).

Next: [getting started](../getting-started.md).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/coming-from/arduino/

# If you know Arduino and C

If you've written `setup()` and `loop()` in C or C++, ThingStudio will feel different in three ways. It uses
Python rather than C, you wire events together instead of writing a loop, and a change goes to the board in
seconds without reflashing.

## Python instead of C

The board runs [MicroPython](../background/micropython.md), which you flash once in place of an Arduino sketch.
Your own code, in function nodes and custom nodes, is Python.

Python is slower than C and uses more memory. That's fine for sensing, switching, displays and networking. It's
the wrong tool for tight timing, such as bit-banging a protocol at microsecond precision or sampling at high
rates.

## Events instead of a loop

There's no `loop()`. Each job is its own chain of nodes, started by an event: a timer, a pin change, a network
message. Jobs don't wait for each other. See [event-driven programming](../background/event-driven.md).

The `interrupt` node works like `attachInterrupt()`. The difference is that your code runs
safely in the main program, not inside the interrupt, so you can do anything there.

## No compile-and-flash cycle

The firmware stays the same. Deploying a flow sends a compiled file to the board, over USB or WiFi, and the
board swaps it in. Changing a flow and trying it again takes seconds.

## What stays the same

ThingStudio checks your pin
numbers against the board before deploying, and refuses pins that would crash it, such as those wired to the
flash chip. See [boards and processors](../boards.md).

Next: [getting started](../getting-started.md).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/getting-started/

# Getting started

Want a look first? [Try the editor in your browser](https://demo.thingstudio.net/) before you install anything.
The demo doesn't connect to a board, but you can build a flow and read the MicroPython it makes.

From a new board to a blinking LED, in six steps:

1. **[Install ThingStudio](#step-1-install-thingstudio)** on your computer.
2. **[Tour the editor](editor-tour.md)**: what each part of the screen does.
3. **[Install MicroPython](installing-micropython.md)** on your board. A standard ESP32 takes the advised
   [custom image](custom-firmware.md).
4. **[Connect your board](connecting.md)** to ThingStudio.
5. **[Install the runtime](installing-runtime.md)**, the part of ThingStudio that runs on the board.
6. **[Blink an LED](first-flow.md)**: build your first flow and deploy it. Or open `tutorials/blink.flow.json`
   (the [tutorials folder](tutorial-flows.md#where-the-folder-is)) with **File → Open…**, point the pin at your
   board's own LED, and deploy.

When something doesn't work, [Debugging](debugging.md) and the [FAQ](faq.md) go by what you see on screen.

You need a board with one of the processors in [Supported hardware](supported-hardware.md), and a USB cable that
carries data, not only power. Installing uses a terminal, or PowerShell on Windows.

## Step 1: Install ThingStudio

ThingStudio is a program you run on your computer. It opens its editor in your web browser. It brings its own
Python, so nothing else needs installing to run it.

There are two ways to install it. Both give you the same program.

- **[Download a package](#download-a-package)** and unpack it. Nothing runs until you start it.
- **[Run the installer script](#run-the-installer-script).** It picks the right package, checks its checksum, and
  adds a `thingstudio` command. Run it again to upgrade.

### Download a package

Download the package for your computer from the
[releases page](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases/latest).
[Installation details](installation-details.md#packages) lists the package for each platform.

**macOS and Linux:** unpack it with `tar -xzf thingstudio-VERSION-PLATFORM.tar.gz`. ThingStudio is the
`thingstudio` file in the unpacked folder.

**Windows:** unzip it anywhere, for example into your Documents folder. ThingStudio is `thingstudio.cmd` in the
unzipped folder. If Windows says "Windows protected your PC", click **More info**, then **Run anyway**. The Windows
package isn't signed.

### Run the installer script

The commands below download the installer script and pipe it straight into a shell. To read the script before
running it, download
[install.sh](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases/latest/download/install.sh) or
[install.ps1](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases/latest/download/install.ps1) and open it in a text
editor.

**macOS and Linux:** run this in a terminal. On a Mac, that's the **Terminal** app, in Applications → Utilities.

```sh
curl -fsSL https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh
```

If the installer says `~/.local/bin` isn't on your PATH, run the command it prints, then open a new terminal.

On Linux, your account must be in the `dialout` group (`uucp` on Arch) to use USB boards. The installer reports this
if your account isn't in the group, and prints the command to fix it.

**Windows:** open PowerShell from the Start menu and run this. It doesn't need administrator rights.

```powershell
irm https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex
```

To upgrade or remove ThingStudio, or build it from source, see
[Installation details](installation-details.md).

## Start ThingStudio

How you start ThingStudio depends on how you installed it:

- **Installer script:** run `thingstudio` in a terminal. If the command isn't found, see
  [If the command isn't found](#if-the-command-isnt-found).
- **Package on macOS or Linux:** run `./thingstudio` in the unpacked folder.
- **Package on Windows:** run `thingstudio.cmd` in the unzipped folder.

The editor opens in your browser at `http://127.0.0.1:8765/`. Leave the terminal open while you work. Press Ctrl-C
there to stop ThingStudio.

ThingStudio also serves this user guide, so it works offline. **Help → User guide** opens it.

### Where it is installed

- **Installer script, macOS and Linux:** the program is in `~/.local/share/thingstudio`, and the `thingstudio`
  command is `~/.local/bin/thingstudio`.
- **Installer script, Windows:** `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Thingstudio`. The `thingstudio` command is in its `bin` folder.
- **Package:** the folder you unpacked it into.

To see which copy your terminal runs, use `command -v thingstudio` in a macOS or Linux shell, or
`Get-Command thingstudio` in PowerShell.

### If the command isn't found

The shell looks for commands in the folders listed in your PATH, and remembers what it found. After an install it can
be out of date in two ways.

**The command's folder isn't on your PATH.** To check, run `echo "$PATH"` and look for `.local/bin`. When it's missing,
the installer prints the line that adds it to your shell's startup file; it prints nothing when the folder is already
on your PATH. Run that line, or add the line `export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"` to the startup file yourself. Then
make the current terminal read the file, or open a new terminal:

| Shell | Run |
| --- | --- |
| zsh (macOS default) | `source ~/.zshrc` |
| bash on Linux | `source ~/.bashrc` |
| bash on macOS | `source ~/.bash_profile` |
| PowerShell | Open a new window. |

**The folder is on your PATH, but the shell hasn't noticed the new command.** In zsh, run `rehash`. In bash, run
`hash -r`.

On Windows, the installer adds the command to the PowerShell window that ran it and to your saved PATH. A PowerShell
window that was already open doesn't see it. Open a new window, or run this in the old one:

```powershell
$env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','User') + ';' + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','Machine')
```

If the command still isn't found, start ThingStudio by its full path, from the list above.

### Remove ThingStudio

[Installation details](installation-details.md#remove) has the commands for the installer script. To remove a package,
delete its folder. Removing never touches your flows or your settings in `.thingstudio`.

## Getting help

When something goes wrong, [Debugging & troubleshooting](debugging.md) and the [FAQ](faq.md) go by what you see on
screen. Questions, and what you've built, go in
[GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/discussions). Bugs go on the
[issue tracker](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/issues), or use **Help → Report a problem**.

## Next

Step 2: [tour the editor](editor-tour.md).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/editor-tour/

# Step 2: Tour the editor

Start ThingStudio if it isn't running: see [step 1](getting-started.md#start-thingstudio).

<figure markdown="span">
  [![The ThingStudio editor with each part labelled](images/editor-parts.png)](images/editor-parts.png)<figcaption>The parts of the editor. Click to see it full size.</figcaption>
</figure>

<!-- The labels on the picture come from EDITOR_PARTS in tools/screenshots.py. Keep the names below in step. -->

## Toolbar

The toolbar runs left to right in the order you work: the flow, the board, then deploy.

- **New, open, save:** the **File** menu.
- **This flow's name:** saved with the flow. The board reports it, so you can tell which flow it's running.
- **Connect to a board:** pick the board's port from the list, then click **Connect**. **⟳** looks for boards
  again.
- **Board type, pin map:** the **Board** menu sets the board the flow is for; **Auto** uses the connected board.
  **Pins…** opens a page listing that board's pins.
- **Deploy flow to board:** **Compile → Deploy** turns the flow into MicroPython and sends it to the board.
- **Board tools, user guide:** the **Tools** menu has board jobs, such as installing the runtime or removing a flow.
  The **Help** menu opens this user guide.

## Palette

**Nodes to add:** every node, in groups such as **General**, **Network** and **Hardware**. Drag a node onto the
canvas, or click it. Type in the filter box to find one. [Custom nodes](custom-nodes.md) appear in the group they
name, or in **General**.

Click a group's name to fold or open it. Only **General** starts open. The editor remembers which groups you
opened, in this browser. While you type in the filter box, every group with a match opens.

## Canvas

The canvas is where you build the flow. The tabs above it, **Sheets of this flow**, spread one flow across several
sheets.

The canvas works like this:

- **Wire two nodes:** drag from one node's output, on its right, to another node's input, on its left.
- **Select:** click a node or a wire. Ctrl-click to select several nodes.
- **Delete:** select, then press Delete or Backspace. Deleting a node removes its wires too.

The editor refuses a wire between ports whose types don't fit. See [Wiring](working-in-the-editor.md#wiring).

## Properties, notes and console

The right-hand side holds the selected node's settings and what the board sends back:

- **Selected node's settings:** the properties panel.
- **Notes on this flow:** the **Notes** panel, free text saved with the flow.
- **Generated MicroPython:** the **Compiled source** panel. Click it to open it. **Download .py** saves it as a
  file. Like the panel, the file holds your WiFi password and broker login.
- **Messages from the board:** the **Device console**, with messages from ThingStudio and the board, including your
  flow's output. Its **Show** menu sets how much it shows: **Normal** for your flow's output, results and errors,
  **Info** to add routine reports such as memory, **Debug** for everything.
- **Run Python on the board:** type a line of Python and click **Send**. It runs on the board alongside the flow.
  See [Commands and the Python prompt](debugging.md#commands-and-the-python-prompt).
- **Escape to REPL:** **Stop flow & open prompt** stops the flow and gives you MicroPython's own `>>>` prompt.
  **Restart ThingStudio** starts the flow again.

To make the notes, compiled source and console column wider or narrower, drag its left edge. Double-click the edge
to reset it.

[Editor in depth](working-in-the-editor.md) covers wire types, node labels, presets, config nodes and node status.

## Next

Step 3: [install MicroPython](installing-micropython.md) on your board.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/installing-micropython/

# Step 3: Install MicroPython

ThingStudio runs on top of [MicroPython](background/micropython.md), so the board needs it first. You install it once
per board.

A new board usually doesn't have MicroPython. If yours already has it, or you're not sure, go to
[step 4](connecting.md). If MicroPython is missing, the console says so when you connect, and links back here.

ThingStudio can install it for you, on the chips it can write.

## Install from ThingStudio

ThingStudio writes the firmware itself: over a serial port for the ESP32 family, and onto a mounted drive for
RP2040, RP2350 and nRF52 boards.

!!! tip "ESP32 without PSRAM? Use a custom image"
    ESP32 boards without PSRAM can be very tight on memory, as the ESP32's WiFi stack and FreeRTOS take quite a
    bit of RAM. We strongly suggest that you flash these boards with one of our
    [custom MicroPython images](custom-firmware.md). They include the runtime and the common libraries, and so
    release significant memory for your flow.

On a classic ESP32 with 4 MB of flash and no PSRAM, an ESP32-C3 or an ESP32-C5, pick
**ThingStudio custom image** as the **Firmware** when the dialog lists one for the chip. Its **Version** list holds
the published releases.
After flashing it, **Install runtime** writes only the boot script.

The list of builds comes from docs.thingstudio.net, so a new image appears without updating ThingStudio. ThingStudio
uses that list only when it carries ThingStudio's signature; offline, it uses the last list it saved, or the one it
was installed with. The line under **Version** says which.

1. Plug the board into USB. A Pico needs **BOOTSEL** held while you plug it in.
2. Choose **Tools → Install firmware…**.
3. Pick **Serial port** or **Mounted drive**, then the port or drive from the list. USB ports come first, shown as
   the path and the adapter's name (for example `/dev/ttyUSB0 -- CH340`). If an ESP32 isn't listed, hold **BOOT**,
   tap **RESET** and click ⟳; the line under the list says how many it found. If it still isn't listed, type the
   path in the box (on macOS a mounted Pico is `/Volumes/RPI-RP2`).
4. Pick the **Chip family**, the **Firmware** (**Official MicroPython (micropython.org)** or **ThingStudio custom
   image**), the **Build** and the **Version**. A board that names its own build is preselected.
5. Click **Flash**. **Erase all flash first** is ticked: it clears an old partition table, which is the usual
   reason a board doesn't boot after a successful install. The dialog shows each line the tool prints; a failure
   says what to fix.

The **Build** matters for the heap as much as for compatibility: an ESP32 with extra PSRAM wants
**ESP32 with PSRAM (WROVER / SPIRAM)**, and a single-core SOLO wants **ESP32 single-core (SOLO / UNICORE)**. Only the
chip families the editor can write are listed, and only builds whose hash is pinned, so what you flash is what was
tested.

The list covers every build ThingStudio pins, so **Or use your own image file** is only for the rest: a build for a
board ThingStudio doesn't list, a chip with no pinned build yet (the ESP32-C5), or an image you downloaded yourself. Pick the `.bin` or `.uf2`; the chip family you
choose decides the address, and the file's own header usually decides the family. **Address**, under **Install
options**, overrides the family's address. A ThingStudio custom image for a classic ESP32 needs `0x0` there: see
[Custom firmware](custom-firmware.md#install-by-hand).

Flashing erases the flow and all settings on the board. Afterwards, [connect](connecting.md) it
and [install the runtime](installing-runtime.md).

## Doing it yourself

For a chip ThingStudio can't write, or a build it doesn't pin, install MicroPython without the editor.

### Get the firmware

Download the firmware for your board from [micropython.org/download](https://micropython.org/download/). Pick your
exact board if it's listed, or the generic build for your chip:

| Chip | Generic build | File type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ESP32 | `ESP32_GENERIC` | `.bin` |
| ESP32-S2 | `ESP32_GENERIC_S2` | `.bin` |
| ESP32-S3 | `ESP32_GENERIC_S3` | `.bin` |
| ESP32-C3 | `ESP32_GENERIC_C3` | `.bin` |
| ESP32-C5 | `ESP32_GENERIC_C5` | `.bin` |
| RP2040 (Pico, Pico W) | `RPI_PICO`, `RPI_PICO_W` | `.uf2` |
| RP2350 (Pico 2, Pico 2 W) | `RPI_PICO2`, `RPI_PICO2_W` | `.uf2` |

For any other chip, see [Other microcontrollers](#other-microcontrollers).

### RP2040 and RP2350: drag and drop

Copy the firmware onto the board as a file:

1. Hold the **BOOTSEL** button while you plug the board into USB.
2. A drive called `RPI-RP2` (or `RP2350`) appears.
3. Copy the `.uf2` file onto it.

The board restarts into MicroPython by itself.

### ESP32 family: esptool

If ThingStudio is connected to the board, click **Disconnect** first. Only one program can use the board's port at
a time. If another program has it open, esptool reports `Resource busy` or `could not open port`.

Install `esptool` once:

```sh
pip install esptool
```

Erase the flash, then write the firmware. `ADDRESS` depends on the chip:

```sh
esptool.py --port PORT erase_flash
esptool.py --port PORT --baud 460800 write_flash ADDRESS firmware.bin
```

| Chip | `ADDRESS` |
| --- | --- |
| ESP32, ESP32-S2 | `0x1000` |
| ESP32-S3, ESP32-C3 | `0` |
| ESP32-C5 | `0x2000` |

`PORT` is the board's serial port. On macOS and Linux it starts with `/dev/`, on Windows it's `COM` followed by a
number. To find it, run `esptool.py flash_id` with no `--port`: esptool searches for the board and prints the port
it found.

If esptool can't talk to the board, put it into download mode and try again: hold **BOOT**, press and release
**RESET**, then release **BOOT**. Boards with a separate USB-serial chip usually do this by themselves. If writing
fails partway, leave out `--baud 460800`.

Press **RESET** when it finishes. A board that uses the chip's own USB (most ESP32-S2 and S3 boards) may show up on
a different port afterwards.

### Without a terminal: Thonny

[Thonny](https://thonny.org) installs MicroPython on the board through a GUI. Open
**Tools → Options → Interpreter** and use **Install or update MicroPython**.

When it's done, close Thonny. Like esptool, it needs the board's port to itself.

Thonny can't install MicroPython on an ESP32-C5. It writes the image at `0`, but a C5 needs `0x2000`, and Thonny
doesn't offer that address. The board then restarts in a loop printing `invalid header`. Use ThingStudio or
esptool instead. ([Thonny issue #3963](https://github.com/thonny/thonny/issues/3963))

### Other microcontrollers

Other chips, such as STM32, nRF or SAMD, each have their own way of installing MicroPython. See your board's page
on [micropython.org/download](https://micropython.org/download/) and the
[MicroPython documentation](https://docs.micropython.org/en/latest/).

[Supported hardware](supported-hardware.md) lists the chips ThingStudio is tested on. Another chip needs a
processor definition: see [Other boards](supported-hardware.md#other-boards).

## Next

Step 4: [connect your board](connecting.md) to ThingStudio.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/connecting/

# Step 4: Connect your board

Connect the board over USB so the editor can talk to it. Start ThingStudio if it isn't running: see
[step 1](getting-started.md#start-thingstudio).

To connect:

1. Plug the board in.
2. Check the port list in the toolbar. When the editor opens it looks for boards, and selects yours if it's the only
   USB device plugged in. If you plugged the board in afterwards, click **⟳** next to the port list.
3. Click **Connect**. It changes to **Connected · Disconnect**. Click that to disconnect.

With more than one USB device plugged in, pick your board from the port list. Port names depend on your operating
system and the board's USB chip. To tell which port is your board, unplug it, click **⟳**, plug it back in and
click **⟳** again. The port that appears is your board.

## What the console says

A board with MicroPython but no ThingStudio runtime gives this message:

```text
No reply from the runtime. MicroPython but no Thingstudio runtime: Tools → Install runtime…
```

You install the runtime in the next step.

If the console says nothing came back, or the board replied but isn't running MicroPython, go back to
[step 3: install MicroPython](installing-micropython.md). Other messages are explained in
[Board won't connect](debugging.md#board-wont-connect).

Once the runtime is installed, the console shows which flow the board is running, if any.

Once a board with WiFi is set up, you can also connect to it over WiFi. See
[Connecting over WiFi](wifi-connection.md).

## Next

Step 5: [install the runtime](installing-runtime.md).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/installing-runtime/

# Step 5: Install the runtime

The runtime is the part of ThingStudio that runs on the board: it receives your flows and runs them. Each board
needs it once. Libraries that a flow's nodes need are installed later, by Deploy.

1. Check the board's port is selected in the port list, as in [step 4](connecting.md).
2. Choose **Tools → Install runtime…**. If you're connected, ThingStudio disconnects first. The console shows
   progress; set the console's **Show** menu to **Info** to see each file.
3. If the board is busy and doesn't stop, the console asks you to press its reset button. On a board without one,
   such as a Pico, unplug it and plug it back in.
4. The board restarts when the install is done. Click **Connect**. If the port has gone from the list, click **⟳**
   first.

After upgrading ThingStudio, the board's runtime may no longer match the editor. Deploy then stops, and the
console says to install the runtime again.

If the install fails, the console says what the board sent back and what to do. See
[Board won't connect](debugging.md#board-wont-connect).

To install the runtime from the command line instead, see
[Command line](command-line.md#installing-the-runtime-from-the-command-line).

## Next

Step 6: [blink an LED](first-flow.md), your first flow.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/first-flow/

# Step 6: Blink an LED

Your first flow: make an LED blink once a second, using three nodes.

Your board should be connected, with the runtime installed: steps [4](connecting.md) and [5](installing-runtime.md).

## Find your LED's pin

Many boards have an LED wired to a GPIO pin. To find it, click **Pins…** next to the **Board** menu. Pins that the
board names, such as `LED`, are listed first. [Supported hardware](supported-hardware.md) lists the boards ThingStudio
has definitions for. For any other board, check its documentation.

The Pico W and Pico 2 W LEDs are wired through the WiFi chip, not a GPIO pin, so `gpio out` can't reach them. On
those boards, or any board without an LED, wire an LED and a 330 Ω resistor from a free GPIO pin to GND. The LED's
longer leg goes towards the GPIO pin.

Don't leave out the resistor. Without it, the LED draws too much current and can damage the board.

## Build the flow

1. Drag a **timer** onto the canvas. Set **interval (ms)** to `500`.
2. Drag a **function** onto the canvas. Replace its **code** with:

    ```python
    msg['payload'] = msg['payload'] % 2
    return msg
    ```

3. Drag a **gpio out** onto the canvas. Set **pin** to your LED's GPIO number.
4. Wire **timer** → **function** → **gpio out**.

This flow is `tutorials/blink.flow.json`, in the [tutorials folder](tutorial-flows.md#where-the-folder-is). Opened from
there, it needs only **pin** set to your LED's GPIO number.

## Deploy

Click **Compile → Deploy**. A successful deploy ends like this in the console:

```text
[deploying "my flow" as 3f2a…]
[deploy OK -- flow is running on the device]
```

The flow name and ID will differ. Set the console's **Show** menu to **Info** or **Debug** to see each stage,
including the board's free memory.

The LED now blinks: on for half a second, off for half a second.

The flow keeps running on the board after you unplug it from your computer and power it another way.

## How it works

The **timer** sends a message every 500 ms. Its payload is a count: 1, 2, 3, and so on.

**gpio out** turns the pin on for any payload that isn't zero. Wired straight to the timer, the LED would switch on
and stay on.

The **function** node turns the count into 1, 0, 1, 0 with `% 2`. That gives on, off, on, off.

## Next

Two tutorials take the flow further:

- [Two more blinks](tutorials/two-more-blinks.md) — the blink again, two more ways: the LED's state on the
  hardware, read and written back in code, or kept in the node with `context`.
- [A sensor display](sensor-display.md) — the next job past blinking: read a sensor and show it on a screen.

## Tell us how it went

Started from a blank board? [Tell us how it went](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/discussions/new?category=onboarding-reports):
where the guide or the tool let you down is the most useful part. To keep it private, email mike@minus1.com.

## If it doesn't blink

Each symptom below has its own fix:

- **Deploy is grayed out:** you aren't connected, so click **Connect**. Deploy is also grayed out after a deploy
  until you change the flow, while the flow is stopped at the Python prompt (**Stop flow & open prompt**), and while
  the board restarts.
- **Compile fails:** usually a mistake in the function node's code, such as a missing quote or wrong
  indentation. The console shows the Python error in red, with its line, and highlights the node. Fix the code and
  deploy again.
- **Deploy works, then the console shows `[NODE_ERROR]`:** the code ran on the board and failed, for example on a
  misspelt name. The message names the error, and the node is highlighted.
- **Deploy fails:** the console says why. See [Board won't connect](debugging.md#board-wont-connect).
- **Deploy works but the LED stays dark:** check the pin number against **Pins…**. Some boards' LEDs light when
  the pin is off; the LED still blinks, the other way round.

For anything else, see [Debugging & troubleshooting](debugging.md).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/installation-details/

# Installation details

How ThingStudio is packaged, where it puts its files, how to upgrade and remove it, and how to build it from source.
[Getting started](getting-started.md#step-1-install-thingstudio) has the install steps.

## Packages

Each [release](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases/latest) has a package for each platform:

| Platform | Package |
| --- | --- |
| macOS, Apple Silicon (M1 and later) | `thingstudio-VERSION-macos-arm64.tar.gz` |
| macOS, Intel | `thingstudio-VERSION-macos-x86_64.tar.gz` |
| Linux, x86_64 | `thingstudio-VERSION-linux-x86_64.tar.gz` |
| Linux, ARM 64-bit (Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 on a 64-bit OS) | `thingstudio-VERSION-linux-aarch64.tar.gz` |
| Windows, x86_64 | `thingstudio-VERSION-windows-x86_64.zip` |

`SHA256SUMS` lists each package's checksum. The macOS packages are signed and notarized by Apple. For a version
other than the latest, open that release from the [releases page](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases).

A package doesn't add a `thingstudio` command; start it from its folder, or by its full path. To upgrade, replace
the folder with a newer one. To remove it, delete the folder. On Linux, add your account to the `dialout` group
(`uucp` on Arch) yourself to use USB boards.

## Installer script

On macOS and Linux, the installer puts ThingStudio in `~/.local/share/thingstudio` and the `thingstudio` command in
`~/.local/bin`. Your settings live in `~/.thingstudio` (see [The ThingStudio folder](thingstudio-folder.md)).

On Windows, it puts ThingStudio in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Thingstudio` and adds the `thingstudio` command to your PATH.
Your settings live in `%USERPROFILE%\.thingstudio`.

To upgrade, run the installer script again.

### Remove

To remove ThingStudio on macOS and Linux:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh -s -- --uninstall
```

On Windows:

```powershell
& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases/latest/download/install.ps1))) -Uninstall
```

Upgrading and removing never touch `~/.thingstudio` (`%USERPROFILE%\.thingstudio` on Windows), or your flows, which
are saved wherever you chose. To start again as a new user, move that folder aside as well: it holds your credentials,
presets, custom nodes and board definitions.

## Tutorial flows

Every install has a `tutorials` folder. [Tutorial flows](tutorial-flows.md#where-the-folder-is) says where it is for each route.

## From source

For working on ThingStudio itself. You need Python 3.10 or later, Node.js 22.12 or later, and `make`. On a Mac,
`make` comes with the Xcode command line tools (`xcode-select --install`).

In the repository folder, run `make`. This builds the editor and the user guide, installs ThingStudio into a `.venv`
folder, and puts the `thingstudio-backend` command on your PATH. Run `make` again after updating the repository. It
only rebuilds what changed. If your `python3` is older than 3.10, name a newer one: `make PYTHON=python3.12`.

Start it with `thingstudio-backend`, or `make run`. On a Mac, start it from Apple's **Terminal** app. macOS blocks
WiFi connections from a copy run from source in other terminals, such as iTerm.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/tutorials/

# Tutorials

[Getting started](../getting-started.md) ends with a blinking LED. The first two tutorials continue from it, each
starting from the flow the last one ends with. The MQTT tutorial starts a new flow, and the sensor display is a separate
project.

1. [Two more blinks](two-more-blinks.md) — the blink again, two more ways: one with the LED's state on the
   hardware, one keeping it in the `function` node with `context`.
2. [Web Blink](blink-from-your-network.md) — the same LED, driven by an `http in` node arriving over
   WiFi: putting the board on your network, finding it again, and what an open port on the board means.

    !!! info "More tutorials coming"

        Web Blink is the last finished tutorial. The two after it are still being worked on, and more are on the way.

3. [Blink from anywhere](blink-from-anywhere.md) — the same LED through an MQTT broker: publishing from the board,
   subscribing to switch it, and why every topic carries a number of your own.
4. [A sensor display](../sensor-display.md) — read a sensor and show it on a touch display. It is a work in
   progress.

The finished flow for each tutorial is in the tutorials folder. [Tutorial flows](../tutorial-flows.md) says where the folder
is and what to change in each flow.

If you've built something past the tutorials, what worked and what stalled is a useful report: what you tried next,
and what happened. [File it on the issue tracker](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/issues).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/tutorial-flows/

# Tutorial flows

If you'd rather not build the tutorial flows from scratch, or you get stuck, their finished flow files are in the
tutorials folder, [below](#where-the-folder-is). Open one with **File → Open…**. Each entry below says what the flow shows
and what to change first.

You'll need to change the flow to match your WiFi setup, and the actual pins that devices, like LEDs, are connected to on
your board. If your board is one of those that already have a definition file made for it, you can set it in the **Board**
drop-down ([Boards and processors](boards.md#picking-the-board)).

## Where the folder is

Every install has a `tutorials` folder. Where it is depends on how you installed:

| Install | Examples folder |
| --- | --- |
| Installer script, macOS and Linux | `~/.local/share/thingstudio/current/tutorials` |
| Installer script, Windows | `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Thingstudio\versions\thingstudio-VERSION-windows-x86_64\tutorials` |
| Package | `tutorials`, inside the folder you unpacked |
| From source | `tutorials`, in the repository folder |

The Windows path contains the version, so it changes when you upgrade.

## Before you deploy

- **Pins are examples.** Set your board's pin in the property panel. **Pins…** next to the **Board** menu lists the
  pins your board has.
- **A flow with a WiFi or MQTT node holds no passwords.** The network name, password and broker address are kept in a
  saved credential on your computer, never in the flow file. Open the node's **WiFi** or **MQTT Broker** field and
  click ✎: fill in your own details and save, or pick one you have already saved from the drop-down. See
  [The ThingStudio folder](thingstudio-folder.md#credentials).

## The flows

In the order that builds up. Each entry lists what to try changing first, and where to read about the node.

### `blink.flow.json`

A `timer` counts, a `function` turns the count into on and off, and `gpio out` drives the LED. Walked by
[Blink an LED](first-flow.md).

- **pin** on [gpio out](nodes/gpio-out.md): your LED's GPIO number. The file has 15.
- **interval (ms)** on [timer](nodes/timer.md): each tick toggles the LED, so the blink rate follows.
- The [function](nodes/function.md) node's **code**, which keeps the count's parity with `% 2`.

### `two-more-blinks.flow.json`

The same blink with the state kept elsewhere. This file reads the LED's pin back with `machine.Pin` to decide the
next level. Walked by [Two more blinks](tutorials/two-more-blinks.md), which also swaps in the `context` version.

- The pin number, in two places: the [gpio out](nodes/gpio-out.md) node's **pin** and the function's
  `machine.Pin(15)`. They have to agree.
- The [function](nodes/function.md) node's **code**: replace it with the `context` version from the tutorial.

### `http-blink.flow.json`

The same LED, toggled from a browser. An `http in` node serves `/toggle` on port 9999, a `function` flips the LED
and builds the reply, and `http response` answers the browser. `wifi status` and `debug` show the connection. It
needs a WiFi network of yours. Walked by [Web Blink](tutorials/blink-from-your-network.md).

- **path** and **port** on [http in](nodes/http-in.md).
- The reply text in the function's **code** (`'LED on'` and `'LED off'`).
- **poll interval (ms)** on [wifi status](nodes/wifi-status.md).

### `blink-from-anywhere.flow.json`

The same LED through an MQTT broker. Clicking `inject` publishes `pressed` to a `button` topic, and `mqtt subscribe`
on an `led` topic feeds a `function` that turns `on`, `1` or `true` into true for `gpio out`; `debug` prints what
arrives. It needs a WiFi network and a broker of yours. Its topics start
`thingstudio/change-this-number/`: replace that number in both before you deploy, because the broker is public. Walked
by [Blink from anywhere](tutorials/blink-from-anywhere.md).

- The number in both **topic** fields, on [mqtt publish](nodes/mqtt-publish.md) and
  [mqtt subscribe](nodes/mqtt-subscribe.md).
- **host** and **port** in the broker form, to use a broker on your own network.
- The [function](nodes/function.md) node's **code**, which decides which messages count as on.

The repository's `test-flows/` folder holds more flows, written for trying one node at a time on a board. They aren't
installed.

## Flows written by an AI assistant

An assistant can write a flow file for you to open the same way. See [Writing flows with an AI assistant](ai-authoring.md).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/tutorials/two-more-blinks/

# Two more blinks

If you've followed the steps in [Getting started](../getting-started.md) you'll now have a board with a blinking LED. This tutorial starts from there and shows you two other methods to get the same effect. In the process you'll directly access the hardware through MicroPython and see how ThingStudio nodes and flows can keep track of past events.

The [Blink an LED](../first-flow.md) flow contained three nodes, a **timer** → **function** → **gpio out**. We'll just be changing the function node in this tutorial.

The first variant is **Read the pin, write it back**: the blink's state lives on the board, in the pin, and the
`function` node runs your own MicroPython to reach it.

The second variant is **Keep the state in the node**: the state lives inside the `function` node itself, in
`context`.

You can build this flow up yourself or start from the finished flow,
[two-more-blinks.flow.json](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/blob/main/tutorials/two-more-blinks.flow.json),
in the [tutorials folder](../tutorial-flows.md#where-the-folder-is), with **File → Open…**. It carries the first of the two
blinks: change `15` in `machine.Pin(15)` to your LED's GPIO number.

If a step misbehaves on the way, start at [Debugging & troubleshooting](../debugging.md).

## Read the pin, write it back

Each message so far decides the LED by counting. Let the pin say where it is instead. Replace the function's code
with this, using your LED's GPIO number in place of `PIN`:

```python
import machine
msg['payload'] = 0 if machine.Pin(PIN).value() else 1
return msg
```

Deploy. The LED blinks as before, but the reason has changed: each message now reads the pin and writes back the
opposite of what it found. The state, what the LED is actually showing, lives on the board between messages, so
the flow can't contradict it.

`machine.Pin` is MicroPython's own pin API. Constructed with a number and no other settings, it takes the pin as it
is and `.value()` reads the level the `gpio out` node has written. The write itself goes out of the function's
output, through to `gpio out`.

The pin fields on gpio nodes are checked against your board at compile time, but code inside a function isn't. If
`PIN` isn't a pin number your board has, the compile check passes and the error arrives when the flow runs, as a
`[NODE_ERROR]` in the console. See [Reading a node error](../debugging.md#reading-a-node-error); **Pins…** next to
the **Board** menu lists your board's pins.

## Keep the state in the node

!!! note "An important point to understand"

    A flow is stateless: each event is handled on its own, without regard to what came before. In general this is
    a good thing:

    - An error shows up with the message that caused it, not in some state built over earlier operations.
    - Recovery is doing nothing: the next message starts clean. A crashed stateful component needs its data
      restored to an acceptable earlier version, with nothing to say which that is.

    When a flow does need to remember, ThingStudio's answer is a **context** — state held between messages, either
    private to one node (`context`) or shared across the whole flow (`flow`). This blink's LED level belongs to one
    function node, so its private store is the one to use. All three stores, `context` and `flow` among them, are
    in [Context, flow and settings](../nodes/function.md#context-flow-and-settings); `settings` even survives a
    reboot.

The pin held the state on the board. The other place is inside the function node itself:

```python
on = not context.get('on', False)
context.set('on', on)
msg['payload'] = on
return msg
```

Deploy again: the same blink. Nothing outside the node holds the state now. `context.get('on', False)` reads this
function node's own memory; `context.set('on', on)` writes it; the `False` is what `.get` answers when nothing is
stored yet, which is why the first message turns the LED on.

For state kept without code, the [change](../nodes/change.md) node stores a flow variable, the same store a
`function`'s `flow.get()`/`flow.set()` reads. A `change` node can store a flow variable but can't flip it, so a toggle
needs a function node.

## Next

The next tutorial, the next job, and the node pages behind the code:

- [Web Blink](blink-from-your-network.md) — the next tutorial: the same LED, driven by an `http in`
  node from anywhere on your WiFi.
- [A sensor display](../sensor-display.md) — the next job: read a sensor and show it on a screen.
- [gpio out](../nodes/gpio-out.md) — what else the node that drives the LED can do.
- [function](../nodes/function.md) — `context`, `flow` and `settings`, and several outputs from one function node.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/tutorials/blink-from-your-network/

# Web Blink

If you've worked through [Two more blinks](two-more-blinks.md), you have a board whose LED blinks on a timer. Here the
timer goes, and a web browser does the switching. You'll put the board on your WiFi network, find it from your
computer, and see what it means for a board to have an open port.

The blink flow was a **timer** → **function** → **gpio out**. The **timer** gives way to an **http in** node, which
runs a web server on the board, and the **function** gains a second output for the reply that goes back to the
browser.

You can build the flow step by step, or start from the finished flow,
[http-blink.flow.json](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/blob/main/tutorials/http-blink.flow.json), in the
[tutorials folder](../tutorial-flows.md#where-the-folder-is), with **File → Open…**.
[Tutorial flows](../tutorial-flows.md#before-you-deploy) says what to change before you deploy.

If a step misbehaves on the way, start at [Debugging & troubleshooting](../debugging.md).

## Build the flow

On the network the request is the event, so the timer goes and the LED holds the level you last asked for.

1. Delete the **timer**.
2. Drag an **http in** onto the canvas. Set **port** to `9999` and **path** to `/toggle`. Leave **method** as `GET`.
3. Select the **function**. Set **outputs** to `2` and replace its **code** with:

    ```python
    on = not context.get('on', False)
    context.set('on', on)
    msg['payload'] = on
    reply = dict(msg)
    reply['payload'] = 'LED ' + ('on' if on else 'off')
    return [msg, reply]
    ```

4. Drag an **http response** onto the canvas.
5. Wire **http in** → **function**. Wire the function's first output to **gpio out** and its second output to
   **http response**.
6. Drag a **wifi status** and a **debug** onto the canvas. Tick **full message** on the **debug** node and wire
   **wifi status** → **debug**.

## The board joins WiFi

The board joins the network named in the flow — so tell the flow which network. Flow files hold no
passwords or other secrets: the WiFi details live in the `.thingstudio` folder in your home directory
(`~/.thingstudio/credentials/`), as **credentials**. Each credential is named, and you can keep
several — one per network — and pick the right one per flow. See
[The ThingStudio folder](../thingstudio-folder.md#credentials).

1. On the `http in` node's property panel, click **+** next to the **WiFi** field to make a new credential (✎
   edits an existing one). Give the credential a name, your network's SSID and its password, and save.
2. The **WiFi** field on the `http in` node (and on the `wifi status` node) picks that credential — one WiFi
   network per flow, shared by every WiFi node in it.

Compile stops with a one-line error if the flow's WiFi has no saved network behind it; the FAQ's
[needs-a-WiFi-network](../faq.md#why-does-compile-fail-with-needs-a-wifi-network) entry is that error.

## Name the board, then deploy

1. Connect the board over USB, as in [Connect your board](../connecting.md), and choose **Tools → Board settings…**.
   Give the board a network name, such as `blink`. A name lets your computer find the board without an IP address.
2. Click **Compile → Deploy**. The board swaps in the flow and joins your WiFi.

A few seconds after the deploy, the console prints the **wifi status** message, with a `payload` of `true`, and the
node's dot shows connected (see [node status](../working-in-the-editor.md#node-status) when the dot is something else). The LED is dark:
nothing drives the pin until a request does.

## Find the board

- **By name:** open `http://blink.local:9999/toggle` in your browser. The name is the one from Board settings plus
  `.local`; port 9999 and path `/toggle` are the **port** and **path** of the `http in` node.
- **By IP:** the `debug` node prints the whole **wifi status** message, which includes `ip`. (In the example file,
  tick **full message** on the `debug` node first; it prints only the payload otherwise.) The fields are listed
  under [wifi status](../nodes/wifi-status.md#wiring). Open `http://<ip>:9999/toggle`.

If `.local` names don't resolve on your network (they don't everywhere, and they don't across VPN tunnels at all —
multicast doesn't pass), the IP address is the dependable one.

The page answers `LED on` or `LED off`, and the LED does what it says. Expect the first answer after an idle stretch
to take up to a second: the board's WiFi wakes on the request (see
[Why do http in requests take a second to answer?](../faq.md#why-do-http-in-requests-take-a-second-to-answer)).

## How it works

The request is the only event this flow gets, and each one is handled on its own: between requests the LED holds its
level, remembered in the `context` toggle from the last tutorial.

The function has two outputs. The first carries the new state to **gpio out**. The second carries `reply` to
[http response](../nodes/http-response.md), which answers the browser. `return [msg, reply]` routes one message to
each output, as in Node-RED; see the [function node](../nodes/function.md).

## The server is open

`http in` runs an unauthenticated server on the board: whatever reaches that network can call every path. Keep those
routes non-sensitive, or keep the board off shared networks. See [http in](../nodes/http-in.md) for what the server
does and doesn't do.

## Next

- [http in](../nodes/http-in.md) — routes, methods, timeouts and the server's limits.
- [Blink from anywhere](blink-from-anywhere.md) — the next tutorial: the same LED through an MQTT broker.
- [mqtt publish](../nodes/mqtt-publish.md) and [mqtt subscribe](../nodes/mqtt-subscribe.md) — the nodes behind it.
- [Connecting over WiFi](../wifi-connection.md) — the board as an editor peer on your network, not just a web
  server.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/tutorials/blink-from-anywhere/

# Blink from anywhere

!!! note "Work in progress"

    This tutorial is still being checked on a board. The example flow compiles, but some steps may not match the editor.

If you've worked through [Web Blink](blink-from-your-network.md), you have a board on your WiFi that switches its LED
when a browser on your network asks. Here an MQTT broker sits in the middle. A broker passes messages between clients,
so your phone or laptop doesn't have to be on the board's network. You'll publish a message from the board, switch the
LED by sending one to it, and see why every topic here carries a number of your own.

This is a new flow, on an empty canvas, with two halves: **inject** → **mqtt publish** sends a message when you click
the button in the editor, and **mqtt subscribe** → **function** → **gpio out** switches the LED when a message
arrives on another topic. The board joins your WiFi with the saved credential from Web Blink.

You can build the flow step by step, or start from the finished flow,
[blink-from-anywhere.flow.json](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/blob/main/tutorials/blink-from-anywhere.flow.json),
in the [tutorials folder](../tutorial-flows.md#where-the-folder-is), with **File → Open…**. Before you deploy, replace
`change-this-number` in both topics (see below), and set the WiFi network and broker as
[Tutorial flows](../tutorial-flows.md#before-you-deploy) describes.

If a step misbehaves on the way, start at [Debugging & troubleshooting](../debugging.md).

## Pick a topic prefix

This tutorial uses `test.mosquitto.org`, a public broker. Anyone who knows or guesses a topic can read it and publish
to it, so every topic starts with a number nobody else will pick: a random one of six or seven digits. Here it is
written `4821937`; use your own.

- `thingstudio/4821937/button` is where the board publishes.
- `thingstudio/4821937/led` is where the board listens.

## Build the flow

Start with an empty canvas (**File → New flow**).

1. Drag an **inject** onto the canvas. Set **payload type** to `string` and **value** to `pressed`.
2. Drag an **mqtt publish**. Set **topic** to `thingstudio/4821937/button`. Click **+** next to **MQTT Broker**: the
   form asks for a name, a host, a port and an optional username and password. Name it `test-mosquitto`, set the host to
   `test.mosquitto.org` and the port to `1883`, and leave the rest blank. Wire **inject** → **mqtt publish**.
3. Drag an **mqtt subscribe**. Set **topic** to `thingstudio/4821937/led`. Its **MQTT Broker** field already shows the
   broker from step 2, because a flow has one.
4. Drag a **function** and replace its **code** with:

    ```python
    msg['payload'] = str(msg['payload']).lower() in ('on', '1', 'true')
    return msg
    ```

5. Drag a **gpio out** and set **pin** to your LED's GPIO number. Wire **mqtt subscribe** → **function** → **gpio out**.
6. Drag a **debug** and wire **mqtt subscribe** → **debug**, to see what arrives in the console.
7. On either MQTT node, pick your WiFi credential in the **WiFi** field: the one from
   [Web Blink](blink-from-your-network.md#the-board-joins-wifi), or make one with **+**. A flow has one
   WiFi network, so the other node shows the same one.

## Deploy

With the board connected, click **Compile → Deploy**. When **mqtt subscribe**'s dot turns green, the board is connected
to the broker. **mqtt publish**'s dot stays blank until its first message.

## Board to world

On your computer, subscribe to everything under your prefix:

```sh
mosquitto_sub -h test.mosquitto.org -t 'thingstudio/4821937/#' -v
```

Click the ▶ on the **inject** node. The terminal prints the topic and `pressed`. A phone does the same with any MQTT
client app: connect to `test.mosquitto.org` on port `1883` and subscribe to the same topic.

## World to board

Publish to the LED topic from the same terminal, or from the phone:

```sh
mosquitto_pub -h test.mosquitto.org -t 'thingstudio/4821937/led' -m on
mosquitto_pub -h test.mosquitto.org -t 'thingstudio/4821937/led' -m off
```

The LED follows, and the editor's console shows each message from the **debug** node. The function node is there because
`gpio out` treats any non-empty text as true, so `off` would switch the LED on. It turns `on`, `1` and `true` into true
and every other message into false.

## Nothing arrives?

- Check that the number in the topics matches everywhere, and that the last part is `button` on the publisher and `led`
  on the subscriber.
- A red dot on an MQTT node, or a console line starting `mqtt connect to`, means the board can't reach the broker. See
  [MQTT broker unreachable](../debugging.md#mqtt-broker-unreachable), which also covers networks that block port 1883.
- If compile stops with "needs a WiFi network", a **WiFi** field is empty. See
  [Why does compile fail with "needs a WiFi network"?](../faq.md#why-does-compile-fail-with-needs-a-wifi-network).

## How it works

A topic is a label on a message. **mqtt publish** sends each message that reaches it to its topic, and **mqtt
subscribe** emits each message that arrives on its topic, with the text as `payload` and the topic it came in on as
`topic`. The broker sits between them and between any other clients.

Both nodes use the flow's one broker, which is why the second node showed the first one's settings.

## The broker is public

Anyone who knows your topic can switch your LED, which is why the topic carries a number and why the messages here
carry nothing private. For anything that matters, use a broker on your own network with a password: set its address in
the broker form instead. The nodes work the same way.

## Next

- [mqtt publish](../nodes/mqtt-publish.md) and [mqtt subscribe](../nodes/mqtt-subscribe.md) — every property, including
  QoS and retain.
- [Tutorial flows](../tutorial-flows.md) — the finished flows for the tutorials, and what to change in each.
- [Tutorials](index.md) — the other tutorials.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/sensor-display/

# A sensor display

!!! note "Work in progress"

    This tutorial is being reworked. The example flow runs, but some steps may not match the editor. The GUI nodes it
    uses are provisional; see [GUI nodes](nodes/gui.md).

If you've followed [Getting started](getting-started.md), you've driven an LED from a flow. This tutorial moves on to
a sensor and a screen. You'll read temperature, humidity and pressure from an I2C sensor, show them with their recent
history on a three-page touch display, and publish them over MQTT. It's a separate project from the blink tutorials,
with its own parts, listed under What you need.

The flow is a **bme280** sensor feeding GUI nodes that draw the readings, with an **mqtt publish** that sends them on.

The finished flow is in the ThingStudio repository:
[`test-flows/gui-headliner-sensor-freenove-s3-4in.flow.json`](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/blob/main/test-flows/gui-headliner-sensor-freenove-s3-4in.flow.json).
Open it in one of two ways:

- **Open the finished flow.** Download it and open it with **File → Open…**, then set your own WiFi and MQTT
  credentials in its config nodes.
- **Build it yourself.** Follow the steps below.

## What you need

The steps use this hardware and setup:

- A Freenove ESP32-S3 4.0" touch display (FNK0104S), with MicroPython and the runtime installed
  ([Getting started steps 3 to 5](installing-micropython.md)). Pick it by hand in the **Board**
  menu. Other boards work too; the pins below are this board's.
- A BME280 sensor board. A BMP280 also works, without humidity. Wire it to 3V3, GND, **SCL 15** and **SDA 16**,
  the touch panel's I2C bus.
- A WiFi network for the clock and MQTT, and an MQTT broker. See [Connecting over WiFi](wifi-connection.md).

## 1. Read the sensor

1. Drag a **bme280** onto the canvas. In its **I2C bus** field, click **+** and make a bus: bus `0`, SCL `15`,
   SDA `16`.
2. Set the bme280's **address** to `0x76`, or `0x77` if your sensor board ties SDO high, and **interval (ms)** to
   `5000`.
3. Drag a **function** node, set **outputs** to `5`, wire the bme280 to it, and use this code:

    ```python
    p = msg['payload']
    t = {'topic': 'temperature', 'payload': p['temperature']}
    h = None
    if p['humidity'] is not None:   # a BMP280 has no humidity
        h = {'topic': 'humidity', 'payload': p['humidity']}
    pr = {'topic': 'pressure', 'payload': p['pressure']}
    ok = {'topic': 'sensor', 'payload': True}
    return [t, h, pr, pr, ok]
    ```

    Each reading goes out on its own output, so each widget gets only its own number. Output 4 is a second copy of
    the pressure, for its journal. Output 5 says the sensor is alive.

To test the sensor first, wire the bme280 to a **debug** node and deploy. A reading appears every 5 seconds. See
[bme280](nodes/bme280.md).

## 2. Show it on the display

1. Drag a **display spi** onto the canvas and set it for the Freenove panel:

    | Property | Value |
    | --- | --- |
    | controller | `st7796` |
    | frame format | `rgb565` |
    | SPI bus | `1` |
    | baudrate | `40000000` |
    | sck, mosi, dc, cs pin | `12`, `11`, `46`, `10` |
    | reset pin | `-1` |
    | backlight pin | `45` |
    | width, height | `320`, `480` |
    | rotation | `1` |
    | orientation | `90° clockwise` |
    | color order | `BGR` |
    | invert colors, data latch order | on |

    Click 💾 to save these as a [preset](working-in-the-editor.md#presets) for next time.
2. Drag a **gui screen** and wire it to the display spi. It takes its width, height and frame format from the
   display, so the panel's size is set in one place.
3. In the gui screen's **touch panel** field, click **+** and make a Touch panel: controller FT6336U, the same I2C
   bus, address `0x38`, width `320`, height `480`.
4. Drag three **gui readout** nodes (temperature, humidity, pressure) and a **gui light** for the sensor. Wire the
   function's outputs 1, 2, 3 and 5 to them. In each readout, set **units**, **decimals**, **lowest value** and
   **highest value**.
5. Lay out the pages: select the gui screen and use the page outline in its properties to add rows of text and
   readouts. See [Laying out pages](nodes/gui.md#laying-out-pages), which also says why the layout is fixed when the
   flow compiles.

Set **stale after** on the readouts and the light. A reading that stops arriving is then dimmed, so a dead sensor
looks different from a steady room.

## 3. Add the history

A [journal](nodes/journal.md) keeps the recent readings, and a **gui histogram** draws them.

1. Wire the temperature output to a journal with **seconds per row** `10`, **rows kept** `156` and **rows per
   roll-up** `6`. Wire its first output to a gui histogram. That histogram shows the last 26 minutes.
2. Wire the journal's second output, one summary per minute, to a second journal with **seconds per row** `0`. Wire
   that journal to a second gui histogram, which shows the last 2.6 hours.
3. Wire output 4, the pressure copy, to a journal with **seconds per row** `60`, and that to a third gui histogram.

Each bar is the average of its row, and the thin line runs from the row's min to its max. Set each histogram's
**bottom at** and **top at** to the range you expect, for example 15 to 30 for temperature. A histograms shows only
the rows its journal kept: give the journal at least as many **rows kept** as the histogram has columns, or the bars
fill the right of the card and leave the rest empty — the compiler warns with the number to raise. See
[Histogram](nodes/gui.md#histogram).

## 4. Add the clock

1. Drag a **timer** with **interval (ms)** `1000`, and two **ntp** nodes. Wire the timer to both.
2. Set one ntp node's **format** to `time` and the other's to `date`. In both, set **UTC offset (hours)** for your
   zone's standard time, and **daylight saving** to **UK / EU: automatic** if that's where you are, otherwise
   **none**. See [ntp](nodes/ntp.md).
3. Add two **gui label** nodes, one for the time with **room for (characters)** `5`, and one for the date with
   `10`. Wire the `time` ntp node to the first and the `date` one to the second.
4. On a new page, give the time label the font `font_seg764` (seven-segment digits) and the date `font_body24`.

Until the board has the time, the labels show `--`.

## 5. Turn the pages
