Add a **gui button** with **mode** `navigate` to each page, so you can turn the pages by touch. See
[Buttons](nodes/gui.md#buttons).

The finished flow also turns the pages by itself every 8 seconds, with a node that isn't in the palette. Skip it when
you build the flow: the buttons turn the pages by touch.

## 6. Publish the readings

Drag three **mqtt publish** nodes, one per reading, with topics such as `thingstudio/headliner/temperature`. Wire
outputs 1 to 3 of the function to them, and pick your MQTT broker and WiFi. See
[mqtt publish](nodes/mqtt-publish.md).

## Deploy

Click **Compile → Deploy**. The display lights, the readings appear within 5 seconds, the histograms fill as the minutes
pass, and the clock starts once the board has the time.

## If it doesn't work

Each symptom below has its own fix:

- **The picture is scrambled:** the **width** and **height** on the display spi must be the panel's own size,
  `320` and `480`, even when the picture is turned; the gui screen follows them. Deploy checks this and says so.
- **Touches land in the wrong place:** see [Touch panels](nodes/touch-panel.md).
- **No readings:** check the wiring and the address (`0x76` or `0x77`), and test with a debug node.
- **The clock stays at `--`:** the ntp node's status says why: no WiFi yet, or the NTP server can't be reached.
  It tries again every 30 seconds.
- **Compile says a node is "disconnected from any source":** a widget has nothing wired to it. Wire it, or reload
  the editor if the wires are there.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/working-in-the-editor/

# Editor in depth

## Wiring

Every port has a type: `int`, `number`, `bool`, `string`, `bytes` or `any`. The editor refuses a wire between
types that don't fit. What each input type accepts:

| Input | Accepts wires from |
| --- | --- |
| `any` | any output |
| `bool` | any output. The value is tested with Python's `bool()`. |
| `number` | `number`, `int`, `string` |
| `int` | `int`, `string` |
| `string` | `string` |
| `bytes` | `bytes`, `any` |

A `string` that isn't a number fails on the board when it reaches a `number` or `int` input, with a `NODE_ERROR`.
An `any` output, such as the output of a [function](nodes/function.md) node, connects only to `any`, `bool` and
`bytes` inputs.

An input can take any number of wires. The node runs once for each message that arrives, whichever wire it came
on. An output can feed any number of inputs.

When an output feeds more than one wire, the first wire gets the message itself and each other wire gets a copy,
made before any of them runs. The wires then run one after another, in the order they were drawn. The copy is
shallow: a list or dict inside the message is shared, so a node that changes `msg['payload']` in place, rather than
replacing it, changes it for the other wires too.

## Typed values

Some nodes take a value you type next to a type you pick: [inject](nodes/inject.md) and
[startup](nodes/startup.md) (**payload type** and **value**), and [change](nodes/change.md) (**literal type** and
**value / source property**). The value is read as that type:

- `bool`: `true` is `True`. Anything else is `False`, including `True` and `1`.
- `number`: a whole number becomes an `int`, any other number a `float`. An empty value is `0`. Write numbers in
  decimal: `0x2000` is not a number.
- `string`: sent as typed.

With type `number`, a value that isn't a number stops the deploy for `change`. For `inject` and `startup` it fails on
the board when the node fires, with a `[NODE_ERROR]`.

## Giving a node a flow label

Every node has a **flow label** field at the top of its property panel. Type something, say `Fire!`, and the canvas
shows it instead of the node's name. Leave it blank to show the name again. Console messages and errors that name
the node use the flow label too.

A `gui button` also has a **board label**, the text drawn on the button. If the board label is blank, the button
shows the flow label.

## Presets

A preset is a named set of property values, such as the pins and size of one display panel. `display spi`,
`display i2c` and the Touch panel config have a **preset** menu at the top of their property panel:

- Pick a preset to copy its values into the node's properties.
- Click 💾 to save the current values as a preset, under a name you choose.
- Click ↻ to read the preset files again.

Applying a preset copies the values once. Later changes to the node or the preset don't affect each other.

Each preset is a JSON file in `~/.thingstudio/presets/<node type>/`, which you can also write by hand. A file that
isn't valid JSON appears in the menu disabled, with the file named. See
[The ThingStudio folder](thingstudio-folder.md#presets).

## Config nodes

A config node holds settings that several nodes share. A node's property panel has a field to pick one; ✎ edits it
and **+** makes a new one. The config nodes are:

- **WiFi:** a saved credential and a security mode: password, open, or [unmanaged](wifi-provisioning.md).
- **MQTT Broker:** a saved credential holding the host, port and optional username and password. One per flow.
- **I2C bus:** the bus number, SCL and SDA pins, and frequency. See [I2C bus](nodes/i2c-bus.md).
- **BLE:** the board's Bluetooth name. Optional; one per flow. See [BLE](nodes/ble.md).
- **BLE peer:** a Bluetooth LE device the board connects to, by address or name. One per device. See
  [BLE peer](nodes/ble-peer.md).
- **Touch panel:** the touch controller, its I2C bus and address, and its size and orientation. See
  [Touch panels](nodes/touch-panel.md).

The WiFi and MQTT Broker configs hold only the name of a saved credential. The SSID, passwords and broker address
are saved by name in `~/.thingstudio/credentials/`, not in the flow file, so a flow you share or commit holds no
secrets. Two flows that use the same credential share its values: edit it once and both change.

Pick a saved WiFi network or broker from the field's list. ✎ opens the saved values, such as a broker's host, port
and login, with the config's other settings; **Save** stores them and **Cancel** discards the changes. **+** makes a
new one: give it a name, fill it in and save. If a flow names a credential that isn't saved on this computer, ✎ says
so, and saving creates it. See [The ThingStudio folder](thingstudio-folder.md#credentials).

A flow has one WiFi network and one MQTT broker. Every node that uses WiFi has a **WiFi** field, and every MQTT node
an **MQTT Broker** field. They all show the flow's one setting: change it on one node and it changes on all. A flow
doesn't need a `wifi status` node to use the network.

## Node status

Some nodes show a colored dot and a line of text under the node while the editor is connected to the board:

| Dot | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Green | connected |
| Amber | connecting |
| Gray | disconnected |
| Red | error |

The dot shows what the board reports, not the editor's guess. It appears once the running flow first reports, and
clears on every deploy until the new flow reports.

These nodes report a status: `wifi status`, `mqtt publish`, `mqtt subscribe`, `ntp`, `i2c device`, `bme280`, `touch`
and a `gui screen` with a touch panel. `adc` and `neopixel` report only a failed read or write, as a red dot. A custom
node reports one if its code does.

## Notes

The **Notes** panel on the right is free text about the flow: what it does, what to wire up, how to use it. It's
saved in the flow file, and opens by itself when you open a flow that has notes. **File → New flow** clears it.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/flow-lifecycle/

# Flow lifecycle

How a flow is saved, opened, deployed and disconnected.

## Save and open

A flow is saved in a `.flow.json` file you choose, so it can live in a project's git repo like any other file. The
file holds the nodes and their properties, the wiring, the canvas layout and the config nodes.

- **File → Save** (⌘S, or Ctrl+S on Windows and Linux) writes to the flow's file. A new flow has no file yet, so the
  first Save asks where, like Save As. The file's name shows next to the flow name.
- **File → Save As…** (⇧⌘S, or Ctrl+Shift+S) always asks where, and that file becomes the flow's file.
- **File → Open…** (⌘O, or Ctrl+O) loads a flow file. Save then writes back to it.
- **Open recent**, in the File menu, lists the last 8 files you opened or saved, newest first, with each one's flow
  name. After a reload the browser asks once for permission to use the file again. A file that has moved or been
  deleted is taken off the list. **Clear recent files** forgets the list, not the files.
- **File → New flow** starts an empty flow with no file.

If the file has changed on disk since you opened or last saved it, for example after a `git checkout`, Save asks
before overwriting it. Say no and use Save As to keep both.

The recent list is kept in your browser, so another browser or a private window has its own. Safari and Firefox
can't save back to a file: there, Save and Save As download the flow, Open uploads one, and there's no recent list.

**The flow name** field is saved inside the file itself and is sent with every deploy, so a connected board's
identity is visible in the console instead of a bare deployment id. It also suggests a filename for Save As (spaces
and punctuation become dashes), but you can type over that suggestion freely.

Custom node packages and saved credentials live in `~/.thingstudio/custom-nodes/` and `~/.thingstudio/credentials/`.
They're shared across flows rather than tied to one project, unlike a flow itself — a saved credential referenced by
name from a config node is never written into the `.flow.json` file. See
[The ThingStudio folder](thingstudio-folder.md).

## Deploy

**Compile → Deploy** compiles the current canvas to MicroPython bytecode and sends it to the connected board,
replacing whatever flow is currently running there.

A successful deploy shows a confirmation in the console and the new flow starts running immediately. The board keeps
the deployed flow and starts it again each time the board starts, with or without the editor. Each start begins every
node afresh: counts, filters, journals, flow variables and a function node's `context` start empty. Only `settings`
keeps its values (see [function](nodes/function.md#context-flow-and-settings)).

A failed deploy leaves the board's current flow running and shows a specific error:

- a compile error — something in the flow itself, such as a missing required property
- a space error — the compiled flow doesn't fit in the board's available flash/RAM
- a library error — see below

After a successful deploy the button grays out: the board is already running exactly what's on the canvas. It
re-enables the moment you change anything (a property, a node, a wire). A change reaches the board only with the
next deploy. A failed deploy leaves it enabled so you can fix the problem and retry.

### Libraries

Some nodes need a library on the board, such as MQTT or a display driver. Deploy installs the libraries your flow uses
and removes ones it no longer uses, so a board holds only what its flow needs. The console lists them on each deploy.
A library already on the board isn't sent again.

A [function node](nodes/function.md) that imports one of these libraries, such as `import mqtt_as`, gets it the same
way. If the board can't take a library, for example because its flash is full, the console names the library and says
why.

**Tools → Check status** re-requests the board's identity — chip type, runtime version, and whichever flow is currently running — without resetting the board or redeploying anything. Useful for confirming what's actually on the board after reconnecting to a session already in progress.

**Disconnect** closes the serial connection. The board keeps running whatever flow was last deployed; disconnecting the editor doesn't stop it.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/thingstudio-folder/

# The ThingStudio folder

ThingStudio keeps its own files in one folder on your computer:

- macOS and Linux: `~/.thingstudio`
- Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.thingstudio`

ThingStudio creates the folder the first time it starts. Your flows are not kept here. They are saved wherever you
choose (see [Flow lifecycle](flow-lifecycle.md#save-and-open)).

## What's in it

| Folder | Holds | Edit by hand? |
|---|---|---|
| `credentials/` | WiFi and MQTT broker logins, saved by name | No, use the editor |
| `presets/` | Saved node settings, one folder per node type | Yes |
| `custom-nodes/` | Your own node types | Yes |
| `boards/` | Board definitions | Yes |
| `processors/` | Processor definitions | Yes |

Every file is plain JSON, except the `.node.py` file of a custom node. The editor reads these folders through the
ThingStudio backend, so they aren't available when the editor talks to the board directly over USB.

## Credentials

A WiFi or MQTT broker config node holds only the name of a credential. The SSID, password, broker address and login
are stored in `credentials/wifi/<name>.json` or `credentials/mqtt-broker/<name>.json`. This keeps secrets out of flow
files you share or commit. Create and edit credentials from the config node (see
[Config nodes](working-in-the-editor.md#config-nodes)).

The files are not encrypted. Anyone who can read your home folder can read them. Don't commit this folder or copy it
to shared storage.

## Presets

A preset is a named set of property values for one node type, such as the pins and size of a display panel. You save
and load presets from a node's property panel (see [Presets](working-in-the-editor.md#presets)). Each one is a file at
`presets/<node type>/<name>.json`. A file that isn't valid JSON appears in the list disabled, with the file named.

## Custom nodes

A custom node is two files with the same base name: `<name>.node.json` and `<name>.node.py`. The first time
ThingStudio starts, it puts two examples here. Deleted examples don't come back. See
[Custom nodes](custom-nodes.md).

## Boards and processors

At every start, ThingStudio writes the built-in definitions into `boards/` and `processors/`, replacing files of the
same name. An upgrade's changes therefore arrive on the next start.

- To keep your own version of a built-in, save it under a different name (for example `my-cyd.json`). It is then a
  board or processor of its own, and is never overwritten.
- Editing a built-in file in place works until the next start, when the built-in replaces it.

See [Boards and processors](boards.md).

## Using a different folder

Start ThingStudio with `--data-dir`:

```sh
thingstudio --data-dir ~/projects/greenhouse/thingstudio-data
```

This keeps separate sets of credentials, presets and custom nodes, for example one per project.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/supported-hardware/

# Supported hardware

The boards, processors, displays, touch panels, sensors and other hardware below have built-in support. "Tested" means flows have
been deployed and run on that hardware. Pin details for boards and processors are in
[Boards and processors](boards.md).

## Boards

Each board below has a definition: a pin cheat sheet that names the board's own pins, such as its LED, marks the
pins that are reserved and why, and lists the pins each SPI and I2C bus can use. **Pins…** in the editor shows it.
See [Seeing a board's pins](boards.md#seeing-a-boards-pins).

| Board | Processor | Tested |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Raspberry Pi Pico | RP2040 | Yes |
| Raspberry Pi Pico W | RP2040 | Yes, including WiFi |
| Raspberry Pi Pico 2 | RP2350 | Yes |
| LOLIN S2 Mini | ESP32-S2 | Yes |
| LuatOS ESP32C3-CORE | ESP32-C3 | Yes, with the adc and neopixel nodes |
| [Kitchen sink](kitchen-sink-board.md) (LuatOS ESP32C3-CORE) | ESP32-C3 | Yes, with the adc, ebutton and neopixel nodes |
| ESP32-C5-340X (ESP32-C5-KITC-A) | ESP32-C5 | Yes, with the ble nodes (scan, advertise, characteristics, UART) |
| CYD (ESP32-2432S028, ST7789) | ESP32 | Yes, display only. |
| Freenove ESP32-S3 Display 4.0" (FNK0104S) | ESP32-S3 | Yes, with the display and touch |
| Pyboard v1.0 | STM32F405 | Yes |
| Seeed XIAO nRF52840 (Sense) | nRF52840 | Smoke tested, including the IMU |
| Wemos D1 R32 | ESP32 | Yes, with an RM68090 parallel TFT shield (rewired, custom node) |

MicroPython can be written onto any board in this list from the editor, with **Tools → Install firmware…**: a
serial port for the ESP32 family, a mounted drive for RP2040, RP2350 and nRF52 boards, or an image file you
downloaded. A board in this list preselects its build, but any board on a supported chip can be flashed the same
way. The Pyboard is the exception: it installs over DFU, which the editor doesn't offer; see
[Install MicroPython](installing-micropython.md).

## Processors without a board definition

Any board with one of these processors can be used by picking the processor from the **Board** menu, for example
**ESP32-C3 (any board)**. Its board-specific pins, such as an LED, aren't labelled.

| Processor | Tested |
| --- | --- |
| ESP32 | Yes, on the CYD |
| ESP32-S2 | Yes, on the LOLIN S2 Mini |
| ESP32-S3 | Yes, on the Freenove board |
| ESP32-C3 | Yes, on a generic ESP32-C3 board, over USB and WiFi; also on the [custom image](custom-firmware.md) |
| ESP32-C5 | Yes, on the ESP32-C5-340X, over USB; also on the [custom image](custom-firmware.md) |
| RP2040 | Yes, on the Pico and Pico W |
| RP2350 | Yes, on the Pico 2 |
| nRF52840 | Smoke tested on the Seeed XIAO nRF52840 (Sense) |

The [ble nodes](nodes/index.md#bluetooth) run on the ESP32, ESP32-S3, ESP32-C3 and ESP32-C5. On other processors
Deploy refuses them.

## Displays

The [GUI nodes](nodes/gui.md) that draw on these displays are provisional.

| Chip | Panel sizes | Node | Tested |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ST7789 | 240x240, 135x240, 240x320 | [display spi](nodes/display-spi.md) | Yes, on the CYD |
| ST7796 | 320x480 | [display spi](nodes/display-spi.md) | Yes, on the Freenove ESP32-S3 4.0" |
| SSD1306 (I2C only) | 128x64, or set width and height | [display i2c](nodes/display-i2c.md) | Untested |

## Touch panels

Touch in the [GUI nodes](nodes/gui.md) is provisional.

| Chip | Node | Tested |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FT6336U | [touch](nodes/touch-i2c.md) | Yes, on the Freenove ESP32-S3 4.0" |

## Sensors

| Chip | Node | Tested |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BME280 | [bme280](nodes/bme280.md) | Yes, on a Pico |
| BMP280 | [bme280](nodes/bme280.md) | Untested |

Other I2C devices can be read with a [function](nodes/function.md) node and the chip's datasheet.

## Other hardware

| Hardware | Node | Tested |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analog input (the chip's ADC) | [adc](nodes/adc.md) | Yes, on the LuatOS ESP32C3-CORE |
| WS2812 / NeoPixel LEDs | [neopixel](nodes/neopixel.md) | Yes, on the LuatOS ESP32C3-CORE |

## Other boards

Other boards that run MicroPython may work. ThingStudio needs a processor definition for the chip, and a board
definition if you want the board's own pins labelled.

You can write definition files yourself: [Adding a board](boards.md#adding-a-board) and [Adding a
processor](boards.md#adding-a-processor) describe every field of the JSON. Or an AI assistant can draft one. Point
it at the board maker's web page for the board, and it can usually write the file in seconds. For a processor, give
it the chip's datasheet. One of the existing files in `~/.thingstudio/boards/` or `~/.thingstudio/processors/` makes
a good example to include. Check the result against the datasheet. A missing reserved pin means the compile won't
stop a flow that crashes the board.

## Reporting hardware

Reports on any board, display or sensor, listed or not, are welcome. Open an issue on
[GitHub](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/issues) with:

- the board, processor and any display or sensor
- the MicroPython version
- what worked and what didn't

A definition file for a new board can be attached to the issue.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/boards/

# Boards and processors

Each board and processor has a definition file that says which pins a flow may use. This page covers picking a board, seeing its pins, what gets checked, and writing your own definition files.

ThingStudio checks every pin in a flow against the board the flow is for. If a pin doesn't exist on that board, or using it would crash the board, the compile stops and says why.

Each board has a definition file, and so does each processor. ThingStudio comes with definitions for the boards and processors below. You can [change them or add your own](#your-definition-files).

## Picking the board

Pick the board a flow is for from the **Board** menu in the toolbar. The default, **Auto**, uses the connected board. Auto recognises a board by the name MicroPython reports for it, and the menu shows what it found, for example **Auto: LOLIN S2 Mini**.

Some boards report only their processor. The CYD, for example, reports itself as a generic ESP32. Pick those boards from the menu by hand. You can also pick a processor without a board, for example **ESP32 (any board)**.

The board menu picks pins, not memory. A classic ESP32 board with no PSRAM can run a GUI flow by flashing the
[custom firmware for classic ESP32](custom-firmware.md), which carries the runtime and the flow libraries in the
firmware.

A board picked by hand stays picked when you reconnect. If you then connect a board with a different processor, the menu goes back to **Auto** and the console says so.

If no board is connected and none is picked, pins are only checked against the range 0–48.

## Seeing a board's pins

Click **Pins…** next to the **Board** menu. It opens the pin cheat sheet, in its own tab, for the board or
processor picked there. The cheat sheet lists, in order:

- the pins the board names, such as its LED
- for boards whose definition has a `header`, such as the Pico family, the physical pins, laid out like the board,
  with power and ground marked
- every pin, with whether it's free, reserved or best avoided, and why
- which pins each SPI and I2C bus can use

The page is read from the definition files each time you click. After changing a file, click **Pins…** again.

If ThingStudio knows the board's processor but not the board, the page shows the processor's pins and says the
board's own ones, like its LED, are missing. It gives a starter file to add them: see
[Adding a board](#adding-a-board). If it doesn't know the processor either, the page says what the board reports:
see [Adding a processor](#adding-a-processor).

## What gets checked

These stop the compile:

- a pin the board or processor doesn't have
- a reserved pin, such as a pin wired to the flash chip
- an output on an input-only pin
- an SPI or I2C bus the processor doesn't have, or a pin that bus can't use
- an SPI speed the processor can't run on those pins

These give a warning, but the flow still compiles:

- a pin to avoid, such as a strapping pin that changes how the board starts
- a pull-up or pull-down on a pin that has no internal pull resistor

A node that needs hardware the board doesn't have, such as an ESP-NOW node on a Pico, is refused the same way. The palette greys out such a node while the board is known.

Warnings appear in the console when you deploy, and at the end of the compiled source.

In the properties panel, a pin field shows the board's name for that pin, such as `LED`. It also flags reserved pins and pins to avoid. On a board whose pins are named rather than numbered, the field is a dropdown of the board's pins. See [Pins that aren't numbers](#pins-that-arent-numbers).

## Built-in boards

| Board | Processor | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Raspberry Pi Pico | RP2040 | LED on GPIO 25 |
| Raspberry Pi Pico W | RP2040 | GPIO 23, 24, 25 and 29 go to the WiFi chip. The LED isn't on a GPIO. |
| Raspberry Pi Pico 2 | RP2350 | GPIO 0–29. LED on GPIO 25. |
| LOLIN S2 Mini | ESP32-S2 | LED on GPIO 15, button on GPIO 0 |
| LuatOS ESP32C3-CORE | ESP32-C3 | Pick by hand. LEDs on GPIO 12 and 13, button on GPIO 9. |
| Kitchen sink (LuatOS ESP32C3-CORE) | ESP32-C3 | Pick by hand. The LuatOS board with a potentiometer (`POT`, GPIO 0), a button (`BUTTON`, GPIO 3) and a NeoPixel (`PIXEL`, GPIO 6) wired on. See [Kitchen-sink board](kitchen-sink-board.md). |
| ESP32-C5-340X (ESP32-C5-KITC-A) | ESP32-C5 | Pick by hand. RGB LED (WS2812) on GPIO 27, button on GPIO 28. Left USB-C is a CH340E on GPIO 11/12, right is native USB on 13/14. If flashing doesn't start: hold BOOT, press RESET, release BOOT. |
| CYD (ESP32-2432S028, ST7789) | ESP32 | Pick by hand. Display, touch, SD, RGB LED and speaker pins are labelled. |
| Freenove ESP32-S3 Display 4.0" (FNK0104S, ST7796) | ESP32-S3 | Pick by hand. Display and touch pins are labelled. 320x480, SPI bus 1. Rotation 1 is portrait. For landscape, set the display's `orientation` to 90 (or 270 for the other way up) and keep the screen and display at 320x480. Display and touch (FT6336U) work. |
| Pyboard v1.0 | STM32F405 | Pins are named `X1`–`X22` and `Y1`–`Y12`. The four onboard LEDs are on `A13`, `A14`, `A15` and `B4` (labelled `LED_RED`–`LED_BLUE`); the user switch `SW` is on `X17`. |
| Seeed XIAO nRF52840 (Sense) | nRF52840 | Pins `D0`–`D10` are labelled. RGB LED on 26, 30 and 6, on when the pin is 0. GPIO 20–25 go to the flash chip. Battery, IMU and microphone pins are labelled; IMU and microphone are on the Sense only. No WiFi. |
| Wemos D1 R32 | ESP32 | Pick by hand. Pins carry their Arduino names, `D0`–`D13` and `A0`–`A5`. A2–A5 are input only. LED on A0 (GPIO 2). |

## Built-in processors

| Processor | GPIO | Reserved |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ESP32 | 0–19, 21–23, 25–27, 32–39 (34–39 input only) | 1, 3 (USB serial), 6–11 (flash) |
| ESP32-S2 | 0–21, 26–46 (46 input only) | 27–32 (flash) |
| ESP32-S3 | 0–21, 26–48 | 27–32 (flash) |
| ESP32-C3 | 0–21 | 12–17 (flash) |
| ESP32-C5 | 0–28 | 16–22 (flash and PSRAM) |
| RP2040 | 0–29 | none |
| RP2350 | 0–47 (0–29 on the RP2350A) | none |
| STM32F405 | X1–X22, Y1–Y12 (named pins, not numbers) | none |
| nRF52840 | 0–47 (P1.x is 32 + x) | none |

The ESP32 runs SPI at up to 27 MHz on most pins. Faster speeds need the bus's own fast pins (SCK 14 and MOSI 13 on bus 1, SCK 18 and MOSI 23 on bus 2).

On the RP2040 and RP2350, each SPI and I2C bus can only use certain pins. The compile error lists the pins that work.

On the nRF52840, any pin works for SPI and I2C. SPI uses buses 2 and 3, up to 8 MHz; I2C uses buses 0 and 1.

The definition files list every pin to avoid, with the reason.

## Your definition files

Definition files live in `~/.thingstudio/boards/` and `~/.thingstudio/processors/`. When ThingStudio starts, it writes
every built-in file there, replacing a file of the same name, so an upgrade's changes arrive on the next start.

To keep your own version of a built-in board, save it under a different name (for example `my-cyd.json`) and give it its
own name in the file. It is then a board of its own in the Board menu, and is never overwritten. Editing a built-in
file in place lasts until the next start.

ThingStudio reads these files when the editor starts, when you connect, and when you deploy. If a file has a mistake, it isn't loaded and the built-in is used instead. The console says what's wrong, and the Board menu lists the file under **Invalid files**.

## Adding a board

Save a JSON file in `~/.thingstudio/boards/`. The file name, without `.json`, is the board's id. Use lowercase letters, digits, `-` and `_`.

A board file can't build on another one. To describe a built-in board with parts you have wired to it, copy the
built-in's file, give it a new file name and `name`, and add a name in `pins` for each part, such as `"POT": 0`.
[Kitchen-sink board](kitchen-sink-board.md) is a built-in made this way.

```json
{
  "name": "My weather station",
  "processor": "esp32-c3",
  "match": [],
  "pins": { "LED": 8, "SENSOR_SDA": 4, "SENSOR_SCL": 5 },
  "avoid": { "9": "Wired to the BOOT button." },
  "notes": "Hand-built, rev 2."
}
```

The fields are:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | Name shown in the Board menu. Required. |
| `processor` | Id of the processor, such as `esp32` or `rp2040`. Required. |
| `match` | Board names MicroPython reports, for Auto. Use `[]` to pick the board by hand. Required. |
| `pins` | Names for pins, shown in the properties panel. Required, can be `{}`. |
| `capabilities` | Hardware this board adds to its processor, such as `["wifi"]`. A board with no radio usually sets `wifi` to `false` instead. |
| `gpio` | The pins this board has, if fewer than its processor. For example `["0-29"]`. |
| `reserved` | Pins that must not be used, each with a reason. |
| `avoid` | Pins that give a warning, each with a reason. |
| `free` | Pins the processor reserves or warns about that are fine on this board. For example `["12-13"]` on an ESP32-C3 board whose flash doesn't use them. |
| `notes` | Anything else worth knowing. |
| `variant` | The MicroPython build that **Tools → Install firmware…** picks for this board, such as `esp32-c3-generic`. Copy it from a built-in board with the same chip, or leave it out. |
| `wifi` | `false` if the board has no WiFi. Hides [connecting over WiFi](wifi-connection.md) for it. Leave it out if unsure. |
| `headerOrder` | `"down"` if the right-hand row is numbered top to bottom, like the left. Leave it out for a header numbered down the left and back up the right, like the Pico's. |
| `usb` | Where the USB connector is, with pin 1 at the top left: `"top"` or `"bottom"`. Shown on the **Pins…** page. Needs `header`. |
| `header` | What each physical pin carries: a pin (a GPIO number, or a named pin), or a label such as `"GND"` or `"3V3"`. Shown on the **Pins…** page. For example `{ "1": 0, "3": "GND", "40": "VBUS" }`. A string that's one of the board's pins is that pin; any other string is a label. |

Naming a pin in `pins` turns off the processor's warning for it, on the grounds that the board uses it on purpose. If the warning still matters, such as a strapping pin on a shield header, repeat it in the board's `avoid`.

Numbers in `header` are physical pin numbers, as printed on the board or its datasheet. A header numbered 1 to N
is drawn in two columns, like the Pico's. For a board with several connectors, name the pins `"P3-1"` and so on.

Pin lists take numbers and ranges: `[0, 2, "4-7"]`. In `reserved` and `avoid`, the key is a pin or a range: `{ "6-11": "Wired to the flash chip." }`. A processor whose pins are named uses the names in the same places: see [Pins that aren't numbers](#pins-that-arent-numbers).

To find the name MicroPython reports, connect the board and look for `chipType` in the console's `[HELLO]` line. The board name is the part before " with ".

## Adding a processor

Save a JSON file in `~/.thingstudio/processors/`, named the same way as a board file. The built-in files in that folder are good examples.

The fields are:

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | Name shown in the Board menu. Required. |
| `match` | Text in the processor name MicroPython reports, such as `ESP32S3`. Case, spaces and `-` are ignored. Required. |
| `nativeArch` | The mpy-cross `-march` value, such as `xtensawin`. Required. |
| `gpio` | Every pin the processor has. Numbers, or names on a processor whose pins aren't numbered. Required. |
| `inputOnly` | Pins that can't drive an output. |
| `noPull` | Pins without internal pull resistors. |
| `capabilities` | Hardware the chip has, such as `["wifi", "ble", "espnow"]` or `["pio"]`. A node that needs one the board lacks is refused. |
| `adc2` | Pins on a second ADC that can't be used while WiFi is up (ESP32 family). |
| `reserved`, `avoid` | As for boards. |
| `spi`, `i2c` | Bus numbers, pins each bus can use, and SPI speed limits. |

## Pins that aren't numbers

Some processors, such as the STM32 on a pyboard, name their pins (`X1`, `A13`) instead of numbering them. In a definition file, a pin is either a number, a range `"4-7"`, or a name: a string that starts with a letter and contains only letters, digits, `_` and `-`. Names go wherever numbers do — `gpio`, `pins`, `reserved`, `avoid`, a bus's pins — and a list can mix both. Ranges work for numbers only; list named pins one by one.

```json
{
  "name": "Pyboard",
  "match": ["STM32F405"],
  "nativeArch": "armv7emsp",
  "gpio": ["X1", "X2", "X3", "X4", "Y1", "Y2", "Y3", "Y4"]
}
```

In the editor, a pin field on a named-pin board is a dropdown of the board's pins rather than a number input.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/kitchen-sink-board/

# Kitchen-sink board

How to wire a test board for the input and output nodes: a potentiometer, a push button and a NeoPixel on a LuatOS
ESP32C3-CORE. Tutorials that need hardware beyond an LED use these parts on these pins, so a flow from one tutorial
runs on a board wired for another. Wire all of it, or only the parts a tutorial needs.

## What you need

- A LuatOS ESP32C3-CORE, the version with a USB-serial chip (CH343). The version with native USB works too, but
  needs GPIO 18 and 19 left free.
- A 10 kΩ potentiometer. Any value from 1 kΩ to 100 kΩ works.
- A push button.
- One WS2812 (NeoPixel) LED, on a breakout or as part of a strip.
- Hookup wire, and a breadboard or stripboard.

## Wiring

The parts connect to these pins. The header pin is the number on the board's pin list; **Pins…** in the editor
shows where each one is.

| Part | Connection | GPIO | Header pin | Name in the editor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Potentiometer | one end | — | 13 (3V3) | |
| | wiper (middle) | 0 | 2 | `POT` |
| | other end | — | 1 (GND) | |
| Push button | one side | 3 | 20 | `BUTTON` |
| | other side | — | 17 (GND) | |
| WS2812 | DIN | 6 | 22 | `PIXEL` |
| | 5V | — | 16 or 31 (5V) | |
| | GND | — | 14 or 32 (GND) | |

The button needs no resistor: set the `ebutton` node's **pull** to `up`. The board also has two LEDs of its own,
`LED_D4` (GPIO 12) and `LED_D5` (GPIO 13), and the `BOOT` button (GPIO 9), so a flow can use those with nothing
wired.

## Pick the board

Choose **Kitchen sink (LuatOS ESP32C3-CORE)** from the **Board** menu. The board reports itself as a generic ESP32-C3,
so Auto can't find it. Pin fields then show `POT`, `BUTTON` and `PIXEL` next to their numbers.

## Check each part

Wire one node to a `debug` node, or to a `neopixel` node, and deploy:

- **Potentiometer**: an `adc` node on pin 0. Turning the knob sends readings to the console.
- **Button**: an `ebutton` node on pin 3, **pull** `up`. Pressing it sends `press` and `release`.
- **NeoPixel**: a `startup` node with **payload type** `number` and **value** `8192` (`0x002000`), into a
  `neopixel` node on pin 6 with **count** 1. The LED lights dim green.

## Other pins

To put the parts on other pins, keep these points in mind:

- **Potentiometer**: GPIO 0–4 can read a voltage. GPIO 5 can too, but not while WiFi is on.
- **Avoid** GPIO 2, 8 and 9: they decide how the board starts. GPIO 11 powers the flash chip.
- **Rename pins** by saving a copy of the board's file under a new name: see
  [Adding a board](boards.md#adding-a-board).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/custom-firmware/

# Custom firmware

A ThingStudio custom image is MicroPython with ThingStudio's runtime and every flow library built in. Stock
MicroPython loads the runtime, the libraries and the flow into RAM. With a custom image, the runtime and libraries
run from flash instead, which leaves the RAM for the flow. On a small board, that is the difference between a flow
starting and failing with `MemoryError`.

There is one image per chip:

| Chip | Image | Written at |
|---|---|---|
| classic ESP32, 4 MB, no PSRAM | `thingstudio-classic-esp32-…bin` | 0x0 |
| ESP32-C3, 4 MB | `thingstudio-esp32-c3-…bin` | 0x0 |
| ESP32-C5, 4 MB, no PSRAM | `thingstudio-esp32-c5-…bin` | 0x2000 |

On stock MicroPython, flows that fit in memory run as usual. [Back to stock MicroPython](#back-to-stock-micropython)
says how to return to it.

The technique works on any board that runs MicroPython: freeze the runtime and the flow libraries into the
firmware. `firmware/` in the repository builds these images, and its README says how to add a chip.

## What it changes

The runtime and the flow libraries are frozen into the firmware, so MicroPython runs them from flash instead of
copying them into RAM.

Because the libraries are already there, Deploy does not send them. The console says so after connecting:

```
[libraries] this flow uses font_body12, … st7796py -- already on the board: font_body12, … st7796py
```

Two things follow from that:

- Deploying over a running flow fits where stock MicroPython runs out. On stock MicroPython, the runtime, the
  libraries and the flow fight over the same memory: an ESP32-C5 redeploying a BLE flow fails with `MemoryError`.
  On the custom image, the same board redeploys it with 100 KB to spare.
- The first deploy after flashing has more memory to work with than any later one. Judge a flow by a deploy over
  another flow, not by the first one.

The image carries no board-specific settings. Pins and displays come from the [board definition](boards.md), so
one image serves any board with that chip.

Each image is rebuilt and tested on a board at every runtime version. The runtime version an image carries is its
**Version** in the Install firmware dialog.

## What you need

- A board with one of the chips in the table above. The S2, S3 and C6 have no custom image, and neither do RP2040
  or RP2350 boards.
- A USB cable that carries data.

## Install from the editor

Flashing erases the board: its saved flow and all settings are gone afterwards.

1. Put the board in download mode if it needs it: hold **BOOT** and tap **RESET**.
2. Choose **Tools → Install firmware…**, pick **Serial port**, then the board's port.
3. Set **Chip family** to the board's chip and **Firmware** to **ThingStudio custom image**. If there is no
   **ThingStudio custom image** for the chip, no image for it has been published yet: use official MicroPython.
4. Pick a **Version**. Each version listed ran on a board before it was published, and the editor checks the
   download against its recorded SHA-256 before writing it.
5. Click **Flash**. The editor writes the image at the address in the table above.
6. [Connect](connecting.md), then choose **Tools → Install runtime…**. It writes only the boot script, `main.py`:
   the runtime is already in the image.

## Install by hand

You need `esptool` and `mpremote` on the computer: `pip install esptool mpremote`.

Each image is attached to the ThingStudio release it was published with. On the
[releases page](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases), open the release whose assets include the image
version you want (the versions are the ones the editor lists), and download three files from it: the image for your
chip, its `.sha256` file and `main.py`.

1. Put the three files in one folder and go there. Check the image against its checksum:

   ```sh
   IMAGE=$(ls thingstudio-*.bin)   # the image you downloaded
   shasum -a 256 -c "$IMAGE.sha256"      # sha256sum -c on Linux
   ```

2. Put the board in download mode if your board needs it, then write the image. Use the chip and address from the
   table above. For a classic ESP32:

   ```sh
   esptool.py --chip esp32 --port /dev/ttyUSB0 write_flash 0x0 "$IMAGE"
   ```

   For an ESP32-C5, `--chip esp32c5` and `0x2000`. Written at 0, a C5 does not boot. On macOS the port looks like
   `/dev/cu.usbserial-14420`. On Windows it is `COM3` or similar.

   To write the downloaded image from the editor instead, use **Or use your own image file** in **Tools → Install
   firmware…** and set **Address**, under **Install options**, to the one in the table. Without it, a classic ESP32
   image goes at the family's `0x1000` and the board does not boot.

3. If you held **BOOT** to get into download mode, press **RESET** now: without it the board stays in its
   bootloader, and `mpremote` fails with `could not enter raw repl`. Then write the boot script, the one file that
   lives on the filesystem rather than in the image:

   ```sh
   mpremote connect /dev/ttyUSB0 fs cp main.py :/main.py
   ```

   `main.py` starts the runtime that is frozen into the firmware. A board with the image and no `main.py` starts at
   the Python prompt instead. The image carries the list of libraries it froze, so Deploy skips them without a file
   on the board.

4. Reset the board. It starts the listener and prints `LISTENER_READY`.

The repository also has `firmware/install.sh`, which runs these steps in one command
(`PORT=/dev/ttyUSB0 firmware/install.sh esp32-c5`). Read it before running it: it erases the filesystem partition,
and its port name comes from `PORT`.

## Connect and deploy

Connect in the editor as usual. Two things confirm the image is running:

- the console's version line reports the image's runtime version, as listed under **Version** in the Install
  firmware dialog
- `[libraries] … already on the board: …` names every library the flow imports

Then deploy the flow.

## Memory and the board

The image does not add RAM. Measured on the CYD (classic ESP32-D0WD, 4 MB, no PSRAM) with a GUI flow, in KB:

| Board state | MicroPython free | Largest block | ESP-IDF free | ESP-IDF largest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Just booted, no flow | 142 | 105 | 129 | 108 |
| GUI flow running | 108 | 50 | 70 | 52 |
| GUI flow running, after two more deploys | 120 | 27 | 18 | 14 |

Read the third row before leaning on deploys: each deploy over a running flow leaves the heaps more fragmented, and
the chip's own heap shrinks as MicroPython takes from it. WiFi and Bluetooth draw from that chip heap, and the
console warns when it is low.

The C3 and C5, measured with each flow running after deploying it over itself, in KB:

| Board | Flow | MicroPython free | ESP-IDF free | ESP-IDF largest |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ESP32-C3 module | MQTT over WiFi | 114 | 36 | 28 |
| ESP32-C5-340X | MQTT over WiFi | 94 | 29 | 17 |
| ESP32-C5-340X | BLE central | 113 | 108 | 88 |

WiFi takes the most from the chip's heap.

Keeping frames small and recovering from a `MemoryError` are covered in [Memory](debugging.md#memory) and
[MemoryError or a library that won't load](debugging.md#memoryerror-or-a-library-that-wont-load).

## Back to stock MicroPython

[Install MicroPython](installing-micropython.md) with a standard build for the board, then
[install the runtime](installing-runtime.md) again. Flashing erases the board's flows and settings, as above.

## Reporting a problem

Reports on any board with these chips are welcome, listed or not. Include the board's name and the console's
version and `[memory]` lines from a fresh boot.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/wifi-connection/

# Connecting over WiFi

The editor can connect to a board over WiFi instead of USB. Once connected over WiFi, everything works the same as
over USB: deploy, the console, **Tools → Check status**, and clicking an inject node.

## What you need

- A board with WiFi and the ThingStudio runtime. Plain Raspberry Pi Pico and Pico 2 boards have no
  WiFi.
- A flow on the board that uses WiFi and has joined your network. The board is only reachable while that flow is
  running. It starts again by itself after a reset.
- A board password, set over USB.
- This computer on the same network as the board.
- On a Mac, ThingStudio started from Apple's Terminal app. See [If it doesn't connect](#if-it-doesnt-connect).

## Set the password and name

1. Connect the board over USB.
2. Choose **Tools → Board settings…**. The top line names the board these settings apply to: its chip, USB port and current name.
3. Enter a network name and a password of 8 to 64 characters, then click **Save to board**.

The name and password are stored on the board, not in the flow. The editor also remembers the password on this
computer. A board with no password only accepts USB.

A new name is used from the next time the board joins WiFi. Reset the board to use it straight away.

## Connect

Click **⟳** next to the port list. Boards on your network appear in the port menu under **WiFi**. Pick one and click
**Connect**.

If the board isn't listed, choose **WiFi address…** and type its name (for example `kitchen` or `kitchen.local`)
or its IP address.

If this computer has no saved password for the board, the editor asks for it.

A board with no password is listed as **no password set**. It won't accept a WiFi connection until you set one.

Connected over USB, the console says whether the board can take a WiFi connection now:

```text
[wifi] kitchen is on a network at 192.168.1.42 (kitchen.local): you can connect over WiFi
[wifi] kitchen is not on a network: WiFi connects need a running flow that joins one
```

## Good to know

- Only one editor can connect over WiFi at a time.
- Board settings can only be changed over USB.
- Installing the runtime and **Tools → Remove flow…** need USB.
- If the board loses power or leaves WiFi range, the editor shows it disconnected within about 30 seconds.
- Deploying a flow that doesn't use WiFi takes the board off the network at its next reset.
- The password is never sent over the network, but the connection isn't encrypted. Use it on a network you
  trust.

## If it doesn't connect

The console says what went wrong:

- **No route to host (Mac):** macOS is blocking local network access. The first time ThingStudio reaches for the
  network, macOS asks whether it may find devices on your local network; choose **Allow**, then click **Connect**
  again (the attempt that raised the question can fail). If you chose **Don't Allow**, turn **thingstudio-python**
  on in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Local Network, then restart ThingStudio. When running from source
  (`thingstudio-backend`), macOS may block it without asking: start it from Apple's **Terminal** app instead, which
  macOS always allows.
- **No answer:** check the board is on, its flow has joined WiFi, and this computer is on the
  same network. If a `.local` name doesn't work, try the IP address, shown in the console when you connect over USB.
- **Wrong password:** the editor asks again. To change it, connect over USB and use **Tools → Board settings…**.
- **Already has a network session:** another editor is connected. Disconnect it first.
- **No password set** or **Connection refused:** the board has no password, so it only accepts USB. Set one over
  USB in **Tools → Board settings…**, then click **⟳**.
- **Board not listed:** click **⟳** again. If it's still missing, check its flow has joined WiFi, or use
  **WiFi address…**. If the console says the WiFi scan didn't run, the reason follows; on a Mac it's usually
  the Local Network permission (see **No route to host** above).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/wifi-provisioning/

# WiFi provisioning

You can leave a flow's WiFi network and password out, and enter them on the board when it first starts. Use this
for a board you hand to someone else, or one that goes on a network you don't have the password for.

## Turning it on

In the flow's WiFi config, set **security** to **Unmanaged** and leave the **credential** blank. See
[Config nodes](working-in-the-editor.md#config-nodes). Deploy as usual.

A flow with MQTT nodes can't use **Unmanaged**: an MQTT node connects to the network itself, so the network's name
and password must be in the flow.

## Entering the network on the board

When the board starts with no saved network, it opens its own WiFi network, **Thingstudio-Setup-XXXX**, with the
password `thingstudio`:

1. Connect a phone or laptop to **Thingstudio-Setup-XXXX**. Most phones open the setup page by themselves. If not,
   browse to `http://192.168.4.1/`.
2. Pick your network from the list, or type its name. Some boards' scans miss nearby networks, so typing always
   works.
3. Enter the password and submit.

Once the board connects, it saves the network and joins it on every later start. If nobody enters a network within
10 minutes, the board carries on starting without WiFi.

## Reopening setup when WiFi fails

By default, setup only runs while no network is saved. If the saved network later becomes unreachable, the board
stays disconnected.

Tick **Allow reprovisioning on connect failure** in the WiFi config to reopen the setup network whenever the saved
network fails. Only do this on a network you control: while the setup network is open, anyone in range who knows its
password can point the board at a different network.

## Changing the setup network's password

There's no field for it in the editor. Connect to the board and type this in the command box under the console
(see [Commands and the Python prompt](debugging.md#commands-and-the-python-prompt)):

```python
import wifi_provision; wifi_provision.set_ap_password('yournewpassword')
```

Then choose **Tools → Reset board (hard)**. Use at least 8 characters: with fewer, the setup network doesn't open.
Set it to `'thingstudio'` to go back to the default.

## Starting over

To make the board forget its saved network and run setup again, type this in the command box, then reset the
board:

```python
import os; os.remove('/_wifi_provision.json')
```

This also clears a changed setup password.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/

# Node reference

Every built-in node has its own page, covering what it does, its properties and its output. This page lists them
all, grouped as in the editor's palette: General, Network and Hardware.

## Kinds of node

Each node is one of three kinds. The kind decides where it can sit in a flow.

- **Source**: starts a message. Has no input. Every chain in a flow begins with one.
- **Transform**: takes a message in, and passes it on, changed, delayed or not at all.
- **Sink**: takes a message in and acts on it. Has no output.

See [flows, nodes and messages](../background/flows-and-nodes.md) for how they fit together.

## Which node do I need?

| To… | Use |
| --- | --- |
| do something at a fixed interval | [timer](timer.md) |
| do something once, when the flow starts | [startup](startup.md) |
| send a test message by hand | [inject](inject.md) |
| respond to a pin changing | [interrupt](interrupt.md), [eswitch](eswitch.md) |
| respond to presses, long presses and double clicks | [ebutton](ebutton.md) |
| read an analog input | [adc](adc.md) |
| read a rotary knob | [encoder](encoder.md) |
| drive an LED strip | [neopixel](neopixel.md) |
| switch an LED or relay | [gpio out](gpio-out.md) |
| dim an LED or set a motor's speed | [pwm out](pwm-out.md) |
| read a temperature, humidity or pressure sensor | [bme280](bme280.md) |
| talk to another I2C device, or find its address | [i2c device](i2c.md) |
| draw on a display | [display spi](display-spi.md), [display i2c](display-i2c.md) |
| show readings as pages on a display | [GUI nodes](gui.md) |
| change a message, or decide where it goes | [function](function.md) |
| set or clear a value between messages | [change](change.md) |
| send only changes, or limit the rate | [filter](filter.md) |
| keep a number's history and show its histogram | [journal](journal.md) |
| show the time of day | [ntp](ntp.md) |
| wait before passing a message on | [delay](delay.md) |
| see what's in a message | [debug](debug.md) |
| send or receive MQTT messages | [mqtt publish](mqtt-publish.md), [mqtt subscribe](mqtt-subscribe.md) |
| call a web API | [http request](http-request.md) |
| serve a web page or API from the board | [http in](http-in.md) and [http response](http-response.md) |
| send or receive UDP packets | [udp send](udp-send.md), [udp receive](udp-receive.md) |
| read BLE beacons and sensors | [ble scan](ble-scan.md) |
| broadcast a reading over Bluetooth | [ble advertise](ble-advertise.md) |
| let a phone, computer or another board read or set a value | [ble characteristic out](ble-characteristic-out.md), [ble characteristic in](ble-characteristic-in.md) |
| send and receive text with a Bluetooth terminal app | [ble uart in](ble-uart-in.md), [ble uart out](ble-uart-out.md) |
| read from, write to, or listen to a BLE sensor or another board | [ble read](ble-read.md), [ble write](ble-write.md), [ble notify](ble-notify.md) |
| know when WiFi connects or drops | [wifi status](wifi-status.md) |
| stop messages while WiFi is down | [wifi gate](wifi-gate.md) |

## General

Nodes that don't need a network or hardware:

| Node | Kind | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [inject](inject.md) | source | Sends one message with a fixed payload when you click it in the editor. |
| [startup](startup.md) | source | Sends one message each time the flow starts. |
| [timer](timer.md) | source | Sends a rising count at a fixed interval. |
| [function](function.md) | transform | Runs your own MicroPython on each message. |
| [delay](delay.md) | transform | Passes each message on after a set wait. |
| [filter](filter.md) | transform | Passes a message on only if it changed enough, or enough time has passed. |
| [change](change.md) | transform | Sets or deletes one message property or flow variable. |
| [journal](journal.md) | transform | Keeps the recent history of a number as average, min and max rows, for a histogram. |
| [debug](debug.md) | sink | Prints a message to the editor's console. |

## Network

These nodes share the flow's WiFi network. A flow has one, set on any WiFi node's **WiFi** field.

| Node | Kind | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [wifi status](wifi-status.md) | source | Reports when the WiFi connection comes up or goes down. |
| [wifi gate](wifi-gate.md) | transform | Passes a message on only while WiFi is connected. |
| [ntp](ntp.md) | in and out | Sets the board's clock from the internet and sends the time. |
| [mqtt subscribe](mqtt-subscribe.md) | source | Sends a message for each MQTT message on a topic. |
| [mqtt publish](mqtt-publish.md) | sink | Publishes a message's payload to an MQTT topic. |
| [http request](http-request.md) | transform | Makes an HTTP request per message and passes on the response. |
| [http in](http-in.md) | source | Serves HTTP from the board, sending a message for each request. |
| [http response](http-response.md) | sink | Answers a request that arrived through `http in`. |
| [udp receive](udp-receive.md) | source | Sends a message for each UDP packet received on a port. |
| [udp send](udp-send.md) | sink | Sends a message's payload as a UDP packet. |

## Bluetooth

These nodes need a board with Bluetooth LE: ESP32, ESP32-S3, ESP32-C3 or ESP32-C5. They share the board's one radio.

| Node | Kind | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [ble scan](ble-scan.md) | source | Sends a message for each Bluetooth LE advertisement nearby. |
| [ble advertise](ble-advertise.md) | sink | Advertises the board's name and a payload over Bluetooth LE. |
| [ble characteristic in](ble-characteristic-in.md) | source | Sends a message when a connected device writes a characteristic. |
| [ble characteristic out](ble-characteristic-out.md) | sink | Sets a characteristic a connected device can read, and notifies it. |
| [ble uart in](ble-uart-in.md) | source | Receives text lines from a Bluetooth terminal app. |
| [ble uart out](ble-uart-out.md) | sink | Sends text to a Bluetooth terminal app. |
| [ble read](ble-read.md) | transform | Reads a characteristic of another BLE device. |
| [ble write](ble-write.md) | sink | Writes to a characteristic of another BLE device. |
| [ble notify](ble-notify.md) | source | Sends each value another BLE device notifies. |

The board's Bluetooth name is set once, in the [BLE config](ble.md). The devices the board connects to are
[BLE peers](ble-peer.md).

## Hardware

Pin numbers are checked against your board before a deploy. See [boards and processors](../boards.md).

| Node | Kind | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [interrupt](interrupt.md) | source | Fires the moment a pin changes. |
| [eswitch](eswitch.md) | source | Reports a debounced switch opening or closing. |
| [ebutton](ebutton.md) | source | Reports presses, releases, long presses and double clicks. |
| [adc](adc.md) | source | Reads an analog pin, sending when the reading moves past its bounds. |
| [encoder](encoder.md) | source | Reports a rotary knob's value as it turns. |
| [neopixel](neopixel.md) | sink | Lights a WS2812 / NeoPixel strip. |
| [gpio out](gpio-out.md) | sink | Sets a pin high or low. |
| [pwm out](pwm-out.md) | sink | Drives a pin with a variable duty cycle. |
| [bme280](bme280.md) | source | Reads a BME280 or BMP280 sensor at a fixed interval. |
| [i2c device](i2c.md) | transform | Reads, writes or scans an I2C device that has no node of its own. |
| [display spi](display-spi.md) | sink | Sends a frame to an SPI color display (ST7789). |
| [display i2c](display-i2c.md) | sink | Sends a frame to an I2C OLED display (SSD1306). |

### Hardware is shared

Each pin, PWM output, I2C bus and SPI bus is set up once, and every node that uses it shares that one setup. Two nodes
can use the same pin only if they set it up the same way. For example, an `interrupt` and an `eswitch` can both read
an input pin with no pull, but a `gpio out` can't drive a pin an `eswitch` reads. When two nodes clash, the compile
stops and names both.

A [function](function.md) or [custom](../custom-nodes.md#pins-and-buses) node gets the same objects with
`runtime.shared()`, for example `runtime.shared('i2c', 0)`.

## Shared settings

Some settings are set once and shared by the nodes that use them:

- **WiFi network** and **MQTT broker**: config nodes, with the real passwords kept outside the flow file. See
  [config nodes](../working-in-the-editor.md#config-nodes).
- **I2C bus**: the pins and clock for a bus, shared by every I2C node on it. See [I2C bus](i2c-bus.md).
- **BLE**: the board's Bluetooth name, shared by the ble nodes. See [BLE](ble.md).
- **BLE peer**: a device the board connects to, shared by the nodes that use it. See [BLE peer](ble-peer.md).
- **Touch panel**: the controller, bus and size of a touch screen, used by a gui screen or a touch node. See
  [touch panels](touch-panel.md).

## Something missing?

A [function](function.md) node covers most gaps: a comparison, a sum, a calculation on a reading. For
something you'll use again, [write a custom node](../custom-nodes.md).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/inject/

# inject

Sends one message with a fixed payload each time you click its ▶ icon while the editor is connected to the board.

## Properties

- **payload type** — `bool`, `number` or `string`. Default `bool`. The output's type follows it, so the editor
  checks the wire against the input it feeds (see [Wiring](../working-in-the-editor.md#wiring)).
- **value** — the value to send, read as the payload type (see
  [Typed values](../working-in-the-editor.md#typed-values)). Default `true`.

## Wiring

**Input** — none. `inject` is a source.

**Output** — a message with `payload` set to the value and `topic` set to an empty string.

## Behavior

The ▶ icon and the rest of the node are separate click targets. The ▶ fires the node. A click anywhere else on the
node opens its property panel, connected or not.

Each click sends one message. `inject` never fires on its own, neither on a schedule nor when the flow starts, so a
flow whose only sources are `inject` nodes does nothing until you click one. To send a message when the flow starts,
use [startup](startup.md). To send one repeatedly, use [timer](timer.md).

## Errors

- **The editor isn't connected.** The console shows `[inject: connect to a device first -- clicking only fires while
  live]` and nothing is sent.
- **The value isn't a number,** with payload type `number`. The deploy goes through; the click fails on the board with
  a `[NODE_ERROR]` naming this node and `inject value 'abc' is not a valid number`. See
  [Reading a node error](../debugging.md#reading-a-node-error).
- **A node error in this node's chain** stops the chain. See
  [Reading a node error](../debugging.md#reading-a-node-error).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/startup/

# startup

Sends one message with a fixed payload each time the flow starts.

## Properties

- **payload type** — `bool`, `number`, `string` or `start reason`. Default `bool`.
- **value** — the value to send, read as the payload type (see
  [Typed values](../working-in-the-editor.md#typed-values)). Default `true`. Hidden with `start reason`.

## Wiring

**Input** — none. `startup` is a source.

**Output** — a message with `payload` set to the value, `topic` set to an empty string, and `reason` saying why the
flow started. With payload type `start reason`, the payload is that same string.

| reason | the flow started because |
| --- | --- |
| `deploy` | you clicked Deploy |
| `power_on` | the board was powered up |
| `hard_reset` | the reset button was pressed |
| `watchdog` | a watchdog timer reset the board |
| `deep_sleep` | the board woke from deep sleep |
| `soft_reset` | software restarted the board, for example `machine.reset()` |
| `unknown` | the board can't tell |

Not every board reports every reason. ESP32 boards report the reset button as `power_on`, because on those
chips the button cuts power to the core.

## Behavior

The flow starts after every deploy and each time the board starts (see [Deploy](../flow-lifecycle.md#deploy)), so
`startup` fires even when the editor isn't connected. Use it for setup work, such as setting an output to a known
state or drawing a first screen.

It fires once per start and never repeats. For a message you send by hand, use [inject](inject.md). For a repeating
one, use [timer](timer.md).

## Errors

- **The value isn't a number,** with payload type `number`. The deploy goes through; when the flow starts, the
  console shows a `[NODE_ERROR]` naming this node and `startup value 'abc' is not a valid number`.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/timer/

# timer

Sends a count that goes up by one at a fixed interval.

## Properties

- **interval (ms)** — the time between messages, in milliseconds. Default 1000. A whole number, 1 or more.

## Wiring

**Input** — none. `timer` is a source.

**Output** — a message with `payload` set to the count, an `int`: 1, 2, 3 and so on. `topic` is an empty string.

## Behavior

The first message goes out as soon as the flow starts, then one each interval. The interval starts once the previous
message has finished going through the chain, so a slow node after the timer, such as a [delay](delay.md), adds its
time to every interval.

Each `timer` node keeps its own count, starting at 1 when the flow starts, even when two share an interval.

## Errors

- **The interval is less than 1.** Deploy stops with `property "intervalMs" 0 is below its minimum, 1`, naming the
  node.
- **The interval isn't a whole number.** Deploy stops with `"intervalMs" must be a whole number of milliseconds`,
  naming the node.
- **A node error in this node's chain** stops the chain. See
  [Reading a node error](../debugging.md#reading-a-node-error).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/function/

# function

Runs your own MicroPython on each message, for anything no other node does.

## Properties

- **code** — the body of a Python function, run once for each message. Default `msg['payload'] = msg['payload']`
  followed by `return msg`. Required.
- **outputs** — how many outputs the node has, 1 to 10. Default 1. `outputCount` in the flow file.

## Wiring

**Input** — any message, as `msg`: a dict with the main value in `msg['payload']`.

**Output** — what the code returns. Return the message to pass it on, or return `None` or nothing to stop it. Every
output has type `any` (see [Wiring](../working-in-the-editor.md#wiring)).

With more than one output, return a list with one entry per output, as in Node-RED:

```python
if msg['payload'] > 100:
    return [msg, None]   # output 1 only
return [None, msg]       # output 2 only
```

The returned list is read entry by entry:

- `None` sends nothing on that output.
- A list of messages sends each of them on that output, in order: `return [[msg1, msg2], None]`.
- A list shorter than the number of outputs leaves the rest empty. Entries past the last output are ignored.
- A plain `return msg`, not in a list, goes to output 1.

With one output, a returned list is passed on as the message itself. Set **outputs** to 2 or more to use the list.

## Behavior

The code is the body of an `async def`, so `return` and `await` work at its top level. `asyncio` and `runtime` are
already defined; import anything else in the code, such as `import machine`. A library ThingStudio provides, such as
`mqtt_as`, is installed on the board when you deploy (see [Libraries](../flow-lifecycle.md#libraries)).

Don't call `time.sleep()` or run a long loop: either stops every other chain while it runs. Use
`await asyncio.sleep(1)` instead (see [The one rule: don't block](../background/event-driven.md#the-one-rule-dont-block)).

Local variables start again for every message. Keep values between messages in `context`, `flow` or `settings`.

### Context, flow and settings

Three stores keep values between messages, each with `get(name, default)` and `set(name, value)`:

- **`context`** — this node only. Two `function` nodes using the same name don't share it.
- **`flow`** — shared by every `function` and [change](change.md) node in the flow, by name.
- **`settings`** — saved on the board, so it survives a restart and a redeploy of the same flow. It is
  `runtime.settings`; see [Persisting values](../custom-nodes.md#persisting-values) for what else it does.

`context` and `flow` start empty each time the flow starts.

```python
count = context.get('count', 0) + 1
context.set('count', count)
msg['payload'] = count
return msg
```

## Errors

- **The code is empty.** Deploy stops with `function node's code is empty`.
- **The code has a syntax error.** Deploy stops and highlights the node.
- **The code raises an exception.** The console shows a `[NODE_ERROR]` naming this node and the exception, and the
  chain stops. See [Reading a node error](../debugging.md#reading-a-node-error).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/change/

# change

Sets or deletes one value, on the message or in a flow variable, then passes the message on.

## Properties

- **operation** — `set` or `delete`. Default `set`.
- **target** — `msg property` or `flow variable`. Default `msg property`.
- **property / name** — the message property or flow variable to change. Default `payload`. Required. A leading
  `msg.` or `flow.` is dropped. The name is one top-level key: `payload.temp` names a property called
  `payload.temp`, not `temp` inside `payload`.
- **value from** — with `set`: `a literal value`, `another msg property` or `a flow variable`. Default
  `a literal value`.
- **literal type** — with a literal: `string`, `number` or `bool`. Default `string`.
- **value / source property** — with `set`: the literal, or the name of the message property or flow variable to
  copy. Default empty. A literal is read as the literal type (see
  [Typed values](../working-in-the-editor.md#typed-values)).

## Wiring

**Input** — any message.

**Output** — the same message, changed when the target is a message property.

## Behavior

One rule per node. Chain `change` nodes for more than one change.

A flow variable is shared by name with every other `change` node and with a [function](function.md) node's
`flow.get` and `flow.set`. There is no node-private store here; use a `function` node's `context` for that.

Copying a property or flow variable that doesn't exist sets the target to `None`. Deleting one that doesn't exist
does nothing.

## Errors

These stop the deploy:

- No property or flow variable name: `change needs a property or variable name`.
- No source name when copying: `change needs a source property or variable name`.
- A `number` literal that isn't a number: `change value "abc" is not a valid number`.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/delay/

# delay

Passes each message on unchanged, after a wait.

## Properties

- **delay (ms)** — how long to hold each message, in milliseconds. Default 1000. Must be 1 or more. A fraction is
  rounded down.

## Wiring

**Input** — any message.

**Output** — the same message, after the wait.

## Behavior

The wait holds the whole chain the message is in, back to its source. The source sends nothing new until the
message has gone all the way through. A [timer](timer.md) set to 200 ms, wired into a 5000 ms `delay`, sends a
message every 5.2 seconds, not every 200 ms.

Messages from different chains don't wait for each other, even when they pass through the same `delay` node.

## Errors

- **The delay is less than 1.** Deploy stops with `property "delayMs" 0 is below its minimum, 1`, naming the node.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/filter/

# filter

Passes a message on only when it's worth sending, and drops the rest. Messages that pass are unchanged.

## Properties

- **mode** — what counts as worth sending. Default `change`.
    - `change` — the payload differs from the last one passed.
    - `deadband` — the payload is a number that has moved at least **threshold** from the last one passed, up or
      down.
    - `rate` — at least **interval** has passed since the last message passed.
- **threshold** — for `deadband`. Default 1. Must be 0 or more. With 0, every number passes, changed or not.
- **interval (ms)** — for `rate`. Default 1000. Must be 1 or more.
- **ignore first message** — for `change` and `deadband`. Default off. When on, the first message only sets the
  starting value.
- **separately for each topic** — default on. Each `msg.topic` is filtered on its own, with its own last value and
  its own first message.

## Wiring

**Input** — any message.

**Output** — the message, unchanged, when it passes.

## Behavior

`change` compares payloads with Python's `==`, so `1` and `1.0` count as the same.

`deadband` compares with the last value it let through, not the last one it received, so a slow drift passes once it
adds up to the threshold. It reads text such as `"21.5"` as a number, so it works on MQTT payloads; the message still
goes out as the original text. Anything else, including `true` and `false`, is dropped.

`rate` drops extra messages. It doesn't queue them or send them later. The first message always passes.

The node tracks up to 32 topics. After that it forgets them all and starts again, and prints
`FILTER_INFO node=ID more than 32 topics, starting again` once.

## Errors

- **`deadband` gets something that isn't a number.** The message is dropped and the console shows a `[NODE_ERROR]`
  naming this node and `deadband needs a number, got str 'abc'`. It is reported once, then again only after a number
  has arrived. The chain keeps running.
- **A threshold below 0 or an interval below 1.** Deploy stops, naming the node and the property.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/journal/

# journal

Keeps the recent history of a number, as rows of average, minimum and maximum, the way RRDtool and Cacti do. Wire
it to a [histogram](gui.md#histogram) to see the history, and to another journal for a longer time scale.

## Properties

- **rows kept** — how many rows the history holds, 1 to 256. Default 60. At 12 bytes a row, 156 rows is under 2 KB.
- **seconds per row** — a row closes once this much time has passed, and holds the average, minimum and maximum of
  the readings in it. Default 60. **0** makes every message one row, which is what a journal fed by another journal
  wants.
- **rows per roll-up** — how many rows go into each roll-up on output 2. Default 0, which sends no roll-up.
- **gaps allowed in a roll-up** — shown when **rows per roll-up** is above 0. From 0 to 1, default 0.5. If more
  than this fraction of the rows in a roll-up are gaps, the roll-up is a gap too. Averages use the known rows only;
  a gap is never counted as zero.

## Wiring

**Input** — `msg.payload` is a number. Text such as `"21.5"` is read as a number, and `True` and `False` as 1 and 0.
A message that also carries `min` and `max`, such as another journal's roll-up, is folded in with them, so a longer
time scale keeps the spikes. With **seconds per row** at 0, a payload of `None` records a gap.

**Output 1, series** — sent each time a row is added. The payload is the journal itself, to wire to a histogram. It
is the live history, not a copy, so it costs no memory per row.

**Output 2, roll-up** — sent every **rows per roll-up** rows: `payload` the average, `min`, `max`, and the input's
`topic`. A gap roll-up has `None` in all three. Wire it to another journal, a readout or MQTT.

## Behavior

A gap is empty, never a copy of the last value. A row with no readings in it is a gap, so choose a row longer than
your sensor's interval: 10 seconds for a reading every 5.

With **seconds per row** set, a row closes when a message arrives after its time is up. A sensor that has gone quiet
adds no rows until it sends again; then the rows it missed are added as gaps, at most one full history's worth. Set
the histogram's **stale after** to dim it meanwhile.

[A sensor display](../sensor-display.md#3-add-the-history) wires two journals in a row, for a 26-minute and a
2.6-hour history.

## Errors

- **The payload isn't a number.** The message is dropped and the console shows a `[NODE_ERROR]` naming this node and
  `journal needs a number, got str 'abc'`. It is reported once, then again only after a number has arrived. The
  chain keeps running.
- **Rows kept outside 1 to 256, or a negative seconds per row.** Deploy stops, naming the node and the property.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/debug/

# debug

Prints each message's payload to the console, to see what is flowing through a wire.

## Properties

- **full message** — default off. When on, prints the whole message, with `topic` and any other fields the source
  adds, instead of only `payload`.

## Wiring

**Input** — any message.

This node has no output.

## Behavior

Each message prints one line: `DEBUG node=ID payload=VALUE`, or `DEBUG node=ID msg=MESSAGE` with **full message** on.
The value is printed as Python shows it, so a string is in quotes: `payload='hello'`. Click the line in the console
to find the node on the canvas.

The board prints the line, so the console shows it only while the editor is connected.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/wifi-status/

# wifi status

Reports the board's WiFi connection state. In a flow with no other WiFi node, it also brings the connection up.

## Properties

- **poll interval (ms)** — how often to check the connection. Default 5000.
- **WiFi** — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow (see
  [Editor in depth](../working-in-the-editor.md#config-nodes)). Pick **unmanaged** to stop this node connecting: use it
  when something else manages the connection, or to leave the network out of the flow and enter it on the board. See
  [WiFi provisioning](../wifi-provisioning.md).

## Wiring

**Output** — a message when the connection changes:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `payload` | `True` when connected, `False` when disconnected |
| `ip`, `subnet`, `gateway`, `dns` | the connection's addresses; empty strings when disconnected |
| `rssi` | signal strength in dBm; `None` when disconnected, or when the board can't read it (ESP32 only) |

A [debug](debug.md) node prints only `payload`. Tick **full message** on it to see the other fields.

## Behavior

This node is optional: other network nodes don't need it. In a flow with MQTT nodes, MQTT manages the WiFi connection
and this node only reports on it.

It sends a message when the connection changes: a connect or disconnect, or a new `ip`, `subnet`, `gateway` or `dns`.
It doesn't send on every poll, except the first, which always reports.

`rssi` drifts constantly, so a change in it sends nothing by itself. It is included, as read at that poll, whenever a
message goes out for another reason. It is a snapshot, not a live reading.

If no connection is ever made, the node reports disconnected, as for any failed connect. Provisioning changes how the
board gets its credentials, not what this node reports.

Once the board is connected, the node shows a status dot on the canvas (see
[node status](../working-in-the-editor.md#node-status)). While the node has the board on a network, the editor can
connect to the board over WiFi. See [Connecting over WiFi](../wifi-connection.md).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/wifi-gate/

# wifi gate

Passes a message through unchanged while the board's WiFi is connected, and drops it while it isn't.

## Properties

- **WiFi** — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow.

## Wiring

**Input** — any message.

**Output** — the same message, unchanged, while the link is up. While it is down, nothing is sent on, as when a
[function](function.md) node returns `None`.

## Behavior

The gate checks the live WiFi link as each message arrives. It doesn't use the last message from
[wifi status](wifi-status.md), which sends only when the connection changes and can be out of date.

Put it between a source that fires on its own schedule, such as a timer or a sensor, and a node that sends over the
network. Messages that arrive while the link is down are dropped instead of failing downstream.

It checks the WiFi link only, not whether a given MQTT broker or HTTP server can be reached. `mqtt publish`,
`mqtt subscribe` and `http request` handle their own connections on top of a working link.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/ntp/

# ntp

Sets the board's clock from the internet and sends the time, as text for a display or as Unix time.

## Properties

- **NTP server** — a host name. Default `pool.ntp.org`.
- **UTC offset (hours)** — your standard time, from -12 to 14 in half hours: `1` for central Europe, `5.5` for India.
  Default 0.
- **daylight saving** — `UK / EU: automatic` adds an hour from 01:00 UTC on the last Sunday of March to 01:00 UTC on
  the last Sunday of October. `none` adds nothing. Default `UK / EU: automatic`. For other countries' rules, choose
  `none` and change the offset yourself.
- **format** — what goes in `payload`. Default `time`. Every message also carries all seven formats, as fields of
  the same names.
- **WiFi** — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow (see
  [Config nodes](../working-in-the-editor.md#config-nodes)). Required.

The seven formats, for 14:05:09 on 14 October 2026 at UTC+1:

| format | `payload` |
| --- | --- |
| `time` | `14:05` |
| `time_seconds` | `14:05:09` |
| `time_12h` | `2:05 pm` |
| `date` | `Wed 14 Oct` |
| `date_iso` | `2026-10-14` |
| `iso` | `2026-10-14T14:05:09+01:00` |
| `unix` | `1791983109`, an int: seconds since 1970 UTC, whatever the offset |

## Wiring

**Input** — any message asks for the time now. Wire a [timer](timer.md) in for a clock that ticks: every second for a
format with seconds, otherwise every 1 to 5 seconds.

**Output** — a new message, not the input one: one after each sync, and one for each input once the board has the
time. Nothing is sent before the first sync, so a [label](gui.md) shows `--` rather than a wrong time. To show the
time and the date on one screen, use two `ntp` nodes, one with `time` and one with `date`.

## Behavior

The node joins the flow's WiFi itself. Once WiFi is up it asks the server for the time, tries again every 30 seconds
until that works, then syncs every hour. Between syncs the board's own clock keeps time. A sync takes up to a second
and holds up the flow while it runs.
