The board's clock is kept in UTC. The offset and summer hour are added to each message, so the hour changes on time.

The status dot shows **waiting for WiFi** until the first sync, then **synced**.

## Errors

- **The sync fails.** The dot shows **NTP from pool.ntp.org failed**, and the first failure in a row also goes to the
  console as a `[NODE_ERROR]` with the reason. A board whose MicroPython has no `ntptime` module gives the reason
  `this firmware has no ntptime module`.
- **No WiFi network, a server that isn't a host name, or an offset outside -12 to 14.** Deploy stops and says which.
- **The output isn't wired.** Deploy warns `sends the time nowhere: wire its output to something`.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/udp-receive/

# udp receive

Listens on a UDP port and emits one message per datagram received.

## Properties

- **port** — local port to listen on (1–65535).
- **poll interval (ms)** — how often the node checks for datagrams. Default 20.
- **WiFi** — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow.

## Wiring

**Output** — one message per datagram:

- `payload` — the raw bytes received, not parsed. To read text or a structured format, decode it in a
  [function](function.md) node.
- `host` and `port` — the sender's address.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/mqtt-subscribe/

# mqtt subscribe

Sends a message for each message that arrives on an MQTT topic.

## Properties

- **topic** — the topic to subscribe to. Required. `+` matches one level and `#` the rest, as usual in MQTT.
- **QoS** — `0` or `1`. Default 0. QoS 2 isn't supported.
- **dynamic subscription** — let messages on the input change the subscriptions (see below). Default off.
- **MQTT Broker** — the flow's MQTT broker, shared by every MQTT node in the flow: change it on one and it changes on
  all (see [Editor in depth](../working-in-the-editor.md#config-nodes)). Required.
- **WiFi** — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow. **unmanaged** isn't accepted in a flow with
  MQTT nodes, because they manage the connection themselves.

## Wiring

**Input** — only with dynamic subscription on. See below.

**Output** — one message per message received:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `payload` | the message body, decoded as UTF-8 text |
| `topic` | the topic it arrived on, which can differ from the subscription when that has a wildcard |
| `retained` | `True` when the broker sent it as a retained message |

## Behavior

The node subscribes to **topic** when the flow starts and keeps the subscription across reconnects. Nodes on the same
broker share one connection and subscribe independently.

The node holds up to 20 messages that haven't been sent on yet. When more arrive, the oldest is dropped.

A subscription may not be confirmed by the broker before an [mqtt publish](mqtt-publish.md) node on the same broker
sends its first message. An early publish can go unheard.

The status dot shows this node's own view of the connection, as for mqtt publish.

### Dynamic subscription

With it on, an input message changes what the node listens to:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `action` | `subscribe` or `unsubscribe` |
| `topic` | a topic string, a `{topic, qos}` object, or a list of either |

An unsubscribe stops this node receiving that topic. Another node subscribed to the same topic keeps receiving it. The
configured **topic** can be unsubscribed too, until the flow is next reloaded.

## Errors

- **The board can't reach the broker.** The dot turns red and the console shows `mqtt connect to HOST:PORT failed after
  3 attempts`, with the reason for each attempt. See
  [MQTT broker unreachable](../debugging.md#mqtt-broker-unreachable).
- **The subscribe fails.** The console shows `mqtt subscribe to HOST:PORT failed`, with the system's error.
- **A message arrives on the input with dynamic subscription off.** The node raises an error rather than ignoring it.
- **An action message has no topic, an unknown action, or a QoS other than 0 or 1.** The node raises an error.

These stop the compile: no MQTT broker or no WiFi network in the flow, an empty topic, a QoS other than 0 or 1, an
unmanaged WiFi network.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/http-request/

# http request

Makes one HTTP request per incoming message and returns the response.

## Properties

- **url** — `http://host[:port]/path`. **HTTPS isn't supported.**
- **method** — `GET` or `POST`. No other methods are supported.
- **timeout (ms)** — how long to wait for the whole request and response. Default 5000.
- **WiFi** — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow.

## Wiring

**Input** — any message. For a `POST`, `payload` is the request body: a string is UTF-8 encoded, and other types are
converted.

**Output** — the response:

- `payload` — the decoded body, as a string.
- `status` — the HTTP status code, an integer.

A response with any status (404, 500, …) is sent on. Test `msg['status'] == 200` yourself.

## Behavior

The first request goes out when the first message arrives, so with a [timer](timer.md) it is one full interval after
the flow starts.

The server must send `Content-Length`: chunked transfer-encoding isn't supported. Redirects aren't followed. The body
must be valid UTF-8.

## Errors

If the connection fails, the request times out or the reply can't be read, nothing is sent on. The console shows the
error, and the next message tries again. There is no failure output. To act on a failure, watch the console.

- A body that isn't valid UTF-8 raises an error.
- The whole body is read into memory at once. A response larger than the board's largest free block fails with
  `MemoryError`. Request a smaller response, or use a board with PSRAM.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/http-in/

# http in

Starts a web server on the board and sends a message for each request to a path.

## Properties

- **port** — the TCP port to listen on (1–65535). Default 8080.
- **path** — the exact path to match, such as `/status`. It must start with `/`. A pattern such as `/user/:id` isn't
  supported.
- **method** — `GET` or `POST`. Default `GET`.
- **response timeout (ms)** — how long to wait for an [http response](http-response.md) node before the client gets a
  500. Default 10000.
- **WiFi** — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow.

## Wiring

**Output** — one message per matching request:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `payload` | `None`. The request body isn't read. |
| `topic` | an empty string |
| `req.method` | `GET` or `POST` |
| `req.path` | the path requested, without any query string |

Every chain that starts here must end at an [http response](http-response.md) node. The message carries a hidden link
to the client's connection, and http response uses it. A node that returns a new message instead of the one it
received, such as a [function](function.md) node, drops the link.

## Behavior

Several http in nodes can share one port. Each claims its own method and path. Two nodes claiming the same method and
path on one port is a compile error.

A request that matches no node gets a 404: that includes a method other than `GET` or `POST`. A query string is
dropped, so `/status?x=1` matches `/status`, and the value isn't available to the flow. Request headers are ignored.

If no http response node replies within the response timeout, the client gets a 500 with the body
`Internal Server Error: no response`. The connection closes after each reply.

The server speaks plain HTTP and has no login. It limits neither the number of requests in flight nor their size, apart
from the board's own memory and sockets. Use it on a network you trust.

## Errors

These stop the compile:

- the port isn't a number from 1 to 65535
- the path doesn't start with `/`
- the response timeout isn't a positive number
- two nodes claim the same method and path on one port. The error names both.

A client that doesn't finish sending its request line and headers within 5 seconds gets a 400.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/http-response/

# http response

Sends the reply to a request that arrived through an [http in](http-in.md) node.

## Properties

None. The reply comes from the message.

## Wiring

**Input** — a message that started at an http in node:

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `payload` | the reply body. A string is sent as UTF-8, bytes as they are, and `None` as an empty body. Anything else is converted to text. |
| `statusCode` | the HTTP status, a whole number. Default 200. |

This node has no output.

## Behavior

The reply has no `Content-Type` header. A client that needs to know the body is JSON has to assume it.

Send one reply per request. Once a reply has gone, another for the same request does nothing. A reply that arrives
after the [response timeout](http-in.md#properties) is too late: the client has already received a 500.

## Errors

- **The message didn't come from an http in node.** The console shows
  `http_response: msg did not come from an http_in node (no request to respond to)`. The same happens when a node
  between the two built a new message and dropped the link. Change the message you received and pass it on.
- **`statusCode` isn't a whole number.** The node raises an error and the client gets the 500 after the timeout.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/udp-send/

# udp send

Sends a message's payload as a UDP datagram to a fixed host and port.

## Properties

- **host** — the destination hostname or IP address. Required.
- **port** — the destination port (1–65535). Default 9999.
- **timeout (ms)** — how long to wait for the board's network stack to accept the datagram. Default 2000.
- **WiFi** — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow.

## Wiring

**Input** — any message. `payload` is the datagram: bytes are sent as they are, a string as UTF-8, and anything else is
converted to text first. `None` sends the text `None`.

This node has no output.

## Behavior

UDP has no acknowledgement. A send that succeeds doesn't mean the datagram arrived, and sending to an IP address that
nobody is listening on raises no error.

A hostname is looked up again for every message.

## Errors

- **The name can't be resolved.** The console shows `udp_send: could not resolve HOST:PORT`. Check the name, or use the
  IP address.
- **The send fails.** The console shows `udp_send to HOST:PORT failed`, with the system's error.
- **The network stack doesn't take the datagram within the timeout.** The console shows a timeout error, without the
  host or port.

These stop the compile: an empty host, a port outside 1–65535, a timeout that isn't a positive number.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/mqtt-publish/

# mqtt publish

Publishes each message's payload to an MQTT topic.

## Properties

- **topic** — the topic to publish to. Required. It is fixed: a message's `topic` is ignored. To publish to several
  topics, use one node for each.
- **retain** — ask the broker to keep the message and give it to later subscribers. Default off.
- **QoS** — `0` or `1`. Default 0. QoS 2 isn't supported.
- **MQTT Broker** — the flow's MQTT broker, shared by every MQTT node in the flow: change it on one and it changes on
  all (see [Editor in depth](../working-in-the-editor.md#config-nodes)). Required.
- **WiFi** — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow. **unmanaged** isn't accepted in a flow with
  MQTT nodes, because they manage the connection themselves.

## Wiring

**Input** — any message. `payload` is the message sent: bytes as they are, a string as UTF-8, and anything else
converted to text first. `None` sends the text `None`.

This node has no output.

## Behavior

Nodes on the same broker share one connection. The node connects when the first message reaches it, so its status dot
stays blank until then (see [node status](../working-in-the-editor.md#node-status)). It shows this node's own view of
the connection, even when an [mqtt subscribe](mqtt-subscribe.md) node shares the broker.

## Errors

- **The board can't reach the broker.** The dot turns red and the console shows `mqtt connect to HOST:PORT failed after
  3 attempts`, with the reason for each attempt. See
  [MQTT broker unreachable](../debugging.md#mqtt-broker-unreachable).
- **The publish fails.** The console shows `mqtt publish to HOST:PORT failed`, with the system's error.

These stop the compile: no MQTT broker or no WiFi network in the flow, an empty topic, a QoS other than 0 or 1, an
unmanaged WiFi network.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/ble-scan/

# ble scan

Listens for Bluetooth LE advertisements, such as beacons and BLE sensors, and sends one message per advertisement.

## Properties

- **name starts with** — only devices whose advertised name starts with this. Default blank. Many devices send their
  name only in reply to an active scan.
- **address** — only this device, as `aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff`. Default blank.
- **manufacturer id** — only advertisements with this manufacturer id, in decimal or hex (`0x0499` is Ruuvi). Default
  blank.
- **service UUID** — only advertisements that list this service or carry data for it: 16-bit (`fcd2` is BTHome)
  or 128-bit. Default blank.
- **active scan** — also ask each device for its scan response, which usually holds its name. Default off.
- **repeat window (ms)** — drops an advertisement identical to the same device's last one within this time.
  Default 1000. `0` sends every one; a changed advertisement is always sent.
- **scan interval (ms)** / **scan window (ms)** — the radio listens for the window once every interval, from 2.5 to
  10240 ms. Defaults 320 and 30. A longer window misses fewer advertisements and leaves WiFi less time.

A blank filter lets everything through. The filters combine: an advertisement must pass every one that is set.

With **active scan** on, a device's scan response arrives as a second message, usually a few milliseconds after its
advertisement, with `scanResponse` set. That's where most devices put their name. Empty scan responses are
dropped.

## Wiring

**Input** — none. `ble scan` is a source.

**Output** — `payload` is the advertising data as bytes. The message also carries:

| field | |
| --- | --- |
| `addr` | the sender's address, `aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff` |
| `addrType` | `public` or `random` (phones use random addresses that change) |
| `rssi` | signal strength in dBm, such as `-60` |
| `connectable` | whether the device accepts connections; `None` for a scan response |
| `scanResponse` | `True` for a device's reply to an active scan, sent as its own message |
| `name` | the advertised name, or `''` |
| `mfrId`, `mfr` | the manufacturer id and the bytes after it, or `None` and `b''` |
| `svcData` | service data, by UUID: `{'fcd2': b'...'}` |
| `services` | the service UUIDs it lists |

Decode the bytes in a [function](function.md) node, with `struct.unpack`.

## Behavior

Every ble scan node in a flow shares one scan, so they must have the same scan interval, scan window and active
scan settings. Each node applies its own filters. A node keeps up to 20 advertisements waiting; if they come faster
than the flow handles them, the oldest are dropped.

The radio is shared with WiFi on an ESP32. A long scan window slows WiFi and MQTT.

It runs on the processors [Supported hardware](../supported-hardware.md#processors-without-a-board-definition) lists for the ble nodes.

## Errors

A bad address, manufacturer id, UUID or scan setting stops the deploy, naming the value. So do two ble scan
nodes with different scan settings, and a board without the ble nodes. The status shows **scanning**, or **scan
stopped by the radio** if the radio ends the scan. If the radio can't start, often because the board is short of
memory, the console says so: hard-reset the board.

An advertisement is untrusted input: anyone nearby can send one, with any name or address.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/ble-advertise/

# ble advertise

Advertises over Bluetooth LE: the board's name, and each message's payload as manufacturer or service data.

## Properties

- **payload goes in** — **manufacturer data**, **service data**, or **nothing (name only)**. Default **manufacturer
  data**.
- **manufacturer id** — for manufacturer data, in decimal or hex. Default `0xFFFF`, which is reserved for testing;
  a product uses its maker's id from the Bluetooth SIG.
- **service UUID** — for service data: 16-bit (`fcd2` is BTHome) or 128-bit. Default `fcd2`.
- **interval (ms)** — how often the advertisement is sent, 20 to 10240. Default 500. Shorter is found faster and
  uses more power.
- **BLE** — the flow's [BLE config](ble.md), whose name is advertised. Without one, the name is `thingstudio`.

## Wiring

**Input** — `payload` replaces the data: bytes as they are, text as UTF-8. With **nothing (name only)** it's
ignored. Pack a number with `struct.pack` in a [function](function.md) node first, for example
`struct.pack('<h', round(t * 100))`. Unwired, the node advertises the name only.

This node has no output.

## Behavior

The board advertises the name from the moment the flow starts. Each message replaces the data, and the board sends
the new advertisement until the next one. Phones and computers (nRF Connect, for example) and other boards with a
[ble scan](ble-scan.md) node see it without connecting. When the flow also has characteristic or UART nodes, the
advertisement accepts connections, so other devices can connect to them.

An advertisement holds 31 bytes. The flags take 3, the name its length plus 2, and the data's header 4 (manufacturer
or 16-bit service) or 18 (128-bit service). The node's status says how many are left for the payload.

A flow has one ble advertise node. It runs on the processors [Supported hardware](../supported-hardware.md#processors-without-a-board-definition) lists for the ble nodes.

## Errors

A name with no room left for data, a bad id or UUID, a second ble advertise node, or a board without the ble nodes
stops the deploy. A payload that isn't bytes or text, or that doesn't fit, is reported on the console with its
size, and the board keeps sending the last advertisement.

Anyone nearby can read an advertisement. Don't put anything private in it.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/ble-characteristic-in/

# ble characteristic in

Sends a message each time a connected device writes a Bluetooth LE characteristic.

## Properties

- **service UUID** — the service the characteristic belongs to: 16-bit (`181a`) or 128-bit. Required. Use the same
  service on the nodes for its other characteristics.
- **characteristic UUID** — 16-bit (`2a6e`) or 128-bit. Required.
- **encoding** — how the bytes written become `payload`: **bytes**, **text** (UTF-8), **int8**, **uint8**,
  **int16**, **uint16**, **int32**, **uint32** or **float32**, little-endian. Default **bytes**. It also sets the
  output's type, so a number encoding can wire into a number input.
- **BLE** — the flow's [BLE config](ble.md), for the board's name. Optional.

For your own service, pick a random 128-bit UUID (an online UUID generator, or `python3 -c "import uuid;
print(uuid.uuid4())"`). 16-bit UUIDs belong to services the Bluetooth SIG has defined.

## Wiring

**Input** — none. `ble characteristic in` is a source.

**Output** — `payload` is the value. The message also carries `conn`, the connection's number, and `uuid`, the
characteristic.

## Behavior

The board becomes a GATT server when a flow has any characteristic or UART node. It advertises its name, accepts
connections, and starts advertising again when a device disconnects. Any Bluetooth LE device that can connect and
write works: an app on a phone or a computer, such as nRF Connect, or another board's [ble write](ble-write.md) node.
All the flow's characteristics are registered once, when the flow starts. Pair a
[ble characteristic out](ble-characteristic-out.md) with the same UUIDs to make one characteristic a connected device
can read, write and subscribe to.

A connected device can write up to 244 bytes at a time. A node keeps up to 20 writes waiting; if they come faster than the
flow handles them, the oldest are dropped.

The node's status shows **advertising, no one connected** or **1 connected**.

## Errors

A missing or malformed UUID, two nodes using one characteristic with different encodings, or a board without the
ble nodes stops the deploy.
A write that doesn't decode (2 bytes sent to an `int32`, text that isn't UTF-8) is reported on the console with its
size and dropped.

Anyone in range can connect and write: there's no pairing. Treat what arrives as untrusted input.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/ble-characteristic-out/

# ble characteristic out

Sets a Bluetooth LE characteristic to each message's payload, for a connected device to read, and notifies the
devices that subscribed.

## Properties

- **service UUID** / **characteristic UUID** — as for [ble characteristic in](ble-characteristic-in.md).
- **encoding** — how `payload` becomes bytes: the same choices. Default **bytes**. A number must fit: `70000`
  doesn't fit an **int16**.
- **notify** — also push each new value to the devices subscribed to it. Default on.
- **BLE** — the flow's [BLE config](ble.md).

## Wiring

**Input** — `payload` is the new value. Unwired, the characteristic exists but stays empty.

This node has no output.

## Behavior

Each message replaces the value. A device that reads gets the whole value; a notification carries up to 20 bytes
unless the device has agreed a larger MTU (most do, up to 244). Only devices connected at the time are notified.

One characteristic out node per characteristic: two would fight over its value. A
[ble characteristic in](ble-characteristic-in.md) on the same UUIDs makes it writable too.

## Errors

A missing or malformed UUID, two out nodes on one characteristic, or a board without the ble nodes stops the deploy. A payload that doesn't fit
the encoding is reported on the console and dropped, and the last value stays.

Anyone in range can connect and read: don't put anything private in a characteristic.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/ble-uart-in/

# ble uart in

Receives text from a connected device over Bluetooth LE, through the Nordic UART Service that terminal apps use.

## Properties

- **one message per line** — default on: text is gathered until a newline (`\n`; a `\r` is dropped), and the line
  is sent without its line ending. Off: one message per write.
- **BLE** — the flow's [BLE config](ble.md).

## Wiring

**Input** — none. `ble uart in` is a source.

**Output** — `payload` is the text. The message also carries `conn`, the connection's number.

## Behavior

Any UART node adds the Nordic UART Service to the board's GATT server. Terminal apps that speak it, on phones and
computers, such as nRF Connect, Serial Bluetooth Terminal and Adafruit Bluefruit, find the board by its name and
connect. Pair it with
[ble uart out](ble-uart-out.md) to answer.

A line over 512 bytes is sent as it is, so a device that never sends a newline still gets through.

## Errors

Bytes that aren't UTF-8 text are reported on the console and dropped. Anyone in range can connect and send: there's
no pairing.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/ble-uart-out/

# ble uart out

Sends text to the devices connected over Bluetooth LE, through the Nordic UART Service.

## Properties

- **end with a newline** — add `\n` after each payload. Default on.
- **BLE** — the flow's [BLE config](ble.md).

## Wiring

**Input** — `payload` as text. Bytes are sent as they are; anything else is sent as `str(payload)`.

This node has no output.

## Behavior

The text goes to every connected device, split into pieces that fit each connection: 20 bytes until the device
agrees a larger MTU. With no device connected, nothing is sent and nothing is kept.

## Errors

A board without the ble nodes stops the deploy. Anyone in range can connect and read what's sent: there's no pairing.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/ble-read/

# ble read

Reads a characteristic of another Bluetooth LE device for each message that arrives, and sends the value on.

## Properties

- **BLE peer** — the [device to read from](ble-peer.md). Required.
- **service UUID** / **characteristic UUID** — the characteristic to read: 16-bit (`2a6e`) or 128-bit. Required.
  Apps such as nRF Connect list a device's UUIDs.
- **encoding** — how the bytes read become `payload`: **bytes**, **text**, **int8** to **uint32**, or **float32**,
  little-endian. Default **bytes**. It also sets the output's type.

## Wiring

**Input** — any message starts a read. Wire a [timer](timer.md) in to read at an interval.

**Output** — the incoming message, with `payload` set to the value read.

## Behavior

The read waits up to 5 seconds for the device's answer, and the message's chain waits with it. For a device that pushes
its values, a [ble notify](ble-notify.md) node needs no polling.

## Errors

A message that arrives while the peer isn't connected, a read that times out or fails, or a value that doesn't
decode (1 byte for a uint16) is reported on the console and the message is dropped.

What a device sends is untrusted input: check it before acting on it.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/ble-write/

# ble write

Writes each message's payload to a characteristic of another Bluetooth LE device.

## Properties

- **BLE peer** — the [device to write to](ble-peer.md). Required.
- **service UUID** / **characteristic UUID** — the characteristic to write: 16-bit or 128-bit. Required.
- **encoding** — how `payload` becomes bytes: the same choices as [ble read](ble-read.md). Default
  **bytes**. A number must fit.
- **wait for the peer's response** — default on: the device confirms each write, and a write it refuses is
  reported. Off: write without response, which is faster; the characteristic must allow it.

## Wiring

**Input** — `payload` is the value to write.

This node has no output.

## Behavior

Nothing is queued: a message that arrives while the peer isn't connected is reported and dropped, so a stale value
is never written after a reconnect.

## Errors

Not connected, a write the device refuses or doesn't confirm within 5 seconds, or a payload that doesn't fit the
encoding is reported on the console.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/ble-notify/

# ble notify

Subscribes to a characteristic of another Bluetooth LE device and sends a message each time it sends a new value.

## Properties

- **BLE peer** — the [device to listen to](ble-peer.md). Required.
- **service UUID** / **characteristic UUID** — the characteristic: 16-bit or 128-bit. Required. It must support notify or
  indicate; nRF Connect shows which.
- **encoding** — how each value becomes `payload`, as for [ble read](ble-read.md). Default **bytes**.
  It also sets the output's type.

## Wiring

**Input** — none. `ble notify` is a source.

**Output** — `payload` is the value. The message also carries `peer`, the device's address or name, and `uuid`, the
characteristic.

## Behavior

The board turns notifications on when it connects, and again after each reconnect. It uses indications when the
characteristic offers no notifications. Up to 20 values wait if they come faster than the flow handles them; then
the oldest are dropped.

## Errors

A characteristic that can't notify or indicate is reported when the board connects. A value that doesn't decode is
reported and dropped.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/ble/

# BLE

The board's Bluetooth name, shared by every ble node in a flow. Optional: without it, the board is called
`thingstudio`.

Each ble node has a **BLE** field. Pick the flow's BLE config, or add one with **+**. A flow has one, since a board
has one radio.

## Settings

- **name** — what other devices show when they find the board, up to 26 bytes. Default `thingstudio`. A [ble advertise](ble-advertise.md) node shares the 31 bytes of
  an advertisement between the name and its payload, so a shorter name leaves more room.

## Behavior

Once a ble node has started the radio, it stays on until the board resets, through every redeploy. A deploy stops
the old flow's scans, advertising and connections, not the radio. It keeps some ESP-IDF memory meanwhile: a hard
reset gives it back.

## Errors

A name over 26 bytes, or two BLE configs in a flow, stops the deploy.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/ble-peer/

# BLE peer

Another Bluetooth LE device the board connects to, such as a sensor or another board. The
[ble read](ble-read.md), [ble write](ble-write.md) and [ble notify](ble-notify.md) nodes name one.

Each of those nodes has a **BLE peer** field. Pick a peer, or add one with **+**. A flow can have several, one per
device. Nodes that name the same peer share one connection.

## Settings

- **address** — the device's address, `aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff`. Default blank. A [ble scan](ble-scan.md) node into a debug node shows
  the addresses nearby.
- **name starts with** — default blank. Used when the address is blank: the first device whose advertised name starts with this.
  Phones change their address every few minutes, so find a phone by name; most sensors and boards keep theirs.
- **timeout (ms)** — how long finding the device and connecting to it may each take. Default 10000.

## Behavior

The board finds the device, connects, finds the services and characteristics the flow's nodes use, and turns on
notifications for the ble notify nodes. The nodes' status follows each step: **finding**, **connecting**,
**discovering**, **connected**. If a step fails or the link drops, the status says why, and the board starts again
from finding after 10 seconds. It never connects to a different device instead.

An ESP32 holds at most 4 Bluetooth connections at once, counting its peers and the devices connected to the board.
A peer over that limit reports a failure at connecting.

## Errors

A peer with neither an address nor a name, a malformed address, or a timeout outside 1000 to 60000 ms stops the
deploy. A step that fails on the board, such as the device not being found or a service it doesn't have, is
reported once on the console, naming the device and the step.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/interrupt/

# interrupt

Sends a message the moment a pin changes state.

## Properties

- **pin** — the GPIO pin. Default 4.
- **edge** — the change to react to: `rising`, `falling` or `both`. Default `rising`.

## Wiring

**Input** — none. `interrupt` is a source.

**Output** — a message with `payload` set to the pin's level, `True` or `False`, read when the node handles the
change. `topic` is an empty string.

## Behavior

The pin's interrupt wakes the node, and the node reads the pin then. Changes that come faster than the flow handles
them are collapsed into one message, so `payload` is the level at that moment, not a record of every change.

The pin has no pull resistor. Wire an external one, or use a module with one built in. For a button or switch, use
[ebutton](ebutton.md) or [eswitch](eswitch.md), which ignore contact bounce and can use the pin's own pull resistor.

## Errors

- **A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently.** Deploy stops and says why. See
  [What gets checked](../boards.md#what-gets-checked) and [Hardware is shared](index.md#hardware-is-shared).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/eswitch/

# eswitch

Reports when a switch opens or closes, ignoring contact bounce.

## Properties

- **pin** — the GPIO pin. Default 4.
- **pull** — the pin's own pull resistor: `none`, `up` or `down`. Default `none`, for a switch with an external
  pull resistor or a module that has one.
- **open level (lopen)** — the pin level that means open: `1` for a switch to ground with a pull-up, `0` for a
  switch to 3V3 with a pull-down. Default `1`.
- **debounce (ms)** — how long a level must hold before it counts. Default 50. Must be 1 or more.

## Wiring

**Input** — none. `eswitch` is a source.

**Output** — a message for each change, with `payload` `True` when the switch closes and `False` when it opens, and
`topic` an empty string. `payload` is a bool, so it can wire straight to a [gpio out](gpio-out.md) to mirror the
switch.

## Behavior

The node checks the pin every **debounce** interval. It sends nothing when the flow starts, only on a change.

## Errors

- **A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently.** Deploy stops and says why. See
  [What gets checked](../boards.md#what-gets-checked) and [Hardware is shared](index.md#hardware-is-shared).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/ebutton/

# ebutton

Reports presses, releases, long presses and double clicks from one button, ignoring contact bounce.

## Properties

- **pin** — the GPIO pin. Default 5. [Kitchen-sink board](../kitchen-sink-board.md) shows a button wired to one.
- **pull** — the pin's own pull resistor: `none`, `up` or `down`. Default `none`, for a button with an external
  pull resistor or a module that has one.
- **sense** — the pin level when the button is not pressed: `auto`, `0` or `1`. Default `auto`, which takes the
  level when the flow starts as not pressed. Set it if the button may be held down at start.
- **suppress** — default off. When on, a click that may be the first half of a double click is held back (see
  Behavior).
- **debounce (ms)** — default 50. Must be 1 or more.
- **long press (ms)** — how long a press must last to count as `long`. Default 1000.
- **double click (ms)** — how soon a second press must follow the first to count as `double`. Default 400. Must be
  less than **long press**.

## Wiring

**Input** — none. `ebutton` is a source.

**Output** — a message for each event, with `payload` one of `press`, `release`, `long` or `double`, and `topic` an
empty string.

## Behavior

The events each action sends depend on **suppress**:

| Action | suppress off | suppress on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a click | `press`, `release` | `press` and `release` together, after **double click** has passed |
| a double click | `press`, `release`, then `press` and `double` together, then `release` | `double`, `release` |
| a long press | `press`, `long`, `release` | `long`, `release` |

With suppress off, every press is reported at once. With it on, a click arrives later but never as part of a double
click or a long press, and a press held longer than **double click** but released before **long press** sends only
`release`.

## Errors

- **double click is not less than long press.** Deploy stops with `property "doubleClickMs" 1000 must be less than
  longPressMs (1000)`, naming the node.
- **A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently.** Deploy stops and says why. See
  [What gets checked](../boards.md#what-gets-checked) and [Hardware is shared](index.md#hardware-is-shared).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/adc/

# adc

Reads an analog pin, and sends the reading when it moves past the set bounds, and at a fixed interval if one is set.

## Properties

- **pin** — the ADC pin. Default 34. [Kitchen-sink board](../kitchen-sink-board.md) shows a potentiometer wired to one.
- **mode** — what counts as a change. Default `relative`.
    - `relative` — the reading has moved more than **delta** from the last one sent.
    - `absolute` — the reading crosses **lower** or **upper**: out of the range, or back into it (see **sense**).
- **delta (counts)** — for `relative`. Default 2000. Must be 1 or more.
- **lower** / **upper** — for `absolute`, in counts from 0 to 65535. Defaults 0 and 50000. **lower** must be less
  than **upper**.
- **sense** — for `absolute`: `outside` to send when the reading leaves the range, `inside` to send when it comes
  back. Default `outside`. Leave it at `outside` in `relative` mode.
- **poll (ms)** — also send the reading at least this often. Default 0, which sends only on a change.

## Wiring

**Input** — none. `adc` is a source.

**Output** — a message with `payload` a dict, and `topic` an empty string:

```python
{'raw': 31250, 'volts': 1.572, 'percent': 47.7}
```

`raw` is the reading, 0 to 65535. `volts` is the pin voltage, to 3 decimal places; on a board that can't measure it,
it is worked out as `raw` over 65535 times 3.3 V. `percent` is `raw` as a percentage of 65535, to 1 decimal place.

## Behavior

A raw reading is noisy, so `relative` with a delta of a few thousand counts suits most sensors. `absolute` suits an
alarm or a threshold.

In `absolute` mode the node sends once per crossing. After a message it waits for the reading to go back to the
other side before it can send again, so a reading that stays outside sends nothing more. If the reading is already on
the **sense** side when the flow starts, the first message goes out at once.

## Errors

- **The pin can't be read.** The node's status dot turns red with the error, and the reading is dropped. See
  [Node status](../working-in-the-editor.md#node-status).
- **An ESP32 ADC2 pin in a flow that uses WiFi.** Deploy stops: ADC2 can't be read while WiFi is on. Use an ADC1
  pin.
- **lower is not less than upper**, in `absolute` mode. Deploy stops with `adc lower (100) must be less than upper
  (50)`.
- **A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently.** Deploy stops and says why. See
  [What gets checked](../boards.md#what-gets-checked) and [Hardware is shared](index.md#hardware-is-shared).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/encoder/

# encoder

Reads a rotary encoder (a quadrature knob) and sends its value each time it turns.

## Properties

- **pin x** / **pin y** — the encoder's two switch pins. Defaults 10 and 11. Both are read with the pins' own
  pull-ups. If the value counts the wrong way, swap them.
- **divide by (div)** — pulses per step of the value: `4` or `2` for a knob that clicks, so one click is one step;
  `1` counts every pulse. Default 1.
- **start value** — the value when the flow starts. Default 0.
- **lowest (blank for none)** / **highest (blank for none)** — whole numbers the value stops at. Default blank.
- **wrap at (blank for none)** — a whole number: the value counts from `0` to one less than it, then wraps. Default
  blank.
- **settle (ms)** — how long to wait after the knob moves before sending the value. Default 100. Must be 0 or
  more.

The value is divided first, then held within lowest and highest, then wrapped.

## Wiring

**Input** — none. `encoder` is a source.

**Output** — a message with `payload` set to the value, `delta` set to how far it moved since the last message
(negative when it went down), and `topic` an empty string.

## Behavior

When the knob moves, the node waits **settle**, then sends the value it has reached. A fast turn gives about one
message per **settle**, not one per pulse. A turn that ends where it started sends nothing.

## Errors

- **start value is below lowest or above highest.** The board reports `Incompatible args: must have vmin <= v <=
  vmax` when the flow starts.
- **lowest, highest or wrap at isn't a whole number.** Deploy stops with `property "vmin" "x" must be a whole number
  (decimal or 0x hex)`, naming the node.
- **A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently.** Deploy stops and says why. See
  [What gets checked](../boards.md#what-gets-checked) and [Hardware is shared](index.md#hardware-is-shared).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/neopixel/

# neopixel

Lights a WS2812 (NeoPixel) strip: sets its pixels from each message, then writes the strip.

## Properties

- **pin** — the strip's data pin. Default 13. [Kitchen-sink board](../kitchen-sink-board.md) shows one LED wired to
  one.
- **count** — how many pixels the strip has. Default 8. Must be 1 or more.
- **order** — the color order of your strip: `GRB`, `RGB`, `RGBW` or `GRBW`. Default `GRB`, which most WS2812
  strips use. The `W` orders are for strips with a white channel.

## Wiring

**Input** — `payload` in one of three forms:

```python
msg['payload'] = 0xff4400                            # one color for the whole strip
msg['payload'] = [0xff0000, 0x00ff00, 0x0000ff]      # one color per pixel, from the first
msg['payload'] = {'index': 2, 'colour': 0x00ff00}    # one pixel; 'color' works too
```

A color is `0xRRGGBB`, 0 to 255 for each of red, green and blue. A strip with a white channel takes
`0xWWRRGGBB`; a plain `0xRRGGBB` leaves white off. A list shorter than the strip leaves the other pixels as they
were; one longer than the strip is cut off.

This node has no output.

## Behavior

Each message sets the pixels it names and writes the whole strip. Pixels a message doesn't name keep their color.

## Errors

- **A payload that isn't a color**, or an index past the end of the strip. The node's status dot turns red with the
  error, and nothing is written. See [Node status](../working-in-the-editor.md#node-status).
- **A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently.** Deploy stops and says why. See
  [What gets checked](../boards.md#what-gets-checked) and [Hardware is shared](index.md#hardware-is-shared).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/gpio-out/

# gpio out

Sets a pin high or low from each message.

## Properties

- **pin** — the GPIO pin. Default 12.

## Wiring

**Input** — `payload`, read with Python's `bool()`: a true value sets the pin high, a false one (`False`, `0`,
`""`, `None`, an empty list) sets it low. A message with no `payload` sets it low. The input is type `bool`, so any
output can wire to it.

This node has no output.

## Behavior

The pin stays where the last message set it. It is set up as an output when the flow starts, before any message
arrives.

## Errors

- **A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently.** Deploy stops and says why. See
  [What gets checked](../boards.md#what-gets-checked) and [Hardware is shared](index.md#hardware-is-shared).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/pwm-out/

# pwm out

Drives a PWM signal on a pin, for dimming an LED, setting a motor's speed, or any other variable duty cycle.

## Properties

- **pin** — the GPIO pin. Default 12.
- **frequency (Hz)** — the PWM frequency. Default 1000. Must be 1 or more.

## Wiring

**Input** — `payload` is the duty cycle as a fraction, from `0.0` (always off) to `1.0` (always on). A value below 0
is taken as 0 and one above 1 as 1. `True` and `False` work as 1 and 0. A string, even `"0.5"`, fails: convert it
first, in a [function](function.md) node. A message with no `payload` sets the duty to 0.

This node has no output.

## Behavior

The duty cycle stays where the last message set it.

## Errors

- **The payload is a string or another non-number.** The console shows a `[NODE_ERROR]` naming this node. See
  [Reading a node error](../debugging.md#reading-a-node-error).
- **A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently.** Deploy stops and says why. See
  [What gets checked](../boards.md#what-gets-checked) and [Hardware is shared](index.md#hardware-is-shared).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/display-spi/

# display spi

Shows a frame on an SPI color TFT panel. The frame comes from a [gui screen](gui.md), or from a
[function](function.md) node that draws with `framebuf`. [Supported hardware](../supported-hardware.md#displays)
lists the display chips.

## Properties

The property panel's **preset** picker saves a panel's whole setup under a name and loads it on another node (see
[Presets](../working-in-the-editor.md#presets)). Pins, size, rotation and color settings differ from board to board,
so check them against your own panel, or use a board's labelled pins (see
[Seeing a board's pins](../boards.md#seeing-a-boards-pins)).

- **controller** — the display chip: `ST7789` or `ST7796 (320x480)`. Default `ST7789`.
- **frame format** — the frame the node takes. Default `rgb565`, full color at 2 bytes a pixel. The indexed formats
  use less memory and fewer colors: `gs4` (16 colors, a quarter of the memory), `gs2` (4 colors, an eighth) and `mono`
  (2 colors, a sixteenth). A gui screen wired to the display draws in this format.
- **palette** — the 16 RGB565 colors the indexed formats use: `gs4` all 16, `gs2` the first 4, `mono` the first 2.
  Shown as swatches under **frame format** when an indexed format is picked; click one to change it, or **reset**
  for the built-in colors. While a gui screen with a [theme](gui.md#themes) is wired to the display, the theme sets
  the palette and this one is ignored.
- **SPI bus** — the hardware SPI peripheral. Default 2.
- **baudrate** — the SPI clock in Hz. Default 40000000.
- **sck pin** / **mosi pin** / **dc pin** — required. Defaults 12, 11 and 13.
- **cs pin** / **reset pin** / **backlight pin** — `-1` when not wired, the default for all three. Some boards tie
  reset or CS in hardware, or have no backlight control.
- **width (px)** / **height (px)** — the panel's own size. Defaults 135 and 240. A gui screen wired to the display
  takes this size.
- **orientation** — default off. `0`, `90`, `180` or `270` turns the picture clockwise, and a gui screen wired to the
  display turns its size and touch to match. With an orientation, set **width** and **height** to the panel's own
  size, **rotation** to how the panel is mounted (0 to 3), and **xstart** and **ystart** to `-1`. See
  [Rotating the screen](gui.md#rotating-the-screen). A flow that reads touch with a [touch](touch-i2c.md) node sets
  the same angle on that node.
- **rotation (0-7)** — the controller's own orientation code. Default 1.
- **color order** — `BGR` or `RGB`, as the panel is wired. Default `BGR`.
- **invert colors** — for a panel that shows the negative. Default off.
- **data latch order (MH bit)** — a controller bit some panels need, with rotation, for the right left-to-right
  order. Default on.
- **xstart** / **ystart** — the panel's offset in the ST7789's larger frame memory. Default `-1`, which takes it from
  the driver's table: `0, 0` for 240x240, `52, 40` for 135x240. Any other ST7789 size needs both set. A wrong offset
  doesn't raise an error: the picture shows clipped or shifted. An ST7796 has no offset; leave both at `-1`.

## Wiring

**Input** — `payload` is the frame, in the **frame format**. A whole frame is exactly the size the format needs:
`width * height * 2` bytes for `rgb565`; for the indexed formats, see Indexed formats below.

A message with a `y` field is a strip: whole rows, written from row `y` down. A gui screen sends strips, so a large
display never needs a whole frame in memory.

This node has no output.

## Behavior

### RGB565 byte order

`framebuf.RGB565` stores each pixel in the processor's byte order, little-endian on an ESP32, but the panel expects
big-endian. The node sends the bytes as they are, so a buffer drawn with `framebuf.FrameBuffer(..., framebuf.RGB565)`
comes out with its colors wrong: an intended green shows red. Swap each pair of bytes after drawing, before
`msg['payload'] = buf`:

```python
for i in range(0, len(buf), 2):
    buf[i], buf[i + 1] = buf[i + 1], buf[i]
```

A color whose two bytes are the same, such as white `0xFFFF` or black `0x0000`, looks right either way, so text on a
plain background can hide the problem.

### Indexed formats

Draw an indexed frame with `framebuf.FrameBuffer(..., framebuf.<FORMAT>)`, with the constant that matches **frame
format**:

| frame format | `framebuf` constant | bits per pixel | palette entries used | 240x320 frame |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `rgb565` | `RGB565` | 16 | none, real color | 153,600 bytes |
| `gs4` | `GS4_HMSB` | 4 | 0–15 | 38,400 bytes |
| `gs2` | `GS2_HMSB` | 2 | 0–3 | 19,200 bytes |
| `mono` | `MONO_HMSB` | 1 | 0–1 | 9,600 bytes |

Pixel values are palette entries, not colors; the node turns each into its palette color as it writes. The indexed
formats have no byte-order problem.

Each row is padded to a whole byte, so a width that isn't a multiple of the pixels per byte (2 for `gs4`, 4 for `gs2`,
8 for `mono`) needs a little more than `width * height * bits / 8`. On a wrong size the node names the size it
expects.

`mono` needs `framebuf.MONO_HMSB`. `MONO_VLSB` (the [display i2c](display-i2c.md) layout) and `MONO_HLSB` give a
garbled picture with no error, because the node can't tell which one was used.

Send the `bytearray` itself (`msg['payload'] = buf`): `bytes(buf)` makes a second copy the board may not have memory
for. For a flow that redraws often, keep the buffer in `context` and reuse it.

## Errors

- **A frame or strip of the wrong size.** The console shows a `[NODE_ERROR]` naming this node, such as
  `display_spi: expected 64800 bytes (...), got 64000`, or for a strip
  `display_spi: a strip must be whole rows of 270 bytes inside the 240-row screen, ...`. See
  [Reading a node error](../debugging.md#reading-a-node-error).
- **An ST7789 size other than 240x240 or 135x240, with xstart and ystart at -1.** The board reports
  `Unsupported display. Only 240x240 and 135x240 are supported without xstart and ystart provided` when the flow
  starts.
- **An orientation with a panel offset**, including the default 135x240 size. Deploy stops: clear the orientation,
  or set **rotation** by hand.
- **An orientation with a rotation of 4 to 7.** Deploy stops; with an orientation, rotation is 0 to 3.
- **A baudrate too fast for the board or for these pins.** Deploy stops and gives the board's limit.
- **A changed palette while a themed gui screen is wired.** Deploy warns that the theme sets the palette.
- **A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently.** Deploy stops and says why. See
  [What gets checked](../boards.md#what-gets-checked) and [Hardware is shared](index.md#hardware-is-shared).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/display-i2c/

# display i2c

Shows a frame on an I2C monochrome OLED panel. The frame is drawn upstream, usually in a
[function](function.md) node with `framebuf`. [Supported hardware](../supported-hardware.md#displays) lists the
display chips.

## Properties

The property panel's **preset** picker saves a panel's setup under a name and loads it on another node (see
[Presets](../working-in-the-editor.md#presets)).

- **controller** — the display chip. Default `SSD1306`.
- **I2C bus** — the bus the panel is wired to. Required. See [I2C bus](i2c-bus.md).
- **address** — the I2C address, 0 to 127. Default `0x3C`, the usual SSD1306 address. In the flow file `addr`, a plain
  number: `60` is `0x3C`.
- **width (px)** — default 128.
- **height (px, multiple of 8)** — default 64.

A flow saved before I2C bus settings existed has its pins on the node. The editor moves them into an I2C bus when it
opens the flow; save the flow to keep the change.

## Wiring

**Input** — `payload` is the frame: a `MONO_VLSB` buffer of exactly `width * height / 8` bytes, `bytes` or
`bytearray`, as `framebuf.FrameBuffer` makes for a 1-bit surface. Send the buffer, not the `FrameBuffer` object.

This node has no output.

## Behavior

Each message replaces the whole picture. The node only shows frames; it has no drawing of its own.

`framebuf`'s `text()` draws a fixed 8x8 font, so a 128x64 panel holds 16 characters on each of 8 lines. This
function node draws a temperature from a [bme280](bme280.md) and sends the frame:

```python
import framebuf
buf = context.get('buf')
if buf is None:
    buf = bytearray(128 * 8)
    context.set('buf', buf)
fb = framebuf.FrameBuffer(buf, 128, 64, framebuf.MONO_VLSB)
fb.fill(0)
fb.text('%.1f C' % msg['payload']['temperature'], 0, 28, 1)
msg['payload'] = buf
return msg
```

A panel can share a bus with a sensor, at the bus's one clock; the default 100000 Hz suits both.

## Errors

- **A frame of the wrong size.** The console shows a `[NODE_ERROR]` naming this node and
  `display_i2c: expected 1024 bytes (128x64 MONO_VLSB), got 1000`. See
  [Reading a node error](../debugging.md#reading-a-node-error).
- **No I2C bus, or an address over 127.** Deploy stops and says which.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/bme280/

# bme280

Reads a BME280 or BMP280 temperature, humidity and pressure sensor at a fixed interval.
[Supported hardware](../supported-hardware.md#sensors) lists the chips.

## Properties

- **I2C bus** — the bus the sensor is wired to. Required. See [I2C bus](i2c-bus.md).
- **address** — `0x76` (SDO to ground, most boards) or `0x77` (SDO to VCC). Default `0x76`. In the flow file, a plain
  number: `118` or `119`.
- **interval (ms)** — how often to read. Default 5000. Must be 100 or more.

## Wiring

**Input** — none. `bme280` is a source.

**Output** — one reading per interval, with `topic` an empty string:

```python
msg['payload'] == {'temperature': 21.43, 'humidity': 48.2, 'pressure': 1012.6}
```

Temperature is in °C, humidity in %, pressure in hPa, each to 2 decimal places. On a BMP280, `humidity` is `None`.
To use one value, pick it out in a [function](function.md) node: `msg['payload'] = msg['payload']['temperature']`.

## Behavior

The first reading goes out when the flow starts. The status dot shows which chip answered, **BME280** or
**BMP280**. A failed read sends nothing; the node tries again at the next interval, so a sensor connected after the
flow starts is picked up.

## Errors

- **Nothing answers.** The dot shows **disconnected**, `no reply at 0x76 on I2C bus 0`. Check the wiring, pins and
  address; see [I2C device not answering](../debugging.md#i2c-device-not-answering).
- **A different chip at the address.** The dot shows **error**, `no BME280/BMP280 at 0x76 (chip id 0x..)`.
- **No I2C bus.** Deploy stops with `bme280 has no I2C bus. Pick one, or add one with +.`


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/touch-i2c/

# touch

Raw touch input, for flows that don't use the GUI: sends a message when a finger lands on a
[touch panel](touch-panel.md) and when it lifts.

A [gui screen](gui.md) reads its own panel, so buttons on a screen don't need this node. One panel feeds either one
gui screen or one `touch` node.

## Properties

- **Touch panel** — the [touch panel](touch-panel.md) to read. Required. Pick one, or add one with **+**.
- **orientation** — the turn of the picture the touches should match: `0`, `90`, `180` or `270` degrees clockwise,
  the angles a [display spi](display-spi.md)'s orientation takes. Default off, which leaves the panel's own axes.
  Set it when the screen is turned and the flow reads touch through this node; a flow with a gui screen sets the
  orientation on the display instead.

## Wiring

**Input** — none. `touch` is a source.

**Output** — one message when a finger lands and one when it lifts:

```python
{'payload': {'x': 120, 'y': 340}, 'topic': 'down'}   # a finger lands
{'payload': {'x': 121, 'y': 338}, 'topic': 'up'}     # it lifts, where it was last seen
```

The coordinates are screen pixels in the turned picture when **orientation** is set, and in the panel's own axes when
it is off. There is nothing to calibrate.

## Behavior

The node reads the panel at the panel's **poll every (ms)**. Nothing is sent while the finger moves, and only one
finger is followed. The status dot shows **FT6336U** while the panel answers.

A panel that stops answering sends nothing until it answers again. A touch that was down at the time gets its `up`
then.

## Errors

- **The panel doesn't answer.** The dot shows **disconnected**, `no reply from FT6336U at 0x38 on I2C bus 0`.
- **No touch panel, or a panel also used by a gui screen or another touch node.** Deploy stops and names them.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/i2c/

# i2c device

Talks to an I2C device that has no node of its own. Each message that arrives does one transfer.

## Properties

- **I2C bus** — the bus the device is wired to. Required. See [I2C bus](i2c-bus.md).
- **operation** — `read bytes`, `write msg.payload` or `scan the bus` (`read`, `write`, `scan` in the flow file).
  Default `read`.
- **address** — the device's 7-bit address, such as `0x29` or `41`. Up to `0x7f`. Required except for `scan`.
- **register** — the register to read or write, such as `0x80`. Up to `0xff`. Leave it empty for a device without
  registers.
- **length (bytes)** — for `read`, how many bytes, 1 to 256. Default 1.

## Wiring

**Input** — any message starts a transfer. For `write`, `payload` is what to send: bytes, a list of numbers 0 to 255,
or one number 0 to 255.

**Output** — the same message, with other fields kept:

- `read`: `payload` is the bytes read. Reading register `0x92` at address `0x29` (a TCS34725's ID) gives `b'D'`.
- `write`: `payload` is unchanged.
- `scan`: `payload` is the list of addresses that answer, as numbers.

## Behavior

The status dot shows whether the device answers. A transfer that fails sends nothing, and the next message tries
again.

## Errors

- **Nothing answers at the address.** The dot shows **disconnected**, `no reply at 0x29 on I2C bus 0`, and the
  message is dropped. For `scan`, `I2C bus 0 not responding`.
- **A payload that can't be written**, such as a bool or a number over 255. The dot shows **error** with the reason,
  and the message is dropped.
- **No address**, for `read` or `write`. The first message fails with a `[NODE_ERROR]`:
  `i2c: set the device address (7-bit, e.g. 0x29)`.
- **No bus, a bus without pins, or an address or register out of range.** Deploy stops and says which.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/i2c-bus/

# I2C bus

The pins and clock of one I2C bus, set once and shared by every node on it. A display and a sensor can sit on the
same bus, each at its own address.

Each I2C node has an **I2C bus** field. Pick a bus, or add one with **+**. A new bus takes the lowest bus number not
yet used in the flow.

## Settings

- **bus** — the chip's I2C peripheral number. Default 0. Each bus number is used once per flow.
- **scl pin** / **sda pin** — the GPIO pins. Required, and different from each other.
- **frequency (Hz)** — the clock. Default 100000, which suits most sensors. Displays that can take it run at 400000.

## Behavior

Changing a bus changes it for every node on it. The bus's two pins are claimed like any other pin, so no other node
can use them (see [Hardware is shared](index.md#hardware-is-shared)).

`runtime.shared('i2c', 0)` in a [function](function.md) node returns the flow's bus 0, already set up, to talk to a
device that has no node of its own. It raises `KeyError` if no node in the flow uses that bus.

## Errors

These stop the deploy:

- No SCL or SDA pin: `I2C bus 0 has no SCL pin set`.
- The same pin for both: `I2C bus 0 uses pin 5 for both SCL and SDA`.
- Two bus settings with the same number, both in use: `Two I2C bus settings both say bus 0`.
- A pin or bus number the board can't use for I2C. See [What gets checked](../boards.md#what-gets-checked).


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/touch-panel/

# Touch panels

The settings of a capacitive touch panel on an I2C bus, set once in a config node. A [gui screen](gui.md) or a
[touch](touch-i2c.md) node picks it.

A gui screen reads its panel itself and turns touches into button presses, with no wire to draw. If the panel stops
answering, the screen's status dot says so, and a button being held is let go without sending.

## Settings

- **controller** — the touch chip. Default `FT6336U`.
  [Supported hardware](../supported-hardware.md#touch-panels) lists the chips.
- **I2C bus** — the bus the panel is wired to. Required. See [I2C bus](i2c-bus.md).
- **address** — the chip's 7-bit I2C address, from `0x08` to `0x77`. Default `0x38`, the FT6336U's.
- **reset pin** — the panel's reset pin. Default blank, for none.
- **poll every (ms)** — how often to read the panel. Default 20; above 50 starts to feel slow.
- **panel width** / **panel height** — the panel's own size in pixels. Defaults 320 and 480.
- **swap x and y** / **flip x** / **flip y** — turn the panel's coordinates into the display's. Default off. If the
  display is turned, tick these until a touch lands where you pressed.

A board definition that has a touch panel labels its pins; see
[Seeing a board's pins](../boards.md#seeing-a-boards-pins).

## Presets

The edit form has a **preset** control, as the display nodes do. Fill in the settings once, press the disk button and
give the set a name, such as `freenove-4in`. In another flow, open a new touch panel and pick that name to fill the
form. The I2C bus isn't saved with it, since it belongs to the flow: pick or add it after loading.

## Rotated screens

When the display a gui screen is wired to has an [orientation](gui.md#rotating-the-screen), the screen turns its
touches to match the picture. A [touch](touch-i2c.md) node turns them by its own **orientation**.

## Other touch chips

For another chip, such as a GT911 or CST820, read it from a [function](function.md) node with
`runtime.shared('i2c', 0)`, using the chip's datasheet and a MicroPython driver for it. See
[MicroPython's machine.I2C](https://docs.micropython.org/en/latest/library/machine.I2C.html) for the I2C calls.

## Errors

These stop the deploy:

- No I2C bus: `the touch panel has no I2C bus. Pick one, or add one with +.`
- An address outside `0x08` to `0x77`.
- A controller other than FT6336U.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes/gui/

# GUI nodes

!!! note "Provisional"

    The GUI nodes are provisional: their properties and the page layout may change between releases.

The GUI nodes show readings on a display as pages of numbers, text, bars, lights, histograms and buttons. A
[gui screen](#gui-screen) draws the pages and sends them to a [display spi](display-spi.md) node; each widget node
shows the `payload` of the messages wired to it. Lay out the pages in the gui screen's property panel: see
[Laying out pages](#laying-out-pages).

The nodes on this page:

- [gui screen](#gui-screen) — one per display.
- [gui readout](#gui-readout) — a number with units.
- [gui label](#gui-label) — text.
- [gui bar](#gui-bar) — a bar between two values.
- [gui light](#gui-light) — on or off.
- [gui button](#buttons) — a touch button.
- [gui histogram](#histogram) — the recent history of a number.

<!-- gui modal: left out until the editor can lay a modal out (its layout is written in the flow file).
- **gui modal** — a full-screen message. Send any payload to open it, `None` to close it. If several are
  open, the highest priority shows and the rest wait. Its output sends how it closed:
  `{topic: <modal's name>, payload: 'ack' | 'timeout' | 'closed'}`. Properties: **screen** (the id of the `gui_screen` it
  belongs to), **priority**, and **timeout** in seconds (`0` never closes by itself). The modal's layout is under its
  screen in the flow file, see [Modals in the flow file](#modals-in-the-flow-file).
-->

On a classic ESP32 without PSRAM, a GUI flow needs the [custom firmware for classic ESP32](../custom-firmware.md):
stock MicroPython runs out of memory loading the display stack.

## gui screen

Draws a display's pages of widgets and sends them to a [display spi](display-spi.md) node.

### Properties

The screen takes its width, height and frame format from the display it is wired to, so set them once on the display.

- **name** — the screen's name, sent as `topic`. Default `screen`.
- **fastest redraw (ms)** — the shortest time between two redraws. Default 200.
- **next/prev wrap round** — whether `next` on the last page goes to the first, and `prev` on the first to the last.
  Default on.
- **grid columns** — the layout grid's columns, 2 to 48. Default 12. See [Laying out pages](#laying-out-pages).
- **grid rows (0 = from the display's shape)** — 0 to 64. Default 0, which keeps the cells roughly square.
- **touch panel (blank: no touch)** — the [touch panel](touch-panel.md) the screen reads, for buttons. Default blank.
- **theme** and the ten role colors — the screen's colors. Default blank, the GUI's own colors. See [Themes](#themes).
- **shared theme config (older flows)** — used only when the theme fields are empty, so a flow saved with a shared
  theme still draws.

### Wiring

**Input** — none. The widgets on its pages get their own wires.

**Output** — the picture, in strips of about 5 KB, each with `y` set to its first row, so a whole frame never has to
fit in memory. Wire it to a display spi node.

## Laying out pages

A display is one fixed panel of a known size, filled by one flow. A page fills it, and its size never changes while
the flow runs. The layout is worked out when the flow compiles: the compiler turns each element's cells into pixel
positions and picks the font for each piece of text, and Deploy sends those numbers. Nothing reflows at runtime, and
the board carries no layout engine. That differs from a web page: nothing responds to a resize or an orientation
change while the flow runs, and a layout is for one panel. A display of a different size means compiling for that
display.

Every screen has a **cell grid**: **grid columns** on the gui screen (12 by default) and **grid rows**
(`0` means "work them out from the display's shape", so cells stay roughly square). A position is a row and a
column, 0-based; a size is a row span and a column span. Nothing is in pixels, so the same layout works on a
different panel.

Select the gui screen node and open **Properties**: each page lists its elements. **⚙** on an element opens
**row**, **col**, **rows** and **cols**; tick **panel** to draw a card behind those cells. **+ add…** puts a
widget, text, page dots or a panel on the page (it starts at row 0, column 0 — set its cells after).
The same widget can be on several pages of a screen (a navigation button on every page, say), and it must have
the same span on each. A widget belongs to one screen.

Text sizes itself: the compiler picks the largest font that fits the element's cells, and Deploy says which
element, on which page, when even the smallest does not fit. Two elements on the same cells, a span outside the
grid, or a panel on top of another panel are also Deploy errors naming the element. The editor doesn't draw the
page; the outline is a view of the flow file's `"screens"` section, which you can also edit by hand.

To put the page dots in a footer, give them the last grid row. The current page's dot is drawn as a pill.

## Widgets

The readout, label, bar, light, button and histogram are widgets: each sits on a page and shows the `payload` of each
message that arrives on its input.

- A widget shows `--` until a value arrives. A `payload` of `None` shows `--` again.
- **stale after (s, 0 = never)**, default 0: a value not updated in that time is dimmed (or underlined, on a
  black-and-white display), so an old reading never looks current.
- **name** is how Deploy names the widget in an error, after its flow label.
- **font (blank = fit the cells)**, where a widget has one: default blank, the largest font that fits its cells.
- A widget that can't draw its value, such as a bar given text, is crossed out and the console shows a
  `[NODE_ERROR]` naming it. The other widgets carry on.

A widget belongs to one screen, and can be on several of its pages.

## gui readout

Shows `payload` as a number with units. A number is drawn with **decimals** places; anything else is drawn as text.

- **caption (above the number)** — a small muted line above the number, such as `Temperature`. Default blank.
- **units** — text after the number. Default blank.
- **decimals** — 0 to 6. Default 1.
- **lowest value** / **highest value** — the range it will show. Defaults 0 and 100. The number's space is sized for
  this range, so the layout doesn't shift as the value changes.

## gui label

Shows `payload` as text.

- **room for (characters)** — how many characters its space is sized for. Default 8.

## gui bar

A bar that fills between two values. A value below **empty at** shows empty, one above **full at** shows full.

- **style** — `solid` (an outline and a fill) or `segments` (a row of cells, lit in the accent color and unlit in the
  track color). Default `solid`.
- **cells** — for `segments`, 1 to 40. Default 10.
- **empty at** / **full at** — defaults 0 and 100. **full at** must be above **empty at**.

## gui light

On when `payload` is true, off when it is false, by Python's `bool()`.

- **style** — `light` (a circle) or `chip` (a filled pill showing a word). Default `light`.
- **chip when on** / **chip when off** — the chip's words. Defaults `On` and `Off`.

## Buttons

A touch button. Its input sets what it shows, and its output sends when it is tapped. A button needs a
[touch panel](touch-panel.md) on its screen to be pressed.

### Properties

- **topic** — the `topic` of the messages it sends. Default blank, the node's id.
- **mode** — what a tap does. Default `momentary`.
    - `momentary` — sends its **sends** value.
    - `toggle` — sends the opposite of its state, and shows its **on shows** or **off shows** text.
    - `navigate` — changes page, to **goes to**. It needs no wires.
- **style** — `box` (outline and text), `filled` (a solid accent button, for the main action) or `switch` (a track
  and knob; it needs `toggle`). Default `box`.
- **value type** — `true / false`, `text` or `number`: the type of what it sends. Default `true / false`.
- **send on** — `release` (when your finger lifts inside the button; lifting outside sends nothing) or `press`.
  Default `release`. The button is drawn inverted while held.
- **board label (drawn on the button)** — `momentary`: the text drawn on it. Default blank, the flow label. A
  `payload` on its input replaces it.
- **sends (the payload)** — `momentary`: what it sends. Default blank.
- **room for (characters, if no text)** — `momentary`: default 8.
- **on sends** / **off sends** — `toggle`: what it sends to turn on and off. Default blank.
- **on shows** / **off shows** — `toggle`: its text. Defaults `ON` and `OFF`.
- **starts on (when nothing is wired in)** — `toggle`: default off.
- **wait for confirmation (s, 5 or more)** — `toggle` with a wired input: how long a tap waits for the input to agree.
  Default 5.
- **goes to** — `navigate`: `next`, `prev`, `back`, `home` or a page name.

A blank value field sends `true` and `false` for `true / false`, `ON` and `OFF` for `text`, and `1` and `0` for
`number`. The gray placeholder shows which.

### Wiring

**Input** — for `momentary`, a `payload` replaces the text drawn on it. For `toggle`, the real state of the thing it
switches; see below.

**Output** — `{'topic': <topic>, 'payload': <value>}` on each tap. A `navigate` button sends nothing.

Deploy warns when a screen has buttons and no touch panel, and when a `momentary` or `toggle` button's output goes
nowhere. A `navigate` button whose **goes to** isn't `next`, `prev`, `back`, `home` or a page on its screen stops the
deploy.

### A toggle that follows the real device

Wire the toggle's input to the device's real state, and its output to whatever switches it:

```
mqtt subscribe (stat/plug/POWER) -> toggle -> mqtt publish (cmnd/plug/POWER)
```

With the input wired, the flow owns the state:

- Before the first report the toggle shows `--` (a dashed outline).
- A tap shows the state you asked for, with a dotted outline, until the input confirms it.
- If the input says something different, the toggle shows what the input says.
- If nothing comes back in time, it returns to the last known state, shows a cross for a moment, and the
  console reports it. See [a toggle goes back](../debugging.md#a-toggle-button-goes-back).

The input is matched against the toggle's *on sends* and *off sends* values. MQTT delivers text, so the text `true`
matches a true/false toggle and `1` matches a number toggle. Anything else shows `--`. Tasmota
reports `ON` and `OFF` as text, so for a Tasmota plug set the value type to text and use `ON` and `OFF`.

Unwired, the toggle keeps its own state and starts as set by *starts on*.

## Histogram

A moving histogram: a row of bars, oldest on the left, newest on the right. It shows what a number can't: which way
it is heading. Wire it to the first output of a [journal](journal.md), or to any node that sends a list of numbers (a
`None` is a gap), such as a spectrum from a function node.

Each bar is a row's average, in the theme's accent color, with a thin line from the row's minimum to its maximum in
the muted color, so the range reads as context behind the value. A gap is empty. A wider space shows more history: it
draws as many bars as fit, newest at the right edge.

- **bottom at** / **top at** — the range of the bars. Defaults 0 and 100. Values outside are cut off at the edge.
- **columns (natural width)**, **column width (px)**, **height (px)** — the natural size, defaults 60, 3 and 48: as
  wide as columns times column width, plus the border. In a layout it can stretch, and then shows more rows.

It shows only the rows its journal kept. With fewer rows than the space holds, the bars sit at the right edge and the
left of the card stays empty; the compiler says how many rows to keep. Raising **rows kept** on the journal fills it.

## Themes

By default a screen draws in the GUI's own colors: white text, gray for stale values, and a green accent for bars and
lights that are on. Full color needs the display's frame format set to `rgb565`; the gray formats use less memory and
send faster, so use them on boards with little RAM. To choose your own colors, select the gui screen and set **theme**
(a starting point) and any of the role colors in its Properties: the screen owns its look, and a screen with no theme
keeps the default colors.

A theme is ten roles, so the widgets stay consistent and one theme works on different panels: **background**, **card**,
**foreground**, **muted** (stale values), **track** (a bar's empty part), **accent** (bar fill, lights on), **text on
accent**, **ok**, **warn** and **alarm**. Start from **dark slate**, **light paper** or **vivid** and change any
color; the preset is a starting point, not a lock. **Vivid** has a near-black background, violet cards and a
cyan accent.

Use the **preset** control in the theme's edit form to save your colors by name under
`~/.thingstudio/presets/gui_theme/`, and apply them to another theme later
([Presets](../working-in-the-editor.md#presets)). The three starting points are built in, so a flow that names one
still compiles without a backend.

A panel with fewer colors than that folds the roles onto the ones it has, rather than refusing the theme:

- a **gs4** panel (16 colors) gets every role as its own color;
- a **gs2** panel (4 colors) keeps background, foreground, muted and accent — cards fold to the background, the track
  to muted, ok/warn/alarm to the foreground;
- a **mono** panel (2 colors) is ink and paper: text, bars and lights are ink, backgrounds are paper.

A **panel** is a card behind a group of widgets: tick **panel** on an element in the layout outline and the cells it
covers sit on a filled, rounded rectangle in the theme's **card** color. It follows the theme.

On an indexed panel (gs4, gs2 or mono) the theme also sets the display's palette while a screen is wired to it — one
theme is the whole color scheme, not two lists to keep in step. A palette set on the display itself is ignored while a
themed screen is wired to it, and Deploy says so in the console.

## Rotating the screen

The screen follows its display's **orientation** (see [display spi](display-spi.md#properties)). It takes the
display's size and turns its layout and its touch to match. At 90 or 270 the usable picture is the panel turned: 480
wide by 320 high on a 320x480 panel. A flow that reads touch with a [touch](touch-i2c.md) node instead of a gui
screen sets the same angle on that node, since there is no display for it to follow.

## Seven-segment digits

The `seg7` fonts (`font_seg748`, `font_seg764`, `font_seg796`) have only `0-9 : . -` and a space, so they suit the
`time` and `time_seconds` formats of the [ntp](ntp.md) node. On a 320-pixel-wide screen `font_seg764` fits `14:05`
(221 px) and `font_seg748` fits `14:05:09` (254 px). `font_seg796` is for wider screens. The font is DSEG by
Keshikan (SIL Open Font License 1.1); see
[third-party licenses](https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/blob/main/docs/third-party-licenses.md).

<!-- Left out until the editor can lay a modal out. Kept for when it can.
## Modals in the flow file

A modal is laid out like a page, but in the screen's `modals` list, next to `pages`. Each entry names the `gui_modal`
node and gives its layout as `elements`. The modal node is not itself placed there; the elements are what the
modal shows (text, and widget nodes wired to it or to the flow):

```json
"screens": { "<screenId>": {
  "pages": [ ... ],
  "modals": [
    { "node": "<modalNodeId>", "elements": [
      { "kind": "text", "text": "Too hot", "row": 0, "col": 0, "rowSpan": 2, "colSpan": 8 },
      { "kind": "widget", "node": "<labelId>", "row": 2, "col": 0, "rowSpan": 2, "colSpan": 12 }
    ] }
  ]
} }
```

Send any payload to the modal node to open it; what is drawn is its layout, so wire a label or readout widget in the
layout to the data you want shown (a modal can hold the same widget a page does). Send `None` to close it (a function node
returning a message whose `payload` is `None`). A navigate button in the layout with target `back` acknowledges it,
and a **timeout** above `0` closes it on its own. The modal node's output says which of the three happened.
-->


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/node-conventions/

# Node conventions

A node moves a message from one point in a flow to the next. These are the rules a custom node follows; the file
format itself is in [Writing custom nodes](custom-nodes.md).

## The message

A message is a dict: `msg = {'payload': ..., 'topic': ..., <anything else>}`.

- **`payload`** is the node's value. It is what the output port's declared type checks against and the one key a
  generic downstream node reads — `debug` prints only `payload`. Put the value you want wired and checked here.
- **`topic`** is a routing string. Set it to a real protocol topic when the node has one, otherwise `''`. Don't put
  the node's own event or state in `topic`; use a named field instead.
- **anything else** rides along under its own name, and only a node written to read that name sees it.

Put one value in `payload` and leave the rest as named fields. The DHT22 example sends the temperature in `payload`
and the humidity in `msg['humidity']`.

## Ports

Port types are `int`, `number`, `bool`, `string`, `bytes` and `any`, the same as built-in nodes, with the same wire
checks. A declared output type must match what the node puts in `payload`. Use `any` when unsure. The ports follow
the kind: a source has one output, a transform one input and one or more outputs, and a sink one input. A sink with
`eventSource` set also has one output; see [Two-faced nodes](custom-nodes.md#two-faced-nodes).

## Kind

Every node is one of three kinds:

- **source** — makes its own messages: on the `intervalMs` schedule, when an event fires (`eventSource`), or once when
  the flow starts (`runOnce`).
- **transform** — one message in, one or more out. Return the message, or `None` to stop it.
- **sink** — consumes a message and produces nothing, unless it is two-faced.

## Errors

A runtime error in your Python is reported from the board, attributed to your node. A `transform` that returns
`None` stops that message; anything it passes on continues. The full list is under [Errors](custom-nodes.md#errors)
