in Writing custom nodes.

## Limits

A custom node has the following limits:

- A polled source's `emit` runs on a timer. To react to an external event, use an event-driven source: see
  [Event-driven sources](custom-nodes.md#event-driven-sources).
- Two instances of the same custom node get independent setup, so don't put two on the same physical resource, such
  as the same pin.
- Your Python runs with the same trust as the `function` node. Read a package before you put it in the folder.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/custom-nodes/

# Writing a custom node for ThingStudio

A custom node is two files sharing a base name: `<name>.node.json` (the
descriptor) and `<name>.node.py` (the behavior), placed in the backend's
`~/.thingstudio/custom-nodes/` directory. ThingStudio loads it for you,
and you drag it onto the canvas like any built-in node.

## Loading a custom node

Put both files in `~/.thingstudio/custom-nodes/` on the computer running
ThingStudio.

The editor loads every package in that folder when it starts, and again
when you switch back to its window. After changing a file, you can also
click **Reload custom nodes** at the bottom of the palette. The console
lists what loaded. Each node appears in the palette under its `group`.

A package with a problem isn't loaded, and the console says which file
and why. The others still load. If two packages use the same `type`, the
first one by file name is loaded and the other is reported.

The folder starts with two examples, `doubler` and `dht22`, under
**examples** in the palette. Read them, change them or delete them.
ThingStudio adds them only the first time it runs, so deleted examples
stay deleted.

## The descriptor: `<name>.node.json`

Example — a node that doubles a numeric payload:

```json
{
  "type": "custom/doubler",
  "kind": "transform",
  "label": "doubler",
  "color": "#6e3b8a",
  "bgcolor": "#3f1f4a",
  "icon": "×2",
  "ports": {
    "inputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "any" }],
    "outputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "any" }]
  },
  "properties": [
    { "name": "factor", "label": "factor", "kind": "number", "default": 2 }
  ]
}
```

**`type`** (required) — unique id, shaped `namespace/name` (lowercase
letters, digits, underscores). Must not start with `thingstudio/` —
reserved for built-in nodes.

**`kind`** (required) — one of:

- `source` — generates messages on its own. 0 input ports, 1 output
  port. Must declare a numeric `intervalMs` property (below) — unless
  `eventSource` is true (it waits on an event) or `runOnce` is true (it
  runs once at flow start).
- `transform` — one message in, one or more out. 1 input port, 1+ output
  ports.
- `sink` — consumes a message, produces nothing. 1 input port, 0 output
  ports.

**`label`** (required) — name shown on the canvas and in the palette.

**`title`** (optional) — the canvas title, when it should differ from
`label`.

**`hidden`** (optional) — hide the node from the palette (a flow file can
still use it).

**`description`** (optional) — a short line shown at the top of the
property panel, like a built-in node's own description.

**`presetType`** / **`screenOutline`** (optional) — show a save/load-preset
control or the screen-layout outline in the property panel, as the relevant
built-in nodes do.

**`color`** / **`bgcolor`** (optional) — CSS colors for the node's
outline and fill. Default is gray.

**`icon`** (optional) — one or two characters shown in the icon chip.

**`group`** (optional) — which palette section the node sorts into.
Defaults to "general". Any name works; a new one gets its own section,
added after the built-in ones.

**`priority`** (optional) — a number controlling order within `group`,
lower first. Omit it and the node sorts after every built-in node in
that group.

**`ports.inputs`** / **`ports.outputs`** — arrays of `{ name, type }`.
`type` is one of `int`, `number`, `bool`, `string`, `bytes`, `any` — the
same types built-in nodes use, with the same wire-compatibility checks.
Use `any` when unsure.

A port type can follow a select property instead of being fixed:

```json
{ "name": "msg", "type": { "property": "payloadType", "map": { "bool": "bool", "number": "number" }, "default": "bool" } }
```

The value of `property` picks the wire type; an unset or unmapped value uses `default`. The property must be a
`select` field, and every key in `map` must be one of its options.

A `transform` may declare more than one output. Return a list to route
messages across them, Node-RED style (e.g. `return [msg, None]` sends to
output 1 only). A `source` has one output; a `sink` none.

**`properties`** (optional) — fields shown in the property panel when
the node is selected:

```json
{ "name": "factor", "label": "factor", "kind": "number", "default": 2 }
```

- **`name`** — identifier. Your Python reads the value by this key.
- **`label`** — shown in the property panel.
- **`kind`** — `text`, `textarea`, `number`, `boolean`, `select`, `configRef`, `pin`, or `target`.
- **`default`** — used when a node instance doesn't set the property.
  Type must match `kind`.
- **`options`** — required for `select`: array of `{ value, label }`.
  `default` must be one of the values.
- **`configType`** — required for `configRef`: the config type the picker
  offers (e.g. `thingstudio/config/i2c-bus`). At compile time the picked
  config's own properties become a dict the node reads — see below.
- **`singleton`** — optional, on a `configRef`: resolve the flow's one
  config of `configType` at compile time instead of an id you store (how a
  built-in uses the shared WiFi setting). Zero or two such configs is a
  compile error.
- **`pinUse`** / **`pinPull`** — optional, on a `pin`: `input` or `output`,
  and the pull (`none`/`up`/`down`). Adding `pinUse` makes the compiler
  claim the pin, so two nodes can't quietly set the same pin up two ways. A
  `pin` without `pinUse` is just a value (checked to exist on the board) —
  use that for a bus line like SCL/SDA.
- **`target`** — a kind for a board-specific node. Its value in Python is a
  dict of the board/processor this flow is compiled for — `boardId`,
  `boardName`, `processorId`, `processorName`, `label`, `capabilities` —
  or `None` if no board is chosen, so guard for that. Use it to identify
  your exact board (e.g. a XIAO nRF52840's own IMU).
- **`nodeId`** — a kind whose Python value is this node's own id (a string).
  Use it to report status about yourself:
  `runtime.report_status(properties['id'], 'connected')`.
- **`help`** / **`placeholder`** / **`min`** / **`max`** / **`step`** /
  **`optional`** / **`rows`** — optional, the same panel hints a built-in
  field has. `rows` sets a `textarea`'s height (default 4). `pin` fields
  take a `number` default; `optional` marks one where
  `-1`/blank means "not wired".
- **`visibleWhen`** — optional: show the field only when another property
  satisfies a condition, e.g.
  `{ "field": "mode", "equals": "deadband" }`. Operators: `equals`,
  `notEquals`, `in` (an array), `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`.

A polled `source` node must declare a numeric property named `intervalMs` — it
sets the poll interval, a whole number of milliseconds, 1 or more. An `eventSource` or `runOnce` source does not need one.

**`requires`** (optional) — hardware the node needs, as `{ "capabilities": ["ble"] }`. The words are the board
definitions' capabilities (`wifi`, `ble`, `espnow`, `pio`, see [Boards](boards.md)). On a board without one, the
palette grays the node out and the compile refuses it, naming the missing capability.

## The behavior: `<name>.node.py`

Ordinary MicroPython. Define exactly one top-level function, named for
your node's `kind`:

- `transform` / `sink` → `async def run(msg, properties):`
- `source` → `async def emit(properties):`

`msg` is a dict with a `payload` key, a `topic` key, and room for any
extra keys you add. `topic` is a routing/identification string — the
`mqtt subscribe` built-in node, for instance, fills it with the real
MQTT topic a message arrived on. Most nodes have no natural topic of
their own; set it to `''` rather than a real value. The key is
required either way — don't leave it out. `properties` is a dict of
the node instance's configured values.

Transform — return the (possibly modified) `msg`, or `None` to stop it
propagating:

```python
async def run(msg, properties):
    msg['payload'] = msg['payload'] * properties['factor']
    return msg
```

Sink — return value is ignored:

```python
async def run(msg, properties):
    print('got:', msg['payload'])
```

Source — called once per `intervalMs`, must return a `msg`:

```python
async def emit(properties):
    return {'payload': 42, 'topic': ''}
```

Anything else — imports, helper functions, setup code — is ordinary
Python.

### Example: a temperature sensor source

`temp_sensor.node.json`:

```json
{
  "type": "myproject/temp_sensor",
  "kind": "source",
  "label": "temp sensor",
  "ports": { "outputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "number" }] },
  "properties": [
    { "name": "pin", "label": "data pin", "kind": "number", "default": 4 },
    { "name": "intervalMs", "label": "read interval (ms)", "kind": "number", "default": 5000 }
  ]
}
```

`temp_sensor.node.py`:

```python
import dht
import machine

_pin = properties['pin']
_sensor = dht.DHT22(runtime.shared('pin', _pin, ('dht22',), lambda: machine.Pin(_pin)))

async def emit(properties):
    _sensor.measure()
    msg = {'payload': _sensor.temperature(), 'topic': ''}
    msg['humidity'] = _sensor.humidity()
    return msg
```

The sensor is built once, at setup, not on every `emit()` call —
top-level code and `emit` share the same `properties`.

Temperature goes in `payload`, not humidity, because `payload` is the
field the port's declared type (`number`, here) checks against, and
the field a generic downstream node reads — `debug` prints
`msg['payload']` and nothing else, whatever else is in `msg`. Put
whichever value you want wired and type-checked that way in `payload`.
Anything else is a passenger: `humidity` rides along in the same `msg`,
but only a node written to look for it specifically will ever read it.

### `nonlocal`, not `global`

Your file's top-level code doesn't run at true module scope — each node
instance gets its own wrapper function, so two instances of the same
custom type never share state. To keep a value across calls, use
`nonlocal`:

```python
_count = 0

async def emit(properties):
    nonlocal _count
    _count += 1
    return {'payload': _count, 'topic': ''}
```

`global` raises `NameError` here — there's no module-level name to find.

### Pins and buses

Get a pin or bus with `runtime.shared(kind, key, settings, make)`, not by building it yourself. The first node to
ask builds it with `make()`; every later node gets the same object. If a later node asks with different `settings`,
the flow stops with an error naming both, instead of one node quietly changing the pin under another.

```python
_pin = runtime.shared('pin', 5, ('in', 'up'), lambda: machine.Pin(5, machine.Pin.IN, machine.Pin.PULL_UP))
_i2c = runtime.shared('i2c', 0)  # fetch a bus another node in the flow set up
```

The built-in nodes use these settings: `('in', 'none' | 'up' | 'down')` and `('out', 'none')` for pins, and `()`
for an ADC (`runtime.shared('adc', 26, (), lambda: machine.ADC(machine.Pin(26)))`). Pins, ADC, PWM, I2C and SPI all
work this way: see [Hardware is shared](nodes/index.md#hardware-is-shared).

### Sharing a config (I2C bus, touch panel)

A `configRef` property lets your node pick one of the flow's config nodes. Its value in
`properties` is that config's own properties as a dict (or `None` if none is picked), so a custom
I2C node can join the same bus a built-in `i2c`/`bme280` node uses:

```json
{ "name": "bus", "label": "I2C bus", "kind": "configRef", "configType": "thingstudio/config/i2c-bus", "default": "" }
```

```python
_i2c = runtime.shared('i2c', properties['bus']['bus'])  # the flow's shared bus, by its number
```

The bus/pins come from the config; keep the same `runtime.shared` key a built-in would use so a
clash is reported, not silently shared. (Network configs — WiFi, MQTT — expose only the
credential's name, not the secret, so a custom node can't make a WiFi connection from one.)

### Cleanup

If your node opens something that needs closing on redeploy — a socket,
typically — register it:

```python
import socket

_sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
runtime.register_cleanup('my_node_socket', lambda: _sock.close())

async def run(msg, properties):
    _sock.sendto(str(msg['payload']).encode(), ('192.168.1.50', 9000))
```

`runtime` is already available — no import needed. Without cleanup, a
redeployed flow can leave the old socket open and fail with
`EADDRINUSE` on the next deploy.

### Libraries you can import

When a node imports one of these, ThingStudio sends it to the board with the flow:

| Library | For |
| --- | --- |
| `ts_ble` | the board's Bluetooth LE radio, shared with the ble nodes (below) |
| `ts_wifi`, `ts_mqtt`, `ts_http_server` | the flow's WiFi, MQTT client and HTTP server, shared with the network nodes |
| `threadsafe_event` | waking a coroutine from a hardware interrupt (see Event-driven sources) |
| `events`, `delay_ms`, `encoder`, `aadc` | Peter Hinch's asyncio switch, button, timer, encoder and ADC drivers |
| `ssd1306`, `st7789py`, `st7796py` | display drivers |
| `bme280_float`, `ft6336u` | the BME280 sensor and FT6336U touch drivers |
| `mqtt_as` | Peter Hinch's asyncio MQTT client |

A library of your own can't be sent yet. Code two of your nodes share goes in each `.node.py`.

For Bluetooth, use `ts_ble.radio()`, not `bluetooth.BLE()`: the board has one radio, and the ble nodes use the same
one. `radio().scan(...)` and `radio().advertise(...)` share it as `ble scan` and `ble advertise` do, and
`ts_ble.decode(adv)` and `ts_ble.build_adv(...)` read and build advertising data. The radio is turned off on each
redeploy.

### Persisting values

`runtime.settings` keeps a value across reboots and redeploys of the same flow. Use it for an application
setting a user changes on the device — units, a colour scheme — not for per-message state, which belongs in a
closure local.

```python
async def run(msg, properties):
    units = runtime.settings.get('units', 'kg')   # the default is yours, not the store's
    runtime.settings.set('units', msg['payload'])
    msg['payload'] = units
    return msg
```

Values are namespaced by the deployed flow's name, so a different flow cannot read or overwrite them. Renaming
the flow starts a fresh namespace. A missing key returns your default. `set` raises `SettingsError` if the board
cannot save (full or read-only flash) — let it surface as a node error rather than assuming the write worked.
`delete(key)` and `keys()` round out the surface.

The store is a plain key/value; it does not know what a value means. Save only what the user changed, and supply
the default at the read. To clear stored values, see [debugging](debugging.md#commands-and-the-python-prompt).

### Event-driven sources

A `source` that reacts to something other than the clock sets `"eventSource": true` and defines a
second function, `async def wait(properties)`, alongside `emit`. `wait` is awaited, so it blocks
until your event fires; then `emit` builds the message. No `intervalMs` is needed.

```json
{
  "type": "custom/button",
  "kind": "source",
  "label": "button",
  "eventSource": true,
  "ports": { "outputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "bool" }] },
  "properties": [{ "name": "pin", "label": "pin", "kind": "pin", "default": 11, "pinUse": "input" }]
}
```

A hardware interrupt (`machine.Pin.irq`) is the usual reason to use `eventSource`. Bridge it into `asyncio`
with the vendored `ThreadSafeEvent` — its `set()` is the one call safe in a hard-IRQ handler — and
register the handler:

```python
import machine
from threadsafe_event import ThreadSafeEvent   # pushed with the flow because you import it

_evt = ThreadSafeEvent()

def _irq(_pin):
    _evt.set()          # a hard-IRQ handler may only do this: no allocation, no print, nothing else

_pin = runtime.shared('pin', properties['pin'], ('in', 'up'),
                      lambda: machine.Pin(properties['pin'], machine.Pin.IN, machine.Pin.PULL_UP))
_pin.irq(trigger=machine.Pin.IRQ_RISING, handler=_irq)

async def wait(properties):
    await _evt.wait()
    _evt.clear()

async def emit(properties):
    return {'payload': True, 'topic': ''}
```

`runtime.asyncio.Event()` is fine when the event is set from other asyncio code; for a real IRQ use
`ThreadSafeEvent`, which survives the hard-IRQ context.

Keep any state the two share at the top of the file (both functions come from one per-instance
closure, so `nonlocal` works across them).

### Run-once sources

A source that runs once, at flow start, sets `"runOnce": true` instead. It defines only `emit`; ThingStudio calls
it once, with no `intervalMs` and no `wait`.

```json
{
  "type": "custom/boot",
  "kind": "source",
  "label": "boot",
  "runOnce": true,
  "ports": { "outputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "string" }] }
}
```

### Two-faced nodes

A `sink` with `"eventSource": true` both consumes and produces: one input, one output, and three functions in
`.node.py`. `run(msg, properties)` handles the input; `wait(properties)` then `emit(properties)` produce the
output. All three come from the same per-instance closure, so they share state through `nonlocal`.

```json
{
  "type": "custom/gateway",
  "kind": "sink",
  "label": "gateway",
  "eventSource": true,
  "ports": {
    "inputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "any" }],
    "outputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "string" }]
  }
}
```

Use it when the node has to react to messages and also act on its own (a clock that echoes a message and then
ticks, or a subscription you can change at run time). A `transform` cannot be two-faced.

## Compile time: `<name>.compile.py`

A package can also include an optional compile-time hook, `<name>.compile.py`, defining one function:

```python
def compile(ctx, properties):
    return {"properties": {...}, "errors": [...]}
```

It runs in the editor when the flow is compiled — never on the board. `properties` is what the flow file holds
for this node; `ctx` describes the flow:

- `ctx["node"]` — this instance: `id`, `type`, `properties`, and `wired` (a boolean per input/output).
- `ctx["flow"]["nodes"]` / `["configs"]` — every node and config, with non-secret properties only.
- `ctx["nodesOfType"]` — every node of this node's type in the flow, including this one: `id`, `type`, and
  non-secret `properties`. Use it when the nodes share a decision (for example, a port's set of routes).
- `ctx["referencedConfigs"]` — the full properties (including credentials) of the configs this node's `configRef`
  fields point at.
- `ctx["target"]` — the board/processor being compiled for, or `None`.

Return a dict (or `None`). Everything is optional:

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `properties` | Extra values merged into what `.node.py` receives. Keys your descriptor doesn't declare are allowed. |
| `claims` | `[{"resource": "GPIO 22", "use": "my device"}]`, checked like a `pin` field. |
| `warnings` | Strings shown in the compile warnings. |
| `errors` | Strings that stop the compile, naming the node. |

The hook is sandboxed: no files, network, clock or randomness. Its result is data only — it cannot return Python
or change the generated code's shape. Limits: 64 KB of properties, 64 claims, 32 warnings and 32 errors, and one
second per hook; a hook that runs too long is stopped.

`wifi status` is an example: its hook derives the flow's WiFi config and whether an MQTT node is present, so its
Python never asks you for the network twice.

## Errors

**Load time** — a malformed `.node.json` is rejected immediately, with
a message naming what's wrong: bad `type`, wrong port count, missing
`intervalMs`, and so on.

**Compile time** — a bad property value on a specific node instance
(e.g. a non-numeric `number` field) errors out naming that node and
property.

**Without the editor** — the [check command](check-a-flow.md) loads the same folder (or `--custom-nodes <dir>`).
Check a flow that uses your node and it reports load and compile errors the same way:

```sh
node dist-cli/thingstudio-compile.mjs --board board:cyd my.flow.json
```

**Deploy time** — `.node.py` is spliced into the flow as-is;
ThingStudio doesn't check it. A typo surfaces as a runtime error (e.g.
`NameError`) reported from the device, attributed to your node.

## Limitations

A polled `source` node's `emit` runs on a fixed `intervalMs` schedule; an `eventSource` source waits on `wait` instead.

Two instances of the same custom node get independent setup. For a `pin` field that declares `pinUse`,
ThingStudio checks it against the board and claims it at compile time; a pin you build in Python yourself (or
read from a plain `number` field) it can't see, so use `runtime.shared()` for those, and a clash is caught when
the flow starts.

Custom node Python runs with the same trust as any other node, including ThingStudio's `function` node. Loading a
package only adds it to the palette; its Python runs on a board only when you place the node and deploy. Only files
you place in the folder are loaded — there's no registry and no URL install — so don't put a package there that you
haven't read.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/ai-authoring/

# Writing flows with an AI assistant

This page is for an AI assistant (or a person) writing a ThingStudio flow file or a custom node in the user's folder,
without the editor. It is complete on its own, with two companions: the generated [node catalog](nodes-catalog.md), and
the `thingstudio-compile` command ([Check a flow without the editor](check-a-flow.md)). With a board attached,
`device_cli.py` deploys and runs the flow ([Command line](command-line.md#deploy-and-run-a-flow-without-the-editor)).
The whole docs set is also one file at `/llms-full.txt` on the docs site, with an index at `/llms.txt`.

## Setting up your assistant

Paste this into the assistant's standing instructions (a project's instructions, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, or a custom
GPT/Gem), so it reads this page before it writes a flow:

```text
When I ask for a Thingstudio flow or custom node, first read the Thingstudio authoring guide:
https://docs.thingstudio.net/ai-authoring/ (the whole docs set is one file at https://docs.thingstudio.net/llms-full.txt).
Write the flow as a .flow.json file, run the thingstudio-compile check with --board for my board and
--layout, fix every error and layout warning until it prints OK, then tell me: the board id you checked against, which credential
names I must create, what you assumed about wiring, and what you could not check.
Never say a flow works on the board unless you deployed it there and saw its output; otherwise say it
passes the check. No HTTPS in http_request.
```

Claude users can add the ThingStudio skill instead: `thingstudio-flow-author-<version>.zip`, from the releases page,
carries this guide, the node catalog, the examples and the check command, so the assistant needs nothing else.
Upload the zip as a skill in Claude, or unzip it into `~/.claude/skills/` for Claude Code. Use the skill whose
version matches your editor. Otherwise the check needs Node and the built `thingstudio-compile.mjs`.

## The loop

1. Write the flow as a `.flow.json` file.
2. Run `node dist-cli/thingstudio-compile.mjs --board board:lolin-s2-mini --layout my.flow.json` (the board ids are `board:cyd`, `board:freenove-s3-4in`,
   `board:lolin-s2-mini`, `board:pico`, `board:pico-2` and `board:pico-w`, or `processor:esp32`, `esp32-c3`, `esp32-s2`,
   `esp32-s3`, `rp2040`, `rp2350` for a bare chip; `--list-boards` shows the current list). Read every error: it names the node and
   says what is wrong. Fix them all, and every `layout:` warning, and run it again until it prints `OK`.
3. Tell the user to open the file in the editor (**File → Open**), choose the board, and deploy. If a board is
   attached and the user asks you to test it, deploy it with
   [`device_cli.py`](command-line.md#deploy-and-run-a-flow-without-the-editor) instead, and report what the board
   printed. That result is for that board only.

The check is the same compile the editor runs, so a flow that passes it opens and compiles in the editor. It loads
the user's custom node packages the way the editor does. It can't check credentials, what a custom node's Python does
on the board, or the hardware. Don't claim a flow works on a board unless you deployed it
there and saw it run; otherwise say it passes the check.

## The flow file

A JSON object. These keys matter:

| Key | What |
| --- | --- |
| `formatVersion` | `1` |
| `flowName` | A name for the flow. |
| `nodes` | `[{ "id", "type", "properties" }]`. `id` is any unique string. `type` is `thingstudio/<kind>`. |
| `edges` | `[[fromId, outputNumber, toId, inputNumber]]`. Numbers start at 0, in the order the [catalog](nodes-catalog.md) lists the ports. |
| `configs` | `[{ "id", "type", "properties" }]`: shared settings (I2C bus, WiFi, MQTT broker, touch panel). |
| `screens` | The pages of any GUI screen, keyed by that node's id. See [GUI](#gui-screens). |
| `panes`, `paneOf` | Optional. Tabs in the editor and which tab each node is on; leave them out and everything lands on one tab. When you edit a file that has them, put new nodes in `paneOf` too (copy the pattern). |
| `layout` | `{ "<nodeId>": { "pos": [x, y] } }`. Optional, but give positions: without them every node lands at 0,0. |
| `notes` | Optional text shown in the editor's Notes panel. Say what the flow is for and how it is wired. |

A property you leave out gets the default listed in the [catalog](nodes-catalog.md). Use the catalog's names and types
exactly: `intervalMs`, not `interval`. Values and ranges are checked by the compile, which says what is allowed.

Give every node a position, laid out as described in [Layout](#layout).

A complete flow, a blinking LED on a LOLIN S2 Mini (its LED is pin 15):

```json
{
  "formatVersion": 1,
  "flowName": "blink",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "tick", "type": "thingstudio/timer", "properties": { "intervalMs": 500 } },
    { "id": "flip", "type": "thingstudio/function",
      "properties": { "code": "msg['payload'] = msg['payload'] % 2\nreturn msg", "outputCount": 1 } },
    { "id": "led", "type": "thingstudio/gpio_out", "properties": { "pin": 15 } }
  ],
  "edges": [["tick", 0, "flip", 0], ["flip", 0, "led", 0]],
  "layout": { "tick": { "pos": [80, 200] }, "flip": { "pos": [300, 200] }, "led": { "pos": [520, 200] } },
  "configs": []
}
```

## Layout

The user reads the flow on the editor's canvas, and the editor shows it exactly where the file puts it. It does not
rearrange the nodes or zoom to fit. Lay it out the way a careful person would:

- **Left to right.** Sources (timers, inputs, subscriptions) on the left, outputs on the right, and every wire running
  to a node further right. Don't wrap a long chain back to the left edge on a second row.
- **Columns about 220 px apart**, left edge to left edge. Nodes are 84-132 px wide, so that leaves about 90 px for the
  wire. Use the same column positions for the whole flow, so columns line up.
- **Tight rows.** Nodes are 34 px tall (a function node with several outputs is taller). Stack branches in one
  column about 36 px apart (y about 70 apart), and separate chains about 66 px apart (y about 100 apart).
- **One chain per job**, stacked top to bottom: inputs and processing first, display or output last. Unwired nodes
  (GUI buttons that only appear on a screen, for example) go together at the bottom left.
- **Straight wires.** A node fed by one node sits at that node's y. When one node feeds several, the first sits level
  with it and the rest stack below; a node fed by several sits level with the first of them, or between them.
- **Start near (80, 80)**, so the flow is on screen when it opens.

`--layout` checks these rules and reports problems as `layout:` warnings. `--relayout` rewrites the positions to
follow them, which makes a good first pass for a new flow. When you edit the user's own flow, keep their layout: place
only the nodes you add, and don't relayout it unless they ask.

## Which node

| To... | Use |
| --- | --- |
| send a message every so often, or once at start | `timer`, `startup`, `inject` |
| read a BME280 / BMP280 | `bme280` (payload is a dict with `temperature`, `humidity`, `pressure`; pick one out in a `function`) |
| read another I2C chip | `i2c` on a shared `i2c-bus` config |
| react to a switch or button | `eswitch` (a debounced switch: open and close events); `ebutton` for press, release, long-press and double-click; `interrupt` for raw edges |
| drive a pin | `gpio_out` (on/off), `pwm_out` |
| change or route a message | `function`; `filter` to pass only changes; `delay` |
| keep a number's history | `journal`, shown by a histogram (`gui_trend`) |
| show the time | `ntp` (two for time and date: `format` `time` and `date`) |
| talk MQTT / HTTP / UDP | `mqtt_publish`, `mqtt_subscribe`, `http_request`, `http_in` and `http_response`, `udp_send`, `udp_receive` |
| draw on a screen | `gui_screen` with `gui_*` widgets, wired to `display_spi` |

## Messages and the function node

Every message is a dict: `msg = {'payload': ..., 'topic': ...}`. `payload` is what nodes read; `topic` is a string, `''`
when there is nothing to say. Other keys ride along.

A function node's `code` is the body of a function in MicroPython (a subset of Python with a small standard library). Return `msg` to pass it on, or `None` to stop. With `outputCount` above 1, return a list with one
entry per output (`None` for nothing, a list of messages for several). `context` keeps state for the node, `flow` for
the whole flow. See [function](nodes/function.md). A syntax error in the code is caught by the check.

A wire is refused if the payload types can't meet (for example a `bool` into a `bytes` input). The check reports it.
Numbers go into `bool` inputs (zero is off), and an `int` into a `number`; a `number` into an `int` is refused.

Addresses are written two ways, because the nodes differ: the `bme280` `address` is a plain number (`118` is `0x76`);
a touch panel config's `address` is text (`"0x38"`). The [catalog](nodes-catalog.md) notes which.

A node that uses the network (`mqtt_publish`, `http_request`, `http_in` and so on) uses the flow's WiFi: add a WiFi config to
`configs` and it is picked up; the node has no WiFi property of its own.

Things to know before you pick a node:

- `http_request` is plain `http://` only (no HTTPS), GET or POST. A reply with any status is passed on with an integer
  `msg['status']`; a failed connection or a timeout sends nothing on and logs an error. So test `msg['status'] == 200`
  in a `function`, and expect no message at all when the server is unreachable.
- `mqtt_subscribe` payloads arrive as text when they decode, otherwise bytes. For a number, use `float(msg['payload'])`
  in a `function`.
- `function` code can `import` standard modules (`json`, `framebuf`, `time`) inside the body.
- `http_in` gives a `payload` of `None` and `http_response` sets no `Content-Type`. Use port 80 unless something else
  on the board already uses it.
- `bme280` has no input: it reads on its own interval. To answer a web request with a current value, keep the
  latest reading with `flow.set('temp', ...)` in a `function` after the sensor, and read it with `flow.get('temp')`
  in a `function` between `http_in` and `http_response` (send a 503 before the first reading arrives).
- To print text on a `display_i2c` (SSD1306), draw with `framebuf` in a `function` and send the buffer: see
  [display i2c](nodes/display-i2c.md#behavior). Its address property is `addr`, a plain number (`60` is `0x3C`).

## Pins: take them from the board

Never guess a pin. List the boards with `--list-boards`, run `--board-info board:<id>` for what each pin does (the
LED, the buttons, the display, the I2C pins) and which to avoid, and check the finished flow with `--board board:<id>`. If the user's board is not listed, say so, ask for the pins, and point them to the MicroPython documentation
for their board (docs.micropython.org). Don't pretend a board is supported.

Things the pin check cannot catch: a pin that exists but is wired to something else on the user's board. When the
user has told you the wiring, use it; when they haven't, say what you assumed.

## Config nodes and credentials

A node that needs shared settings names a config by id: `"i2cConfigId": "cfg-i2c"`, with the config in `configs`:

```json
{ "id": "cfg-i2c", "type": "thingstudio/config/i2c-bus", "properties": { "bus": 0, "scl": 15, "sda": 16, "freq": 100000 } }
```

The [catalog](nodes-catalog.md) lists each config type's fields. WiFi and MQTT configs hold a **credential name**:

```json
{ "id": "cfg-wifi", "type": "thingstudio/config/wifi", "properties": { "credentialName": "home", "security": "password" } }
```

**Never write a password, SSID or broker secret into a flow file.** Write a `credentialName` and tell the user which
names to create in the editor's credential store (they are saved there, not in the file). The check uses stand-ins
for them and says so.

## GUI screens

A touch or plain display is two nodes wired together, `gui_screen` then `display_spi`, plus widget nodes (`gui_label`,
`gui_readout`, `gui_bar`, `gui_trend`, `gui_led`, `gui_button`) that you wire data into. Where each widget sits is in
`screens`:

```json
"screens": { "<screenId>": { "pages": [
  { "name": "main", "elements": [
    { "card": true, "row": 0, "col": 0, "rowSpan": 1, "colSpan": 12 },
    { "kind": "text", "text": "Living room", "row": 0, "col": 0, "colSpan": 8 },
    { "kind": "widget", "node": "<readoutId>", "row": 1, "col": 0, "rowSpan": 4, "colSpan": 12 },
    { "kind": "pagedots", "row": 15, "col": 4, "colSpan": 4 }
  ] }
] } }
```

Rules that cause most failures:

- The screen's `width` and `height` are the **panel's own size** (320 × 480 for the Freenove 4") whatever the orientation.
  Portrait needs nothing more: leave `orientation` empty and use the board's `rotation` (1 for the Freenove). To turn
  the picture, set the `orientation` property of `display_spi` to `"90"`, `"180"` or `"270"` (clockwise), not the
  screen's size.
- A navigate button's `target` is `next`, `prev`, `back`, `home` or the `name` of a page in `screens`; when you edit an
  existing flow, read the page names from its `screens` section.
- Fonts are chosen to fit an element's cells; nothing in a layout is in pixels. A character no font has is an
  error.
- A widget is placed once per page, drawn the same on every page it is on. Its cells decide its size.
- A page is a cell grid: the gui screen has `gridColumns` (12 by default) and `gridRows` (`0` = from the display's
  shape). Every element has `row`, `col` (0-based) and spans; an element outside the grid, two on the same cells,
  or one whose text cannot fit is an error naming it and the page.
- With an `orientation`, `xstart` and `ystart` must be `-1`, which means "no offset" (the CYD example flow uses 0,
  which an orientation refuses; `-1` is always allowed). At `"90"` or `"270"` the picture is the panel turned, so a
  320 x 480 panel gives 480 wide by 320 high to lay out.
- A modal is laid out in `screens.<screenId>.modals`, not in `pages`: see the format below.
- A histogram (`gui_trend`) takes a journal's first output, and a journal takes numbers: `sensor → journal → histogram`.

A modal (`gui_modal`, with `screen` set to the `gui_screen` node's id) is listed next to `pages`. Its `elements` are
what it shows, and not the modal node itself:

```json
"modals": [ { "node": "<modalNodeId>", "elements": [
  { "kind": "text", "text": "Too hot", "row": 0, "col": 0, "rowSpan": 2, "colSpan": 8 },
  { "kind": "widget", "node": "<labelId>", "row": 2, "col": 0, "rowSpan": 2, "colSpan": 12 }
] } ]
```

Any message opens it; a message with `payload` `None` closes it; `timeout` (seconds, `0` for never) closes it by
itself; a navigate button with `target` `back` acknowledges it. Its output sends `'ack'`, `'timeout'` or `'closed'`.

Placement keys, in `screens` (a page is `{"name", "elements": [...]}`; a modal is `{"node", "elements": [...]}`):

| Element | Keys |
| --- | --- |
| any element | `row`, `col` (0-based cells), `rowSpan`, `colSpan` (default 1), `card` (draw a panel behind), `align` |
| `widget` | `kind: "widget"`, `node` (the widget node's id) |
| `text` | `kind: "text"`, `text` |
| page dots | `kind: "pagedots"` |
| panel | `card: true` (no `node` or `text`) |

No element takes a font, height, width, gap or padding: fonts follow the cells and spacing is the screen's gutter. The button's own behaviour (`mode`, `target`,
`onValue`, ...) is on the node: see the [catalog](nodes-catalog.md). For a toggle that follows a real device (a smart
plug), `gui.md` has the wiring.

Read [GUI nodes](nodes/gui.md) for the details, and copy from
`test-flows/gui-headliner-sensor-freenove-s3-4in.flow.json` (a sensor display with histograms, a clock and MQTT) and
`test-flows/gui-touch-freenove-s3-4in.flow.json` (buttons).

## Custom nodes

If no node does the job and a function node is not enough, write a custom node: `<name>.node.json` and
`<name>.node.py`. [Writing custom nodes](custom-nodes.md) is complete on its own. The two files go in `~/.thingstudio/custom-nodes/` on the
computer running ThingStudio. The check command loads that folder (or the one given with `--custom-nodes <dir>`), so
check a flow that uses the node: a bad descriptor is reported by file, and the node's wires, properties and compile
hook are checked like a built-in's. What the Python does on the board isn't checked: test its body on its own with
sample messages.

## Examples to copy

| Task | File |
| --- | --- |
| Blink an LED | `tutorials/blink.flow.json` |
| Read and set a GPIO pin, keep state in the node | `tutorials/two-more-blinks.flow.json` |
| Blink an LED from an HTTP request (WiFi, `http in`) | `tutorials/http-blink.flow.json` |
| Publish to MQTT | `test-flows/basic-mqtt.flow.json` |
| Call a web service | `test-flows/basic-http-request.flow.json` |
| A BME280 reading | `test-flows/bmp280-test-flow.flow.json` |
| A sensor on a display, with histograms and a clock | `test-flows/gui-headliner-sensor-freenove-s3-4in.flow.json` |
| Touch buttons | `test-flows/gui-touch-freenove-s3-4in.flow.json` |

## When you hand the flow back

Tell the user, briefly: that it passes the check (and with which `--board`), which credential names to create, which
board to choose in the editor, what you assumed about wiring, and what you could not check.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/check-a-flow/

# Check a flow without the editor

`thingstudio-compile` compiles and checks a flow file from the command line, with the same errors the editor gives.
Use it in a script, in CI, or to let an AI assistant check a flow it has written.

## Build it

From the `editor/` folder:

```text
npm ci --ignore-scripts
npm run build:cli
```

This writes `dist-cli/thingstudio-compile.mjs`, one script that needs only Node 22 or later.

## Use it

```text
node dist-cli/thingstudio-compile.mjs my-flow.flow.json
```

A good flow prints one line:

```text
OK  my-flow.flow.json: 25 nodes, 21 wires, 4 configs, 38980 bytes of MicroPython, 0 warnings
```

A bad one lists every problem it found:

```text
FAIL  my-flow.flow.json: 2 errors
  error: wire from node t1 output 4 to node g1 input 1: node t1 has no output 4 (it has 1)
  error: node x1: unknown node type "thingstudio/teleporter"
```

The exit code is 0 for a valid flow, 1 for a flow with errors, and 2 for a bad command or a file it can't read.

## Options

- `--board board:freenove-s3-4in` checks pins against that board. `--list-boards` shows the choices. Without a
  board, pins are checked against the widest range and a warning says so.
- `--board-info board:freenove-s3-4in` prints that board's labelled pins (the LED, the display, the I2C pins), the
  GPIOs that exist, and the ones to avoid or that are reserved, as JSON.
- `--out flow.py` writes the generated MicroPython.
- `--json` prints the result as JSON: `ok`, `errors`, `warnings`, `notes`, `stats` and the `source`.
- `--strict` makes warnings fail the check.
- `--layout` also checks the layout: wires run left to right, nodes are close but don't overlap, and the flow starts
  on screen. Problems come back as `layout:` warnings (so `--strict` fails on them). The rules are in
  [Layout](ai-authoring.md#layout).
- `--relayout` rewrites each file's node positions to follow those rules, then checks it. It changes positions only,
  and it overwrites the file.
- `--describe timer` prints a node's type, ports and properties with their defaults. `--describe-all` prints every
  node and config node (add `--json` for JSON). The same list is on the [node catalog](nodes-catalog.md) page,
  generated from the code.
- `--custom-nodes ~/my-nodes` loads custom node packages from that folder. Without it, the check loads
  `~/.thingstudio/custom-nodes/` when it exists, as the editor does. `--no-custom-nodes` loads none.
- `--no-syntax` skips the MicroPython syntax check. `--arch` sets its `-march`; the default is the `--board`'s
  processor (`rv32imc` for an ESP32-C3 or C5), or `xtensawin` without a board.

## What it checks

- The file is a flow file, and every node type exists.
- Every wire joins real ports, and is one the editor would accept. The editor drops a wire it refuses when it opens the file.
- A property the file leaves out gets the editor's default, as when you open the file in the editor.
- The flow compiles: pins, properties, GUI layouts, nodes with nothing wired to them.
- Custom node packages load as they do in the editor. A package that doesn't load is named with its file and the
  reason, and its nodes' wires and properties are checked like a built-in node's.
- The generated code is valid MicroPython. This uses the same `mpy-cross` the editor deploys with, and catches a
  typo in a function node's code before you deploy.

## What it doesn't check

- **WiFi and MQTT credentials.** The secrets are in the backend, so the check uses stand-in values and says so in a
  note. A missing credential shows up when you open the flow in the editor.
- **What a custom node's Python does.** It is checked for syntax, not run. Test its body on its own with sample
  messages.
- **A real board.** It can't tell you the display is wired right, or that the memory is enough. Deploy does that;
  [Command line](command-line.md#deploy-and-run-a-flow-without-the-editor) can deploy and run a flow without the
  editor.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/command-line/

# Command line

Options for starting ThingStudio, a way to install the runtime and run flows without the editor, and a check for a
flow file. To check a flow file from the command line, see [Check a flow without the editor](check-a-flow.md).

## Starting options

Add these after `thingstudio` (or `thingstudio-backend`, from source). `thingstudio --help` lists them all.

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--no-browser` | Don't open the editor in a browser. Open `http://127.0.0.1:8765/` yourself. |
| `--port N` | Serve the editor on port `N` instead of 8765. |
| `--data-dir DIR` | Use `DIR` instead of `~/.thingstudio`. See [The ThingStudio folder](thingstudio-folder.md#using-a-different-folder). |
| `--log-level LEVEL` | How much ThingStudio prints in its terminal: `DEBUG`, `INFO` (default), `WARNING` or `ERROR`. |

If you restart ThingStudio with the editor still open, that tab reconnects and no new one opens.

## Installing the runtime from the command line

Useful for scripting, or setting up several boards at once. It needs a copy of the source repository. Click
**Disconnect** in the editor first, so the port is free.

```sh
pip install mpremote
python3 test-flows/deploy_runtime.py --port PORT
```

`PORT` is the board's port, as shown in the editor's port list. When it finishes, click **Connect** in the editor.

`device_cli.py runtime install` does the same thing and resets the board afterwards; see below.

## Deploy and run a flow without the editor

`device_cli.py` is a small command line for a board on USB serial. It does what the editor does, without a browser:
find the board, check the runtime, deploy a flow, fire inject nodes, run console commands and watch the output.

```sh
python3 test-flows/device_cli.py list          # USB serial ports
python3 test-flows/device_cli.py hello         # runtime version, chip, running flow
python3 test-flows/device_cli.py flow deploy my-flow.flow.json \
    --mpy-cross ~/mpy-src/mpy-cross/build/mpy-cross
python3 test-flows/device_cli.py trigger inject0001
python3 test-flows/device_cli.py exec "settings.namespaces()"
python3 test-flows/device_cli.py watch
```

- If there is one USB serial port, `--port` is not needed. Use `--port` or `THINGSTUDIO_PORT` otherwise.
- `flow deploy` compiles the `.flow.json` with the same compiler as the editor, then deploys it. It takes the flow
  name from the file's own `flowName`. That name is also the `settings` namespace, so check it is what you expect.
- `--trigger NODE_ID` (repeatable) fires inject or startup nodes after deploy, for testing without clicking.
- `--json` prints one JSON object per line, for scripts.
- Disconnect in the editor first: only one program can hold the serial port.
- `flow deploy` needs a native `mpy-cross`. The build recipe is in `device-runtime/test/README.md`, or set
  `THINGSTUDIO_MPY_CROSS` to one you already have.

`python3 test-flows/device_cli.py <command> --help` lists every option. `test-flows/README.md` has ready-made test
flows and their expected output.


---

Source: https://docs.thingstudio.net/nodes-catalog/

# Node catalog

<!-- Generated by `node dist-cli/thingstudio-compile.mjs --describe-all --markdown`. Do not edit by hand: a test fails when it is out of date. -->

This is the flow-file reference. It lists every node a `.flow.json` can use, with the exact names a flow file needs:
the node's type, its ports, and its properties with their types, defaults and allowed values. The editor's code
generates it, so it matches what the compiler accepts.

It does not explain how to use a node. Each entry links to the node's page, which says what the node does and what
each property means. To build a flow in the editor, start from the [node reference](nodes/index.md). To write or check
a flow file without the editor, see [Check a flow without the editor](check-a-flow.md) and [AI authoring](ai-authoring.md).

In a flow file a node's type is `thingstudio/` followed by the type shown here: `wifi_status` is written
`thingstudio/wifi_status`. A property's editor label is the name the node's page uses for it. A port described as
"message, payload bool" carries a message whose `payload` is a bool.

Ports are numbered from 0 in a flow file's `edges`: `[fromNodeId, outputNumber, toNodeId, inputNumber]`, in the order listed here.

## general

### change

Sets or deletes one value on each message, then passes the message on.

Type: `change`. Kind: transform. Palette group: general.

Properties explained: [change](nodes/change.md)

- Inputs: message, any payload
- Outputs: message, any payload

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `operation` | operation | string | `"set"` | one of `set`, `delete` |
| `scope` | target | string | `"msg"` | one of `msg`, `flow` |
| `property` | property / name | string | `"payload"` |  |
| `valueFrom` | value from | string | `"literal"` | one of `literal`, `msg`, `flow` |
| `valueType` | literal type | string | `"string"` | one of `string`, `number`, `bool` |
| `value` | value / source property | string | `""` |  |

### debug

Prints a message's payload to the console.

Type: `debug`. Kind: sink. Palette group: general.

Properties explained: [debug](nodes/debug.md)

- Inputs: message, any payload
- Outputs: none

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `fullMessage` | full message | boolean | `false` |  |

### delay

Holds each message for a set time, then passes it on unchanged.

Type: `delay`. Kind: transform. Palette group: general.

Properties explained: [delay](nodes/delay.md)

- Inputs: message, any payload
- Outputs: message, any payload

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `delayMs` | delay (ms) | number | `1000` |  |

### filter

Passes a message on only when it is worth sending, and drops the rest.

Type: `filter`. Kind: transform. Palette group: general.

Properties explained: [filter](nodes/filter.md)

- Inputs: message, any payload
- Outputs: message, any payload

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mode` | mode | string | `"change"` | one of `change`, `deadband`, `rate` |
| `threshold` | threshold | number | `1` |  |
| `intervalMs` | interval (ms) | number | `1000` |  |
| `ignoreFirst` | ignore first message | boolean | `false` |  |
| `perTopic` | separately for each topic | boolean | `true` |  |

### function

Runs your own MicroPython on each message.

Type: `function`. Kind: transform. Palette group: general.

Properties explained: [function](nodes/function.md)

- Inputs: message, any payload
- Outputs: message, any payload (the number of outputs is the node's `outputCount` property)

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `code` | code | string | `"msg['payload'] = msg['payload']\nreturn msg\n"` | the body of a MicroPython function; `msg` in, return the message, None, or a list with one entry per output |
| `outputCount` | outputs | number | `1` | how many outputs, 1 to 10 |

### inject

Sends one message with a fixed payload when you click its ▶ icon.

Type: `inject`. Kind: source. Palette group: general.

Properties explained: [inject](nodes/inject.md)

- Inputs: none
- Outputs: message, payload bool

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `payloadType` | payload type | string | `"bool"` | one of `bool`, `number`, `string` |
| `payloadValue` | value | string | `"true"` |  |

### journal

Keeps the recent history of a number as rows of average, minimum and maximum.

Type: `journal`. Kind: transform. Palette group: general.

Properties explained: [journal](nodes/journal.md)

- Inputs: message, any payload
- Outputs: series (any); rollup (any)

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `rows` | rows kept | number | `60` | how many rows are kept, 1 to 256 |
| `stepSeconds` | seconds per row (0 = one row per message) | number | `60` | seconds per row; 0 makes every message its own row |
| `steps` | rows per roll-up (0 = none) | number | `0` | rows per roll-up to the second output; 0 sends none |
| `xff` | gaps allowed in a roll-up (0 to 1) | number | `0.5` | 0 to 1: a roll-up becomes a gap if more than this fraction of its rows are gaps |

### startup

Sends one message with a fixed payload each time the flow starts.

Type: `startup`. Kind: source. Palette group: general.

Properties explained: [startup](nodes/startup.md)

- Inputs: none
- Outputs: message, payload bool

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `payloadType` | payload type | string | `"bool"` | one of `bool`, `number`, `string`, `reason` |
| `payloadValue` | value | string | `"true"` |  |

### timer

Sends an increasing count at a fixed interval.

Type: `timer`. Kind: source. Palette group: general.

Properties explained: [timer](nodes/timer.md)

- Inputs: none
- Outputs: message, payload int

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `intervalMs` | interval (ms) | number | `1000` | milliseconds between messages; the payload is a count that rises 1, 2, 3.. |

## GUI

### bar

Shows `msg.payload` as a bar that fills between two values.

Type: `gui_bar`. Kind: sink. Palette group: GUI.

Properties explained: [bar](nodes/gui.md)

- Inputs: message, any payload
- Outputs: none

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | name | string | `""` |  |
| `style` | style | string | `"solid"` | one of `solid`, `segments` |
| `segments` | cells | number | `10` |  |
| `lo` | empty at | number | `0` | the value at which the bar is empty |
| `hi` | full at | number | `100` | the value at which the bar is full |
| `staleAfter` | stale after (s, 0 = never) | number | `0` | seconds without a new value before it dims; 0 = never |

### button

A touch button: its input sets what it shows, and it sends a message when tapped.

Type: `gui_button`. Kind: sink. Palette group: GUI.

Properties explained: [button](nodes/gui.md)

- Inputs: message, any payload
- Outputs: message, any payload

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | topic | string | `""` |  |
| `mode` | mode | string | `"momentary"` | one of `momentary`, `toggle`, `navigate`; momentary, toggle or navigate |
| `style` | style | string | `"box"` | one of `box`, `filled`, `switch` |
| `valueType` | value type | string | `"bool"` | one of `bool`, `string`, `number`; bool, string or number: the type of what it sends |
| `fireOn` | send on | string | `"release"` | one of `release`, `press`; release (default: the finger lifts inside the button) or press |
| `text` | board label (drawn on the button) | string | `""` | what is drawn on the button; empty uses `name` |
| `value` | sends (the payload) | string | `""` | momentary: what it sends; empty sends true, 'ON' or 1 by valueType |
| `maxChars` | room for (characters, if no text) | number | `8` | room for this many characters (a value replaces the text) |
| `onValue` | on sends | string | `""` | toggle: what it sends to turn on |
| `offValue` | off sends | string | `""` | toggle: what it sends to turn off |
| `onText` | on shows | string | `"ON"` |  |
| `offText` | off shows | string | `"OFF"` |  |
| `initial` | starts on (when nothing is wired in) | boolean | `false` |  |
| `pendingTimeout` | wait for confirmation (s, 5 or more) | number | `5` | toggle with a wired input: seconds to wait for the input to confirm before going back |
| `target` | goes to | string | `""` | navigate: next, prev, back, home or a page name from `screens` |

### label

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

### screen

Draws a display's pages of widgets and sends the screen to a display spi node.

Type: `gui_screen`. Kind: source. Palette group: GUI.

Properties explained: [screen](nodes/gui.md)

- Inputs: none
- Outputs: frame (bytes)

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | name | string | `"screen"` |  |
| `minInterval` | fastest redraw (ms) | number | `200` | least milliseconds between screen updates |
| `wrap` | next/prev wrap round | boolean | `true` | whether next/prev wrap around at the ends of the pages |
| `gridColumns` | grid columns | number | `12` |  |
| `gridRows` | grid rows (0 = from the display's shape) | number | `0` |  |
| `touchPanelConfigId` | touch panel (blank: no touch) | string | `""` | the touch-panel config to read touches from; empty for none; the id of a `thingstudio/config/touch-panel` config |
| `themeConfigId` | shared theme config (older flows) | string | `""` | the id of a `thingstudio/config/gui-theme` config |
| `themePreset` | theme | string | `""` | one of `dark-slate`, `light-paper`, `vivid`, `` |
| `bg` | background | colour | none |  |
| `card` | card | colour | none |  |
| `fg` | foreground | colour | none |  |
| `muted` | muted (stale values) | colour | none |  |
| `track` | track (bar and cell background) | colour | none |  |
| `accent` | accent (bars, lights) | colour | none |  |
| `on_accent` | text on accent | colour | none |  |
| `ok` | ok | colour | none |  |
| `warn` | warn | colour | none |  |
| `alarm` | alarm | colour | none |  |

### histogram

A moving histogram: a row of bars, oldest on the left, newest on the right.

Type: `gui_trend`. Kind: sink. Palette group: GUI.

Properties explained: [histogram](nodes/gui.md)

- Inputs: message, any payload
- Outputs: none

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| `lo` | bottom at | number | `0` | value at the bottom of the bars; the range is fixed |
| `hi` | top at | number | `100` | value at the top of the bars; the range is fixed |
| `columns` | columns (natural width) | number | `60` | natural width in bars; in a layout it can stretch to show more |

## hardware

### adc

Reads an ADC pin and sends a message when the reading leaves, or returns to, a set range.

Type: `adc`. Kind: source. Palette group: hardware.

Properties explained: [adc](nodes/adc.md)

- Inputs: none
- Outputs: message, any payload

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `pin` | pin | number | `34` | the ADC pin to read; on ESP32, use an ADC1 pin if the flow uses WiFi (ADC2 can't with the radio on) |
| `mode` | mode | string | `"relative"` | one of `relative`, `absolute`; relative (current value +- delta) or absolute (lower..upper) |
| `delta` | delta (counts) | number | `2000` | relative mode: how far the reading must move from the last sent one to fire |
| `lower` | lower | number | `0` | absolute mode: the low bound |
| `upper` | upper | number | `50000` | absolute mode: the high bound |
| `sense` | sense | string | `"outside"` | one of `outside`, `inside`; outside (fire when the value leaves the bounds) or inside (fire when it returns) |
| `pollMs` | poll (ms) | number | `0` | also send every this many ms; 0 = only on a bounds crossing |

| `intervalMs` | interval (ms) | number | `5000` | milliseconds between readings, at least 100 |

## network

### ble advertise

Advertises over Bluetooth LE: the board's name, and each message's payload as manufacturer or service data.

Type: `ble_advertise`. Kind: sink. Palette group: network.

Properties explained: [ble advertise](nodes/ble-advertise.md)

- Inputs: message, any payload
- Outputs: none
- Needs hardware: ble (checked against the board at compile time)

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `field` | payload goes in | string | `"manufacturer"` | one of `manufacturer`, `service`, `none`; manufacturer (payload after a 2-byte manufacturer id), service (after a service UUID) or none (name only) |
| `mfrId` | manufacturer id | string | `"0xFFFF"` | manufacturer id, decimal or hex with 0x; 0xFFFF is for testing |
| `serviceUuid` | service UUID | string | `"fcd2"` | service UUID for service data: 16-bit (fcd2, BTHome) or 128-bit |
| `advIntervalMs` | interval (ms) | number | `500` | how often the advertisement is sent, 20-10240 ms |
| `bleConfigId` | BLE | string | `""` | the flow's BLE config, whose name is advertised; name and payload share 31 bytes; the id of a `thingstudio/config/ble` config |

### ble characteristic in

Sends a message each time a connected device writes a Bluetooth LE characteristic.

Type: `ble_characteristic_in`. Kind: source. Palette group: network.

Properties explained: [ble characteristic in](nodes/ble-characteristic-in.md)

- Inputs: none
- Outputs: message, payload bytes
- Needs hardware: ble (checked against the board at compile time)

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `serviceUuid` | service UUID | string | `""` | the service it belongs to: 16-bit (181a) or 128-bit; nodes for one service's characteristics share it |
| `charUuid` | characteristic UUID | string | `""` | the characteristic a connected device writes: 16-bit or 128-bit |
| `encoding` | encoding | string | `"bytes"` | one of `bytes`, `text`, `int8`, `uint8`, `int16`, `uint16`, `int32`, `uint32`, `float32`; how the written bytes become payload: bytes, text, int8/uint8/int16/uint16/int32/uint32 or float32 (little-endian); sets the output type |
| `bleConfigId` | BLE | string | `""` | the id of a `thingstudio/config/ble` config |

### ble characteristic out

Sets a Bluetooth LE characteristic to each message's payload for a connected device to read, and notifies subscribed devices.

Type: `ble_characteristic_out`. Kind: sink. Palette group: network.

Properties explained: [ble characteristic out](nodes/ble-characteristic-out.md)

- Inputs: message, any payload
- Outputs: none
- Needs hardware: ble (checked against the board at compile time)

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `serviceUuid` | service UUID | string | `""` | the service it belongs to: 16-bit (181a) or 128-bit |
| `charUuid` | characteristic UUID | string | `""` | the characteristic a connected device reads: 16-bit or 128-bit; one out node per characteristic |
| `encoding` | encoding | string | `"bytes"` | one of `bytes`, `text`, `int8`, `uint8`, `int16`, `uint16`, `int32`, `uint32`, `float32`; how payload becomes bytes: as for ble_characteristic_in; a value that doesn't fit is reported and dropped |
| `notify` | notify | boolean | `true` | also push each value to subscribed devices |
| `bleConfigId` | BLE | string | `""` | the id of a `thingstudio/config/ble` config |

### ble scan

Listens for Bluetooth LE advertisements, such as beacons and BLE sensors, and sends one message per advertisement.

Type: `ble_scan`. Kind: source. Palette group: network.

Properties explained: [ble scan](nodes/ble-scan.md)

- Inputs: none
- Outputs: message, payload bytes
- Needs hardware: ble (checked against the board at compile time)

| Property | Editor label | Type | Default | Allowed values and notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `namePrefix` | name starts with | string | `""` | only devices whose advertised name starts with this; many send a name only to an active scan |
| `addr` | address | string | `""` | only this device, aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff |
| `mfrId` | manufacturer id | string | `""` | only this manufacturer id, decimal or hex with 0x (0x0499 Ruuvi) |
| `serviceUuid` | service UUID | string | `""` | only advertisements listing this service or carrying its data: 16-bit (fcd2, BTHome) or 128-bit |
| `active` | active scan | boolean | `false` | also request each device's scan response (usually its name) |
| `repeatMs` | repeat window (ms) | number | `1000` | drop an advertisement identical to the same device's last one within this time; 0 sends all |
| `scanIntervalMs` | scan interval (ms) | number | `320` | how often the radio listens, 2.5-10240 ms; every ble_scan in a flow must agree |
| `scanWindowMs` | scan window (ms) | number | `30` | how long each listen lasts, up to the interval; longer misses less and leaves WiFi less time |
